questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness, and wheezing for 4 weeks. Absolute eosinophil count >5000/μL. Chest X-ray shows a miliary pattern. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia

The clinical features along with elevated absolute eosinophil count and miliary pattern in chest x-ray are suggestive of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a hyperresponsive pulmonary syndrome that occurs in response to trapped microfilariae within the lung parenchyma. It is a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.

Clinical features:

The patient has a history of residence in a filaria endemic area and usually presents with nocturnal paroxysmal wheeze and cough. Other manifestations include weight loss, low-grade fever, and lymphadenopathy. Hepatosplenomegaly may be seen due to the trapping of microfilariae in the reticuloendothelial system.

Investigations:

• Eosinophilia > 3000/μL, leucocytosis
• X-ray chest: Mottled opacities or military lesions in the middle and lower lung fields, increased bronchovascular markings
• PFT: Restrictive changes in most cases and obstructive defects in half
• Elevated levels of IgE and Antifilarial antibody titers
• Microfilaria are sequestrated in the lungs and hence not found in blood

Treatment: Diethylcarbamazine(DEC) at a daily dosage of 4-6 mg/kg for 14 days.

Differntial Diagnosis:

• Bronchial asthma
• Loffler syndrome
• Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
• Churg strauss syndrome
•

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia

•

Hypereosinophilic syndromes

Other options:

Option A:  The classical symptoms of bronchial asthma are wheezing, dyspnea, and cough which is worse at night and keeps the patient awake in the early morning hours. Chest auscultation reveals rhonchi throughout the chest. The chest x-ray is usually normal but hyperinflation may be seen in severe patients.

Option B: Miliary TB occurs due to the hematogenous spread of tubercle bacilli. Clinical features are nonspecific and depend on the site of involvement. Common manifestations include fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Blood investigations may reveal anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, leukemoid reactions, and polycythemia. Chest x-ray shows a military reticulonodular pattern in some cases.

Option D: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is an inflammatory response to various inhaled antigens. The clinical presentation can be acute, subacute, and chronic. History of exposure to the offending antigen is present. Chest x-ray findings are nonspecific and can show ground-glass opacities or ill-defined micronodular opacities.
questions.learning: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia — The clinical features along with elevated absolute eosinophil count and miliary pattern in chest x-ray are suggestive of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text:
Match the following

A) Depression
1) The feeling goes away as soon as you leave the hospital

B) Suicide
2) State of emotional and physical exhaustion caused by prolonged stress, relieved after relaxation

C) Burnout
3) Difficult to diagnose due to the shell of physician's pride

D) Overworking
4) Women physicians, substance abuse, relationship troubles
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A-3,B-4,C-2,D-1

The correct option is A-3,B-4,C-2,D-1.

• Depression - Difficult to diagnose due to the shell of physician's pride
• Suicide - Women physicians, substance abuse, relationship troubles
• Burnout - State of emotional and physical exhaustion caused by prolonged stress, relieved after relaxation
• Overworking - The feeling goes away as soon as you leave the hospital

Depression in doctors:

• Rates of depression are high in doctors.
• It is difficult to diagnose depression in doctors as they won't seek medical help because of the fear of being judged personally and professionally.
• Depression if untreated is a significant risk factor for suicide.

Suicide in doctors:

The risk of suicide is more among female physicians. Risk factors for suicide can be:

• Personal factors: Underlying psychiatric disorders, relationship troubles, stress, trauma, etc.
• Structural factors: It refers to the condition in which the doctors work. These include increased managerialism, paperwork, rushed patient interaction, inability to time off or rest, work pressure, etc.
• Endemic factors: Exposure to trauma and deaths.

Burnout:

It is classified in ICD 11 as an occupational phenomenon. It is defined as a syndrome resulting from chronic workspace stress that has not been managed successfully. It has three dimensions:

• having a feel of energy depletion or exhaustion
• Feeling of negativism or cynicism related to the job, or having increased mental distance from the job
• decreased professional efficacy.

It is a phenomenon related to occupational context and is not classified as a medical condition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the site of action of amphotericin B in fungi?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cell membrane

The site of action of amphotericin B in fungi is the cell membrane.

Amphotericin B binds to the ergosterol in the cell membrane of fungi and forms pores or channels. They increase the permeability of the membrane to ions and cause leakage of cytosolic molecules. This leads to a loss of integrity of the cell membrane and causes fungicidal effects.

Recent evidence suggests that the amphotericin B sequesters ergosterol from lipid layers, much like a sponge, resulting in fungal cell death.
questions.learning: Cell membrane — The site of action of amphotericin B in fungi is the cell membrane. Amphotericin B binds to the ergosterol in the cell membrane of fungi and forms pores or channels.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a 20-year history of chronic alcohol use (about 500 ml daily) presents with sensation of insects crawling on his skin, agitation, and irritability. He reports that his last drink was 3 days ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are classic for Delirium Tremens (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. DT typically develops 48 to 72 hours (3 days) after the last drink. The sensation of insects crawling on the skin is known as formication (Magnan’s sign), a specific type of tactile hallucination associated with severe withdrawal or cocaine use. Alcohol intoxication (Option A) would present with slurred speech and ataxia while drinking. Tolerance (Option C) refers to the need for increasing amounts of alcohol to achieve the same effect. "Reaction due to alcohol" (Option D) is too vague a term for this specific clinical syndrome. DT is a medical emergency characterized by confusion, hallucinations, and autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, hypertension). Management requires high doses of benzodiazepines (like diazepam) and intensive supportive care, as it carries a significant mortality rate if left untreated
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms are classic for Delirium Tremens (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. DT typically develops 48 to 72 hours (3 days) after the last drink.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town, there are 2500 live births within 6 months. During the same period, 5 women died due to peripartum infection, 5 women died due to electrocution, 2 died due to obstructed labour and 3 died due to postpartum haemorrhage. What is the maternal mortality ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 400 per 100000 live births

MMR = Number of maternal deaths in a period x 100,000 (or 1000)/Number of live births in the same period

In this scenario, only 10 women died due to causes related to pregnancy (5-peripartum infection,2- obstructed labour and 3-postpartum haemorrhage). Only they can be included in the statistics.

So, MMR here = 10 x 100000/2500 = 400 per 100,000 live births.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with ear wax and was subjected to syringing to remove the wax. She developed a syncopal episode while doing the procedure when the tip of the syringe touched the ear canal. Which of the nerves is responsible for this episode of syncope?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arnold's nerve

The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.

When the vagus nerve is stimulated, a parasympathetic response occurs leading to braycardia and decreased blood flow into the brain which causes syncope.

Nerve supply of External auditory canal:

* Anterior wall and roof- the auriculotemporal branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) (Option A).

* Posterior wall and floor - the auricular branch of Vagus (Arnold's nerve). Cough response while cleaning the ear canal is mediated by the vagus which also supplies the larynx.

* Posterior wall also receives sensory supply by the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.learning: Arnold's nerve — The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.

questions.text: An image of a mascot is shown below. Identify the national health programme associated with this mascot.
questions.explanation: The mascot "Sapna" is the official symbol of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in India. She is central to the "Sparsh" Leprosy Awareness Campaign, which aims to reduce social stigma and encourage the early detection of leprosy at the community level. Regarding the distractors, the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (Option B) uses symbols like the "TB Champion" or the Nikshay logo. The Malaria (Option C) and Polio (Option D) programs have their own distinct campaign materials, such as the "Do Boond" icons for polio. Sapna was specifically designed to educate children and villagers about the signs of leprosy, such as skin patches and loss of sensation. Therefore, identifying this mascot is crucial for community medicine practitioners in India

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme is deficient in Von Gierke's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose-6- phosphatase

Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes von Gierke's disease (Type I GSD).

These patients have hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, and hypotonia overlap. Further, in von Gierke's disease, there are increased serum lactate levels and hyperuricemia.

Other options:

Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes Her's disease (Type VI GSD). It results in the accumulation of glycogen in the liver causing hepatomegaly and mild hypoglycemia. Hypotonia is not seen.

Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes McArdle syndrome (Type V GSD) which presents with poor exercise tolerance, low lactate levels following exercise, and accumulation of glycogen in muscles.

Glycogen debranching enzyme is deficient in Cori's disease - Type III glycogen storage disease (GSD) in which hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and growth retardation can be seen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the child shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Umbilical hernia

The hernia appears which as a soft bulge at the umbilicus and covered by normal skin points towards umbilical hernia.

An umbilical defect is present at birth and normally closes as the umbilical cord stump heals within a week. If this process is delayed, herniation may develop during the neonatal period. Umbilical hernia occurs in up to 10% of infants and is more common in premature babies.

It usually appears within a few weeks after birth, often symptomless, but increases in size during crying and assumes a classic conical shape. Both sexes are equally affected, though the incidence is significantly higher in black infants compared to white. Obstruction and strangulation are extremely rare below the age of 3 years.

Treatment of Umbilical Hernia in Children

* Conservative management is preferred for children under 2 years of age when the hernia is symptomless, as about 95% resolve spontaneously. Parental reassurance is essential during this period.

* If the hernia persists beyond 2 years or is large and symptomatic, surgical repair is indicated.

* Surgery involves making a small curved incision below the umbilicus, defining and opening the neck of the sac, reducing the contents, excising the redundant sac, and closing the defect in the linea alba.

Other options:

Option A: In paraumbilical hernia, the hernia is beside the umbilicus & push it to one side taking a crescent shape and the defect in the median raphe is immediately adjacent to the true umbilicus.

Option B: Spigelian hernia is a type of interparietal hernia that occurs at the level of the arcuate line through the Spigelian point.

Option C: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle. Femoral hernia is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
questions.learning: Umbilical hernia — The hernia appears which as a soft bulge at the umbilicus and covered by normal skin points towards umbilical hernia. An umbilical defect is present at birth and normally closes as the umbilical cord stump heals within a week.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness, back pain, and recurrent infections. Evaluation reveals an M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis. Which factor is most important in determining the prognosis in this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of bone pain, recurrent infections, and an "M spike" on electrophoresis is diagnostic of Multiple Myeloma. The International Staging System (ISS), which is the standard model for determining prognosis in these patients, relies on two specific laboratory values: serum albumin and serum beta-2 microglobulin. Beta-2 microglobulin serves as a marker for tumor burden and renal function; higher levels indicate a poorer prognosis. Albumin reflects the patient's general nutritional and inflammatory status; lower levels are associated with more aggressive disease. IgG (Option A) is the most common paraprotein but is not a component of the ISS. IgM (Option B) is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia. While LDH (Option C) can be used in the Revised-ISS, the classic ISS relies primarily on the combination of albumin and beta-2 microglobulin for its three prognostic stages

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding following 7 weeks of amenorrhea. She is found to be in hemodynamic shock, and serum β-hCG testing is positive. On abdominal examination, a palpable mass is detected in the lower abdomen. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a young, sexually active woman with a history of amenorrhea (7 weeks), vaginal bleeding, a positive pregnancy test (beta-hCG), and hemodynamic shock is a classic medical emergency pathognomonic for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy (Option D). The shock is caused by massive intra-abdominal hemorrhage following the rupture of the fallopian tube. The mass felt in the lower abdomen likely represents a pelvic hematocele (clotted blood). Pyelonephritis (Option A) causes fever and flank pain but not amenorrhea and shock. A gastrointestinal stromal tumor (Option B) is an unrelated oncological diagnosis. Red degeneration of a fibroid (Option C) occurs during pregnancy and causes severe pain but would not typically lead to acute hemodynamic collapse and shock. Therefore, immediate surgical intervention via laparotomy or laparoscopy is required to save the patient’s life

Correct answer: D. 5%

The WHO has set the target of at least 5% expenditure of each country's GNP on healthcare

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the diagnostic test for carcinoid tumors?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine neoplasms that can secrete excessive amounts of serotonin. The most definitive diagnostic screen for carcinoid syndrome is measuring 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels. 5-HIAA is the primary end-metabolite of serotonin. For accurate results, patients must avoid serotonin-rich foods like bananas, walnuts, and pineapples before the test. 24-hour urinary catecholamines (Option A) are used to diagnose pheochromocytoma. Serum calcitonin (Option B) is a marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Serum chromogranin A (Option C) is a useful general marker for neuroendocrine tumors but is less specific for the carcinoid syndrome than urinary 5-HIAA. Carcinoid syndrome typically presents with flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing, often occurring only after the tumor has metastasized to the liver. Imaging studies like OctreoScan or Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT are used to localize the primary tumor and assess the extent of metastasis
questions.learning: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine neoplasms that can secrete excessive amounts of serotonin. The most definitive diagnostic screen for carcinoid syndrome is measuring 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels.

questions.text: Which among the following is not a part of urban health care system?

Correct answer: A. Subcenter

Subcenters are not a part of the urban healthcare system. Its seen only in rural health care system.

The urban healthcare system has a primary healthcare center or PHC at the primary level. It will be the first point for OPD (consultation), basic laboratory diagnosis, drug and contraceptive dispensing, and counseling about communicable and non-communicable disease. The first referral unit will be Urban CHCs. There are other referral centres like sub-district hospitals, district hospital. Referrals from these are taken up by medical colleges and super specialty hospitals

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Two vacccines - Measles and the pentavalent vaccine are used during an immunisation programme. Which of these vaccines has to be discarded?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG, JE, Measles vaccines and Rota virus.

All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

Open vial policy  is applicable for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV and liquid pentavalent vaccine.

Pearl PF2122: Open Vial Policy

Open vial policy allows for reuse of partially used multidose vials of applicable vaccines under the Universal Immunization Programme in subsequent sessions up to 4 weeks subject to certain conditions and thereby reducing vaccine wastage.

It is applicable only for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV, liquid pentavalent vaccine, rotavirus vaccine(new version with the VVM on the side), and JE vaccines (inactivated). It is not applicable to BCG and measles vaccines.

Vaccine vials opened in session-site can be used in more than one session up to four weeks if expiry date has not passed, if storage and transport was appropriate, no contamination has occurred in vial septum, asepsis in withdrawing was practiced and if vaccine vial monitor has not reached discard point.

Open vials should not be submerged in water. All open vials should have a record of date and time of opening. At the end of a session, all vaccines should be returned to the cold chain point and segregated as re-usable and non-reusable. All open vials of BCG, measles must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

In case of any adverse events following immunization, all open vials should not be discarded until investigation is complete. All vials must be transported in zipper bags in the vaccine carrier and recorded in stock register. Ice packs used should be well sealed.
questions.learning: Measles Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG, JE, Measles vaccines and Rota virus. All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the type of skin graft used in this image?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a split-thickness skin graft that has been "meshed". Meshing involves passing the harvested skin through a machine that creates a series of small, diamond-pattern slits. This allows the graft to be expanded to cover a much larger surface area than the original donor site, which is particularly useful in extensive burn management. Furthermore, the holes allow for the drainage of serum and blood, preventing the graft from lifting off the wound bed. Options B and C are variants of split-thickness grafts, but "Split thickness" (Option A) is the standard and most correct term for this appearance. A local flap (Option D) involves moving a piece of skin and its underlying blood supply from an adjacent area, which would not have this "mesh" appearance. While meshed grafts heal with a characteristic "lattice" scar, they are essential tools for providing coverage to large wounds that cannot be closed primarily
questions.learning: The image demonstrates a split-thickness skin graft that has been "meshed". Meshing involves passing the harvested skin through a machine that creates a series of small, diamond-pattern slits.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the hemorrhage shown in the following image?
questions.explanation: Subdural hemorrhage The CT image shows a crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdense collection along the surface of the brain, which is characteristic of a subdural hemorrhage (SDH). This occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, commonly following trauma. The blood spreads over the cerebral convexity and is not limited by suture lines, but it is restricted by dural reflections like the falx cerebri. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Extradural (epidural) hemorrhage: Appears biconvex (lens-shaped) and is limited by sutures; usually due to middle meningeal artery injury. (B) Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Blood is seen in sulci and basal cisterns (star-shaped pattern), not as a crescentic collection. (C) Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Appears as a localized hyperdense lesion within brain tissue, not along the surface.
questions.learning: Subdural hemorrhage — The CT image shows a crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdense collection along the surface of the brain, which is characteristic of a subdural hemorrhage (SDH).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman is diagnosed with type Il diabetes mellitus. She has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following statement is correct about the management of this patient?
options: Metformin is contraindicated in all stages of CKD
Pioglitazone is avoided as it is exclusively metabolized by kidneys
Glipizide can be used in renal disease
Linagliptin can be used only after dose reduction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glipizide can be used in renal disease

In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus with chronic kidney disease (CKD), the choice of antidiabetic drugs depends on their renal clearance and risk of hypoglycemia.

• Glipizide is a short-acting sulfonylurea that is primarily metabolized in the liver and produces inactive metabolites, making it safer in patients with renal impairment compared with other sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide). Therefore, it can be used in CKD.

Key related facts:

• Metformin is not contraindicated in all CKD stages; it is avoided mainly when eGFR <30 mL/min due to risk of lactic acidosis.
• Pioglitazone is metabolized in the liver, not kidneys, so renal metabolism is not the reason for avoiding it.
• Linagliptin is excreted via the bile and does not require dose adjustment in CKD.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman in her first trimester presents with lymphadenopathy and past history of toxoplasmosis. Current serology shows IgG Toxoplasma positive. What is the most appropriate advice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Safe to continue pregnancy

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection that can cause congenital infection if acquired during pregnancy. Transmission usually occurs via:

• Undercooked meat
• Cat feces
• Contaminated food or soil

| Serology Result | Meaning

| --------------- | -------

| IgG positive, IgM negative | Past infection

| IgM positive | Recent infection

| IgG negative | No immunity

In this case: IgG positive = past infection

This means the mother already developed protective immunity.

Therefore fetal infection risk is extremely low.

Classic triad:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Hydrocephalus | CSF obstruction

| Intracranial calcifications | Brain damage

| Chorioretinitis | Eye involvement

However, this occurs only if infection is acquired during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes, while central vision remains intact, and there is no history of recent trauma. Which condition best explains his visual field disturbances?
questions.explanation: A patient with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes has a left-sided homonymous hemianopia, indicating a lesion in the right visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma. The fact that central vision remains clear is the defining feature of macular sparing. This specific pattern strongly suggests a lesion in the occipital cortex, most commonly due to a stroke involving the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The macula is spared because the macular representation in the visual cortex has a dual blood supply from both the PCA and the middle cerebral artery. A standard homonymous hemianopia (Option B) would include the loss of central vision if the lesion was in the optic tract. Quadrantanopia (Option A) involves only one-fourth of the visual field. Heteronymous hemianopia (Option C) affects opposite sides in both eyes (e.g., bitemporal), characteristically seen in chiasmal lesions. Accurate field testing is vital for localizing neurological lesions
questions.learning: A patient with difficulty seeing from the left side in both eyes has a left-sided homonymous hemianopia, indicating a lesion in the right visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the function of tubuloglomerular feedback?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regulate GFR

Tubuloglomerular feedback regulates glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

As the rate of ﬂow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases, and, conversely, a decrease in ﬂow increases the GFR.
questions.learning: Regulate GFR Tubuloglomerular feedback regulates glomerular filtration rate (GFR). As the rate of ﬂow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases, and,…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient was posted for dilatation and curettage and a Sim's sound was introduced into the uterus but there was no resistance felt. What is the next line of management in the given options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate laparascopy

As the Sim's sound goes into without any resistance it suggests that there is a perforation for which acute management is needed, that is immediate laparoscopy.

Sims uterine sound is used in dilatation and curettage. The instrument can cause uterine perforation and is hence introduced into the uterine cavity by keeping it in the midline and ensuring it is not forced. It is held like a pencil with the thumb and the first 2 fingers.

After introducing the instrument, a gentle resistance is felt when it meets the fundus and the distance from the fundus to the external os is measured by score marks along the length of the sound.

Note:

Operative hysteroscopy with Versapoint does not require cervical dilation, thus avoiding cervical incompetence, cervical lacerations, and uterine perforation.

Karman’s type suction cannulas made of plastic, reduce the risk of uterine perforation during suction evacuation procedures. (Suction Evacuation is a procedure by means of which products of conception are sucked out of the uterus with a cannula attached to a suction apparatus.)
questions.learning: Immediate laparascopy As the Sim's sound goes into without any resistance it suggests that there is a perforation for which acute management is needed, that is immediate laparoscopy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mitochondrial sheaths are found in which part of the sperm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Middle piece

Mitochondrial sheaths are found in the middle piece of the sperm.

The middle piece is the segment of the sperm located just behind the head and neck.

It contains a spiral arrangement of mitochondria, forming the mitochondrial sheath around the central axoneme.

These mitochondria generate ATP, which provides the energy required for the flagellar movement of the sperm, enabling motility.

Other options:

Option A: Tail: Comprises the middle piece, principal piece, and end piece and is primarily responsible for motility.

Option C: Principle piece: Longest part of the tail which contains fibrous sheaths around the axoneme but lacks mitochondria.

Option D: Connecting piece: Links the head of the sperm to the tail (neck region). Does not contain mitochondrial sheaths.
questions.learning: Middle piece Mitochondrial sheaths are found in the middle piece of the sperm. The middle piece is the segment of the sperm located just behind the head and neck.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What type of MRI image is given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Susceptibility weighted image

The image shown is a susceptibility-weighted image(SWI) as it clearly demonstrates microhemorrhages as hypointense foci.

SWI is a form of MRI sequence that is especially sensitive to substances that distort the local magnetic field. Compounds with diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic properties will interact with the local magnetic field and produce distraction. This would lead to a loss of signal in these areas.

Deoxyhemoglobin, hemosiderin, and ferritin are paramagnetic. Bone minerals and dystrophic calcifications are diamagnetic in nature.

The main clinical use is the identification of microhemorrhages/blood products or calcium that are not detected in other MRI sequences.

Other options:

Proton density image:

It is based on the number of nuclei in the area that is imaged. In PD-weighted image tissues with a higher density of protons produce stronger signals and appear brighter. PD weighted image can be identified by comparing fluid with the fat signal. Fluids in these images appear greyish white similar or the appearance of fat in the body.

Gradient echo sequences(GRE):

It uses gradient fields to generate transverse magnetization. In areas of hemorrhage, the iron that is present in the hemoglobin produces its own local magnetic field and dephases the spinning nuclei. This is useful to identify hemorrhagic contusions in the brain and pigmented villonodular synovitis.

Inversion recovery sequences:

This MRI sequence is used to selectively null certain tissues. It can be:

• Short tau inversion recovery(STIR) where fat is nulled. Fluids appear bright and fat appears dark in these images.
• Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR) or double inversion recovery(DIR where fluid is nulled.- The fluid(CSF) normally appears dark and lesions appear to be brighter on these images.

FLAIR image-
questions.learning: Susceptibility weighted image — The image shown is a susceptibility-weighted image(SWI) as it clearly demonstrates microhemorrhages as hypointense foci.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In serological investigation of hepatitis B virus infection, presence of hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is an indicator of:
options: Active replication of virus in the liver
Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Active replication of virus in the liver

Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is a marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity. Its presence indicates that the virus is actively replicating in hepatocytes and the patient has a high risk of transmitting the infection.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute liver failure: HBeAg indicates viral replication, not the severity of liver damage.
• C. Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus: Chronic HBV is diagnosed by HBsAg positivity for >6 months; HBeAg may be positive or negative.
• D. Inactive carrier phase of infection: Characterized by HBeAg negativity, anti-HBe positivity, low/undetectable HBV DNA, and normal ALT.
questions.learning: Active replication of virus in the liver Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is a marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity. Its presence indicates that the virus is actively replicating in hepatocytes and the patient has a high risk of transmitting…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of the Bishop score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type of maternal pelvis

The type of maternal pelvis is not a component of the Bishop score.

The Bishop score is a scoring system used to assess labor induction outcomes. It is based on the station of the head, dilation, effacement (or length), position, and consistency of the cervix noted by doing a vaginal examination.

Note: In the modified Bishop score (1991), the effacement is replaced by the cervical length in cm.
questions.learning: Type of maternal pelvis — The type of maternal pelvis is not a component of the Bishop score. The Bishop score is a scoring system used to assess labor induction outcomes.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In an industrial worker with suspected intraocular foreign body after an injury involving a hammer and iron chisel, which imaging modality is best for accurately localizing the foreign body, particularly if it is metallic?
questions.explanation: When a metallic foreign body is suspected in the eye (e.g., from an iron chisel), a Computed Tomography (CT) scan is the best and most appropriate imaging modality for localization. CT provides excellent spatial resolution and is highly sensitive for detecting radiopaque materials like iron or steel. MRI (Option A) is strictly contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected; the powerful magnetic field can cause the metal to move or heat up, leading to catastrophic intraocular damage or blindness. A plain X-ray (Option C) can detect the presence of metal but is poor for precise anatomical localization. B-mode ultrasound (Option D) can be useful but is often difficult to perform in an acutely traumatized globe and is less definitive than CT. Therefore, for an industrial "hammer and chisel" injury, CT is the safest and most accurate tool for surgical planning
questions.learning: When a metallic foreign body is suspected in the eye (e.g., from an iron chisel), a Computed Tomography (CT) scan is the best and most appropriate imaging modality for localization.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient who was on ventilator and being ventilated for past few days suddenly pulls out of the endotracheal tube. What is the next step of management?
options: Watch for spontaneous breaths and reintubate if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Watch for spontaneous breaths and reintubate if needed

About half of self-extubated patients may not require re-intubation. Pre-extubation FiO2, PaO2/FiO2, and ventilator mode, as well as gender, may be useful in determining the likelihood that a self-extubated patient will require re-intubation and also watch for spontaneous breathing.
questions.learning: Watch for spontaneous breaths and reintubate if needed About half of self-extubated patients may not require re-intubation. Pre-extubation FiO2, PaO2/FiO2, and ventilator mode, as well as gender, may be useful in determining the likelihood that a…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A teenage individual who was raised as a girl presents with primary amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, there is tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia, with normal testosterone levels. Which genotype is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of tall stature, small firm testes, and gynecomastia in a phenotypic male (who may have had ambiguous gender assignment earlier) are classic for Klinefelter syndrome. This condition is characterized by a 47,XXY genotype. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome often experience primary testicular failure, which may result in testosterone levels ranging from low to low-normal, accompanied by elevated gonadotropins. A 45,X genotype (Option A) corresponds to Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature and a female phenotype. Genotype 46,XX (Option B) represents a normal female karyotype. The 47,XYY genotype (Option D) typically produces tall males with normal fertility who are often asymptomatic. Thus, the specific triad of eunuchoid proportions, gynecomastia, and small testes identifies the 47,XXY genotype
questions.learning: The clinical findings of tall stature, small firm testes, and gynecomastia in a phenotypic male (who may have had ambiguous gender assignment earlier) are classic for Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 6-foot-5-inch man undergoing a routine physical examination was found to have an early diastolic murmur. His family pedigree chart is given below. Identify the mode of inheritance of this condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autosomal dominant

The patient's height and the presence of early diastolic murmur in the given clinical scenario are suggestive of Marfan syndrome. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant disorder. The family pedigree confirms the mode of inheritance.

The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart.

Patients with Marfan syndrome have pleiotropic manifestations:

• Skeletal systems - Tall and decreased upper to lower segment ratio with long arms, hands, and fingers
• Deformities of the chest wall, vertebral column, and foot arches
• Cardiovascular abnormalities - mitral valve prolapse leading to mitral regurgitation and dilatation of aortic root leading to aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, and rupture.
• Ocular - superio-temporal lens dislocation
questions.learning: Autosomal dominant — The patient's height and the presence of early diastolic murmur in the given clinical scenario are suggestive of Marfan syndrome. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant disorder.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A known patient of tuberculosis, on INH for the past 3 months complains of numbness, tingling and burning sensation in all the extremities. What could be vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

Isoniazid (INH) therapy in tuberculosis can cause vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, leading to peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, burning sensation).

• INH forms complexes with pyridoxine and increases its excretion
• This leads to ↓ availability of pyridoxal phosphate (active B6)
• Pyridoxal phosphate is required for neurotransmitter synthesis (e.g., GABA)

Deficiency results in:

• Peripheral neuropathy
• Paresthesia (glove and stocking pattern)

Prevention: Always give prophylactic vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH therapy

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin B12: Causes neuropathy but not specifically linked to INH
• Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Causes beriberi/Wernicke’s
• Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided should cover at least _______
options: 1/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement
2/3 of the total protein requirement + ½ of total energy requirement
½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement
½ of the total protein requirement + 2/3 of total energy requirement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement

Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided must cover at least ½ of the total protein requirement and 1/3 of total energy requirement to children in schools.

The MDM scheme is also called School Lunch Programme and has been operational since 1961 in India. Currently, it functions under the broad coverage of the Minimum Needs Programme.

Some other principles of the MDM are:

• The meal provided under the MDM should only be a supplement and not a substitute to home diets.
• The cost of the meals should be reasonably low.
• The meal should be easy to cook in schools.
• Locally available foods must be used, for as far as possible.
• The menu should be regularly changed to avoid monotony.
questions.learning: ½ of the total protein requirement + 1/3 of total energy requirement Under the Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme, supplementary nutrition provided must cover at least ½ of the total protein requirement and 1/3 of total energy requirement to children in schools.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Na, K

Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+

Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential.

K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. They are responsible for repolarization phase of action potential. Also, the postassium channels return slowly to their closed state, which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization.

The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below.

1. Resting state - Both channels are closed

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters into the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs.

6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: Na, K Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+ Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential. K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When a public health worker periodically visits the community every 15 days to actively collect blood smears for malaria testing, what type of surveillance is this practice called?
questions.explanation: Surveillance is a cornerstone of epidemiological programs. "Active surveillance" occurs when health authorities "actively seek out" cases in the community. The scenario described—a health worker traveling to households to collect blood smears—is the standard definition of active surveillance used in malaria control programs. "Passive surveillance" (Option C) occurs when authorities simply record data from patients who voluntarily come to health centers. "Sentinel surveillance" (Option A) involves collecting detailed data from a few "watchtower" sites to represent the larger population trends. In India’s malaria program, active surveillance is critical for early case detection and prompt treatment to break the transmission cycle. It is more expensive and labor-intensive than passive surveillance but provides much more accurate data on the actual disease burden in remote areas. Therefore, the health worker's proactive outreach constitutes active case finding
questions.learning: Surveillance is a cornerstone of epidemiological programs. "Active surveillance" occurs when health authorities "actively seek out" cases in the community.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient stopped alcohol consumption for 3 days and presented with irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are:

* Altered sensorium with disorientation

* Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations

* Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, hypertension. And sweating

* Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy

* Altered sleep-wake cycle

Other options:

Option B - Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits, or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by:

* Global confusion

* Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex

* Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait

* Vestibular dysfunction

It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome.

Option C - Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient:

* Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory

* Anterograde amnesia

* Confabulation

Option D - Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of a heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. These patients have a clear sensorium, unlike the patients having delirium tremens.

Note: Tremulousness is the first alcohol withdrawal symptom.

Pearl PF1275: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome

Manifestation

Symptoms/signs

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation, presented with severe abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements. On examination, her uterus is tender. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, tender uterus and loss of fetal movements in a pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Abruptio placenta is the partial/total separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery.

The bleeding may be either

* Revealed - Blood dissects downwards between membranes and uterine wall to escape through the cervix. Or,

* Concealed -Blood accumulates between the detached placenta and uterus. Or,

* Mixed

Risk factors for abruption placenta include prior abruption history, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and pregnancy-associated hypertension. The haemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This compromises fetal circulation leading to fetal distress.

Depending upon the degree of placental abruption and its clinical effects, the cases are graded as follows:

Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3

Vaginal bleeding is slight
Vaginal bleeding mild to moderate
Bleeding is moderate to severe or concealed.

Uterus irritable, minimal tenderness

Uterine tenderness is always present
Uterine tenderness is marked.

Maternal BP and fibrinogen unaffected
Maternal pulse increased, BP maintained
Shock is pronounced

FHS good
Fetal distress present
Fetal death is the rule

Maternal shock absent
Maternal shock absent
Associated coagulation defect or anuria may complicate

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment over or very close to the cervical os. Vaginal bleeding is usually painless in this condition. Fetal condition is generally good until bleeding is severe which occurs in later stages. High-risk factors include multiparty, previous cesarean, or myomectomy scar in the uterus.

In preterm labour, fetal movements are not compromised. Polyhydramnios does not present with bleeding PV.
questions.learning: Abruptio placenta — The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, tender uterus and loss of fetal movements in a pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Varicella

Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnant women as it is a live vaccine.

The live attenuated varicella virus vaccine is currently recommended for children between 12 to 18 months of age who have not had chickenpox.
questions.learning: Varicella Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnant women as it is a live vaccine. The live attenuated varicella virus vaccine is currently recommended for children between 12 to 18 months of age who have not had chickenpox.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which drug is indicated for a 55-year-old premenopausal woman with early invasive breast cancer that is ER-positive, PR-positive on immunohistochemistry, and has lymph node involvement?
questions.explanation: In a 55-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive, PR-positive early invasive breast cancer with lymph node involvement, multimodal therapy is indicated. 1. Tamoxifen is the standard endocrine therapy in premenopausal women, acting as a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) to block estrogen effects on tumor cells. 2. Anastrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is typically used in postmenopausal women, but may also be used in premenopausal patients with ovarian suppression. 3. Trastuzumab is indicated if the tumor is HER2-positive, which is often evaluated alongside ER/PR status in such cases. Thus, depending on receptor status (including HER2) and treatment plan, all three drugs may be part of therapy, making option (D) the best answer
questions.learning: In a 55-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive, PR-positive early invasive breast cancer with lymph node involvement, multimodal therapy is indicated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is known as the_______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secondary attack rate

The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.

It is calculated by the following formula:

Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.
questions.learning: Secondary attack rate — The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Heparan sulfate

The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is heparan sulfate. It prevents filtration by repelling negatively charged proteins.

Collagen type IV, fibronectin, entactin are structural components of basement membrane.
questions.learning: Heparan sulfate — The protein in the glomerular basement membrane responsible for charge-dependent filtration is heparan sulfate. It prevents filtration by repelling negatively charged proteins.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the virus given in the following replication cycle.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Herpes simplex virus

The given image shows the life cycle of the herpes simplex virus (HSV).

The herpes virus capsid is icosahedral and encloses a core containing a linear double-stranded DNA genome. The nucleocapsid is surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from the modified host cell nuclear membrane. The envelope carries glycoprotein spikes.

Steps of HSV replication:

The virus enters the cell by fusing with the plasma membrane, and viral DNA is released from the capsid at the nuclear pore. This is followed by circularization of the genome and transcription of immediate-early genes.

α-Proteins are products of immediate-early genes. These proteins stimulate the transcription of early genes. β-proteins are products of early genes. These proteins function in DNA replication, to yield concatemeric DNA. Transcription of late genes gives rise to γ-proteins. These primarily consist of viral structural proteins and participate in virion assembly.

Viral DNA is cleaved from concatemers and then packaged into capsids. Enveloped viral particles collect in the endoplasmic reticulum and are then transported by a vesicular movement to the cell surface.

Image shows replication cycle of herpes simplex virus.

Other options:

Option A) The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virus is spherical, enveloped RNA virus. The nucleocapsid has an icosahedral shell and a cone-shaped core, enclosing the ribonucleoproteins. The genome icomprises two identical single-stranded, RNA copies, with the reverse transcriptase enzyme, which is a characteristic feature of retroviruses.

The images below show the structure of the HIV virus and its life cycle.

Option C: The hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus with an outer envelope and an inner nucleocapsid. The viral genome consists of two linear strands of DNA in a circular configuration. One of the strands (the plus strand) is incomplete resulting in partially double stranded and partially single-stranded DNA. The images below show the structure and life cycle of the hepatitis B virus.

Option D: Coronavirus are enveloped RNA viruses with a genome consisting of positive sense unsegmented single-stranded RNA. They have petal-shaped surface projections. Coronavirus nucleocapsids develop in the cytoplasm and mature by budding into cytoplasmic vesicles. The images below show the structure and life cycle of coronaviruses.
questions.learning: Herpes simplex virus — The given image shows the life cycle of the herpes simplex virus (HSV). The herpes virus capsid is icosahedral and encloses a core containing a linear double-stranded DNA genome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent respiratory infections, persistent wheezing, failure to thrive, and hyperviscous secretions due to dysfunction of a transmembrane regulator channel. Which ion channel is primarily affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride channel

The clinical presentation is consistent with cystic fibrosis (CF), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene.

The CFTR protein is a chloride channel located on the apical surface of epithelial cells in the:

• Respiratory tract
• Pancreas
• Intestine
• Sweat glands
• Hepatobiliary system
• Reproductive tract

Defective chloride transport leads to:

• Decreased chloride secretion
• Increased sodium and water reabsorption
• Thick, dehydrated mucus causing airway obstruction and recurrent infections.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channel: ENaC activity is secondarily increased, but the primary defect is in the CFTR chloride channel.
• B. Potassium channel: Not involved in cystic fibrosis.
• D. Calcium channel: Not involved in cystic fibrosis.
questions.learning: Chloride channel — The clinical presentation is consistent with cystic fibrosis (CF), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old man reports a respiratory tract infection four weeks ago, followed by gradually progressive weakness that began in the lower limbs and later involved the upper limbs, making standing and walking difficult for the past two weeks. Examination reveals absent reflexes with preserved pain sensation and proprioception. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy that often follows a viral or bacterial respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni). The hallmark of GBS is symmetric, "ascending" muscle weakness that starts in the lower extremities and moves upward. The most critical diagnostic clinical findings are "areflexia" (lack of reflexes) and the relative sparing of sensory functions, as seen in this patient. Myasthenia gravis (Option B) presents with fatigable weakness, mostly affecting ocular and bulbar muscles, and does not typically follow an ascending pattern. Polymyositis (Option C) causes subacute proximal muscle weakness and would not present with areflexia. Multiple sclerosis (Option D) is a central nervous system disorder that typically presents with patchy, non-symmetric neurological deficits (like optic neuritis or sensory changes) rather than global ascending paralysis. The most dangerous complication of GBS is respiratory failure due to diaphragmatic weakness. Diagnosis is confirmed by "albuminocytologic dissociation" in the CSF (high protein, normal cell count)
questions.learning: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy that often follows a viral or bacterial respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked in the image drains into:
options: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins

The image shows the thoracic duct which drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins.

Thoracic duct begins in the abdomen at T-12 vertebral level as the continuation of cisterna chyli.

* It is usually beaded due to its numerous valves.

* It drains the body below the diaphragm (lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen) and left half of the body above the diaphragm (thorax, upper limb, head and neck).

* Thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm and ascends through the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and the azygous vein.

* At T-5 level, it deviates to the left side and ascends to pass the thoracic inlet.

Tributaries of the thoracic duct:

* Bilateral (right and left) descending thoracic lymph trunks which convey lymph from lower intercostal spaces (6 – 11).

* Left upper intercostal lymph trunks, which convey lymph from the upper intercostal spaces (1-5).

* Mediastinal lymph trunks

* Left subclavian lymph trunk

* Left jugular lymph trunk

* Left bronchomediastinal lymph trunk

The lymph passes through larger lymphatics and eventually collect into two large trunks, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which in turn drain into the brachiocephalic veins.

* Thoracic duct- drains both lower limbs, left upper limb, abdomen, left halves of thorax, and left side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded green in the image).

* Right lymphatic duct- drains right upper limb, and right halves of thorax, and right side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded blue in the image).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which incision is most commonly used for an appendectomy?
questions.explanation: The McBurney incision, also known as the gridiron incision, is the classic surgical approach for an open appendectomy. It is made at the McBurney point, located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. This muscle-splitting incision follows the fiber direction of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles, allowing for rapid access with minimal muscle damage. Kochers incision (Option B) is a subcostal incision used for cholecystectomy or biliary tract surgery. Midline incisions (Option C) are utilized for emergency laparotomies requiring wide exposure of multiple quadrants. The Battle incision (Option D) is a pararectual incision that is now largely historical due to the risk of damaging nerves supplying the rectus abdominis muscle. Due to its direct access to the cecal base and superior wound healing characteristics, the McBurney incision remains the preferred standard for localized, uncomplicated acute appendicitis when a laparoscopic approach is not utilized
questions.learning: The McBurney incision, also known as the gridiron incision, is the classic surgical approach for an open appendectomy. It is made at the McBurney point, located one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are contraindications for non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation in patients with respiratory failure? I. Craniofacial abnormalities II. Significant burns III. Respiratory failure with PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg IV. Cardiovascular instability Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) (e.g., CPAP or BiPAP) provides ventilatory support without endotracheal intubation. It is most beneficial in acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and selected immunocompromised patients.

However, NIPPV requires a well-fitting mask, an intact airway, hemodynamic stability, and patient cooperation. Certain conditions make its use unsafe or ineffective.

The following are contraindications to NIPPV:

• I. Craniofacial abnormalities: Prevent proper mask seal and may make mask application impossible.
• II. Significant facial burns: Prevent mask fitting and increase the risk of tissue injury.
• IV. Cardiovascular instability (e.g., shock, life-threatening arrhythmias): Requires immediate invasive airway management and hemodynamic support.

III. Respiratory failure with PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg is not a contraindication. In fact, hypercapnic respiratory failure due to COPD is one of the strongest indications for BiPAP, provided there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not associated with annular lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urticaria

Urticaria is not associated with annular lesions. It is characterized by wheals.

Urticaria is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by itchy wheals, which develop due to evanescent edema of dermis.

A weal is a descriptive term for transient, well‐demarcated, superficial pink or pale swellings of the dermis due to reversible exudation of plasma in the skin that fade, usually within hours, without leaving a mark . Weals are usually very itchy and associated with a surrounding red flare when they arise. Lesions begin as erythematous macules, which rapidly evolve into pale pink edematous wheals with a surrounding flare.

Option A: Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs. Characteristic lesions are circular, usually sharply marginated with a raised edge with central resolution.

Option B: Pityriasis Rosea (PR) is an unknown etiology, self-limiting condition that typically lasts between 2 to 10 weeks. It is characterized by a herald patch, followed by a secondary eruption with typical lesions that are oval, annular, erythematous, and plaque-like with a collarette of scales. These lesions commonly appear on the trunk in a "fir tree" pattern along lines of cleavage. Differential diagnoses include guttate psoriasis, secondary syphilis, and drug rash. There is no specific treatment for PR; symptomatic treatment is usually sufficient.

Option D: Porokeratosis is a clonal expansion of keratinocytes which differentiate abnormally. But they are not hyperproliferative. It may present as single or multiple lesions and may be localized or disseminated. Porokeratoses present with single or multiple papules or plaques which develop into annular lesions with a thin raised border.
questions.learning: Urticaria Urticaria is not associated with annular lesions. Urticaria is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by itchy wheals, which develop due to evanescent edema of dermis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An elderly patient presents to the outpatient department with the deformity shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hand in the image shows ulnar deviation (ulnar drift) of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, along with joint deformity and muscle wasting, which are classic features of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that primarily affects the MCP and PIP joints, leading to progressive deformities such as ulnar deviation, swan neck, and boutonnière deformities. Unlike osteoarthritis, which causes hard bony nodules at DIP joints (Heberden’s nodes), this image shows joint misalignment rather than isolated nodules, pointing toward RA. The deformity appears more inflammatory and deforming, rather than just degenerative. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Rickets: Seen in children, not elderly (B) Osteomalacia: Causes bone softening, no joint deformity (C) Osteoarthritis: Primarily affects DIP with nodules, not ulnar deviation
questions.learning: The hand in the image shows ulnar deviation (ulnar drift) of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, along with joint deformity and muscle wasting, which are classic features of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about polycythemia vera is true?
options: Risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with the degree of thrombocytosis
Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation
It is protective against H.pylori infection
Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common cause of mortality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation

Generalized pruritus seen in polycythemia vera (PV) is a consequence of the activation of mast cells by JAK 2 mutation.

Other options:

Option A: The risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with erythrocytosis, not the degree of thrombocytosis.

Option C: In polycythemia vera, there is an increased risk of H.pylori infection.

Option D: Thrombosis is the major cause of mortality in polycythemia vera. The incidence of acute leukemia in patients not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation therapy is low.

PV is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder in which red cells, granulocytes & platelets accumulate in the absence of a physiological stimulus. The most common mutation seen in PV is the JAK2 mutation.

Clinical features of polycythemia vera are:

• Thrombosis is the most common manifestation and is the major cause of mortality. Uncontrolled erythrocytosis causes increased viscosity of the blood causing thrombosis of the vessels. Patients may present with stroke, transient ischemic attacks, myocardial infarction, and Budd-Chiari syndrome.
• Aquagenic pruritis is generalized itching following a warm bath or a shower due to increased mast cells and histamine.
• Erythromelalgia is erythema and pain in the fingers, hands, and feet due to increased platelet stickiness.
• Splenomegaly due to increased destruction of RBCs in the spleen
• Gout is due to the excessive proliferation of the marrow cells leading to elevated uric acid levels.
questions.learning: Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation Generalized pruritus seen in polycythemia vera (PV) is a consequence of the activation of mast cells by JAK 2 mutation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with a history of cholelithiasis, presented with vomiting and abdominal pain. The abdominal radiograph showed Rigler’s triad. Which of these is not a component of Rigler’s triad?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Large bowel obstruction

Rigler’s triad is seen in gallstone ileus and consists of

• Pneumobilia
• Small bowel obstruction
• Ectopic gall stone (usually in the right iliac fossa)

This should not be confused with Rigler’s sign and Rigler's notch sign.

Rigler's Sign:

Seen in pneumoperitoneum. Here, the air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall unlike normally, where the air is seen only in the intraluminal side of the bowel.

Rigler's notch sign:

Refers to indentation seen in the border of a solid lung mass, which is thought to represents a feeding vessel, thus suggesting the presence of bronchial carcinoma. But, this is not specific and can also be seen in granulomatous infections.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which glycosaminoglycan is essential for preserving the transparency of the cornea?
questions.explanation: The transparency of the cornea is vital for vision and depends on the precise, regular arrangement of collagen fibrils within the stroma. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are essential components of the corneal extracellular matrix that help maintain this organization. Keratan sulfate (Option A) is the most abundant GAG in the corneal stroma, accounting for about 60% of the total GAG content. It plays a critical role in regulating collagen fibril diameter and spacing, which prevents the scattering of light. Hyaluronic acid (Option B) is primarily found in the vitreous humor. Chondroitin sulfate (Option C) and Dermatan sulfate (Option D) are also present in the cornea but in much smaller quantities compared to keratan sulfate. Deficiencies or abnormalities in keratan sulfate can lead to corneal opacification, as seen in certain genetic macular corneal dystrophies. Therefore, keratan sulfate is the primary biochemical mediator of corneal clarity

questions.text: A patient is found to have a solitary thyroid nodule. What is the first step in his management?

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with chronic liver disease presents with progressive abdominal distension and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory evaluation is requested to assess his nutritional status and liver synthetic function. The clinician orders serum total protein and serum albumin levels. Which of the following assays is not typically used for the estimation of total serum protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bromocresol green assay

Bromocresol green (BCG) is not used for estimating total serum protein. It is a dye-binding assay that specifically measures serum albumin. At an acidic pH, bromocresol green binds selectively to albumin, producing a green-colored complex whose intensity is proportional to the albumin concentration.

In contrast, total serum protein includes albumin as well as globulins, and is commonly measured using assays that detect peptide bonds or protein-dye interactions.

Other Options:

• Option A. Biuret assay: Incorrect. The Biuret method is the reference method for estimating total serum protein. Copper ions react with peptide bonds in an alkaline medium to produce a violet-colored complex.
• Option B. Bradford assay: Incorrect. The Bradford assay uses Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye, which binds to proteins and is widely used for total protein estimation, especially in research laboratories.
• Option C. Lowry's assay: Incorrect. The Lowry method combines the Biuret reaction with the reduction of the Folin-Ciocalteu reagent, making it a highly sensitive method for total protein estimation.
questions.learning: Bromocresol green assay Bromocresol green (BCG) is not used for estimating total serum protein. It is a dye-binding assay that specifically measures serum albumin.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man has a history of recurrent sinus infections and chronic productive cough since childhood. High-resolution CT of the chest shows bronchiectasis, and a chest radiograph demonstrates dextrocardia with complete situs inversus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia. Impaired ciliary motility leads to defective mucociliary clearance and abnormal embryonic left-right axis determination.

The classic triad consists of:

• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis
• Situs inversus (or dextrocardia)

Other features include:

• Recurrent otitis media
• Chronic productive cough
• Male infertility (immotile sperm)
• Female subfertility/ectopic pregnancy due to impaired fallopian tube cilia

Why not the other options?

• A. Cystic fibrosis: Also causes recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis, but is associated with pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, elevated sweat chloride, and does not cause situs inversus.
• C. Young syndrome: Characterized by bronchiectasis with obstructive azoospermia, but ciliary function is normal and situs inversus is absent.
• D. Primary immunodeficiency: May cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not produce the characteristic combination of bronchiectasis with situs inversus.

High-yield pearl

| Disorder | Key defect | Characteristic features

| -------- | ---------- | -----------------------

| Kartagener syndrome (PCD) | Defective dynein arms → impaired ciliary motility | Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + situs inversus

| Cystic fibrosis | CFTR mutation | Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑ sweat chloride

| Young syndrome | Unknown cause | Bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia; no situs inversus

| Primary immunodeficiency | Immune defect | Recurrent infections without laterality defects
questions.learning: Kartagener syndrome Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The given image is an x-ray of a 22-year-old female. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell tumor

The given x-ray showing a lytic lesion at the end of a long bone with a soap-bubble appearance suggests a giant cell tumor (GCT) or osteoclastoma.

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults of age 20 to 40 years with a slight female predominance. It is a benign but locally aggressive tumor. It is exclusively seen in adults and affects the ends of long bones, involving metaphysis/ epiphysis of long bones. GCT is most commonly seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus, and distal radius. Common presenting complaints are swelling and vague pain. Sometimes, the patient presents for the first time with a pathological fracture through the lesion.

Important x-ray features of a GCT:

• A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis
• Eccentric location, most often subchondral
• Expansion of the overlying cortex
• Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap-bubble appearance.
• No calcification within the tumor
• No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor

Histologically, GCTs consist of undifferentiated spindle cells profusely interspersed with multi-nucleated giant cells. The tumor stroma is well-vascularized with bands of cellular or collagenous fibrous tissue. The image below shows the histopathology of osteoclastoma.

The treatment of choice for GCT is extended curettage and bone grafting.

• GCT in the relatively insignificant bone like the distal ulna, clavicle, and proximal fibula is treated by resection without reconstruction.
• Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.
• Radiation can be used for spinal or sacral tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor that usually appears as well-circumscribed round or oval lytic lesions in the center of the epiphysis of a long bone. It presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. It is most commonly seen in ages 10-20 years.

The following is an x-ray image of the knee showing chondroblastoma:

Option B: Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors commonly present in adolescents. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. They are usually painless. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

The following is an x-ray image of the knee showing osteochondroma of the distal knee:

Option D: Aneurysmal bone cyst is a tumor that affects all age groups but generally occurs more commonly in adolescents with an equal male: female distribution. It usually occurs in the metaphysis of long bones (like femur and tibia) and the posterior elements of vertebral bodies. Patients usually present with pain and swelling. Radiographically, ABC is seen as an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion with well-defined margins.

The following is an x-ray image of the knee showing ABC:

The image below shows common locations of various bone tumors:
