questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Klenow fragment lacks the activity of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5'→3' Exonuclease

Klenow fragment lacks 5’ → 3’ exonuclease activity.

DNA polymerase I is an enzyme involved in DNA replication. It has polymerase activity along with both 3' → 5' and 5' → 3' exonuclease activity. When the 5' → 3' exonuclease domain is removed, the remaining fragment is called Klenow fragment. It retains the polymerization and proofreading activities of DNA polymerase I.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with fever and vesicular lesions on the upper limb and the lower limb. Neck stiffness was present. Similar lesions were present on the palms, soles, and oral cavity. CSF analysis revealed normal glucose levels and elevated lymphocytes and protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Coxsackie viral meningitis and Hand Foot Mouth disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackie viral meningitis and Hand Foot Mouth disease

The presence of characteristic vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity is suggestive of Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) caused by the coxsackie virus. The presence of neck stiffness and CSF showing elevated lymphocytes with normal glucose and elevated protein levels are suggestive of viral meningitis. Coxsackie A viruses can lead to aseptic meningitis.

HFMD is a viral infection commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16, which belongs to the subgroup of enteroviruses. In larger outbreaks, other viruses such as enterovirus 71, coxsackie A viruses 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, and coxsackie B viruses 2 and 5 can also cause the disease.

HFMD typically presents as a mild illness with vesicular lesions on the tongue, posterior pharynx, buccal mucosa, palate, and lips. Lesions may also appear on the hands, fingers, buttocks, and groin, with a higher prevalence on the hands. These vesicles usually resolve within a week.

Infections with enterovirus 71 can be more severe with neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations. Coxsackievirus A16 infections occasionally lead to complications such as encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and shock. Coxsackievirus A6 can cause a severe and atypical form of HFMD.

Diagnosing HFMD typically relies on clinical examination of the characteristic lesions. Confirmatory testing can involve viral culture using samples such as blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), urine, and mucosal swabs. However, RT-PCR testing is more sensitive and specific for detecting the viral genome even when cultures are negative.

Treating HFMD involves mainly supportive care as there is no specific proven antiviral agent for enteroviruses. In cases of enterovirus 71-related cardiopulmonary disease, milrinone is suggested as an effective treatment. Immunoglobulins have been utilized to manage severe cases, although outcomes vary.

Apart from HFMD, coxsackie A viruses can cause herpangina characterized by febrile vesicular pharyngitis with ulcerating small vesicles on the oral fauces, palate, uvula, and posterior pharyngeal wall.

On the other hand, coxsackie B viruses can cause pleurodynia or Bornholm disease, myocarditis, and pericarditis in newborns, as well as orchitis and juvenile diabetes.

Other options:

Option C: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) presents similarly with vesicular lesions but lacks typical herpetic signs. The absence of atypical symptoms like mouth pain, drooling, and characteristic herpetic lesions rule out HSV gingivostomatitis. HSV-induced encephalitis causes anosmia, focal seizures and behavioural changes due to cortex or limbic system damage.

The image shows a typical HSV vesicular lesion below:

Option A: Bacterial meningitis with sepsis is unlikely given the vesicular lesions' distribution pattern (bacteria are less likely to cause vesicles in the oral cavity). Moreover, CSF findings in bacterial meningitis usually show decreased glucose, elevated neutrophils, and elevated protein levels.

Option D: Tuberculous meningitis is less likely as there is no history of TB exposure provided. In most cases, CSF findings in tuberculous meningitis demonstrate elevated lymphocytes and protein levels, along with decreased glucose.
questions.learning: Coxsackie viral meningitis and Hand Foot Mouth disease The presence of characteristic vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity is suggestive of Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) caused by the coxsackie virus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was eating a custard apple when a seed suddenly became lodged in the throat, causing coughing and respiratory distress. On palpation, a knob-like structure was felt, and auscultation revealed an audible thud. What is the likely location of the obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trachea

A history of cough, respiratory distress, a palpable knob and on auscultation, an audible thud in a child suggests a foreign body lodged in the trachea.

The classical signs associated with tracheal foreign bodies: (1) asthmatoid wheeze (2) audible slap produced from foreign body contact with the trachea, and (3) palpable thud over the trachea.

The next step in managing this patient is to obtain a chest X-ray, followed by bronchoscopic removal of the foreign body.

Although foreign body aspiration accounts for most cases in children, there is an approximate 20% incidence among adults. The most common site of foreign body lodging is the bronchus. Foreign body aspiration into the airway has three stages: immediate symptoms of coughing and choking, an asymptomatic interval, and later complications such as fever, atelectasis, and pneumonia.

When a patient presents with a history of choking, detailed history taking and physical examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx, neck, and lungs are necessary.

The next step for suspected foreign body aspiration is to obtain a chest X-ray, including the abdomen, despite most foreign bodies being radiolucent.

Secondary findings on the X-ray can indicate foreign body involvement, such as air trapping, atelectasis, obstructive emphysema, asymmetric hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or consolidation. While a CT scan has high accuracy, it is not typically performed due to radiation risks.

The treatment of choice for a foreign body in the airway is its endoscopic removal with a rigid instrument, usually a bronchoscope, by a specialist otolaryngologist or pulmonologist. Bronchoscopy must be performed even if there is a high suspicion of an airway foreign body despite negative or inconclusive imaging.

Other options:

Option A:  Respiratory distress is seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx. Inspiratory stridor would be heard due to the narrowing of the airway at the level of the vocal cords, which is critical for airflow.

Option B:  When a foreign body is in the bronchus (typically right main bronchus due to its more vertical orientation), it characteristically causes expiratory stridor or wheeze, decreased breath sounds on the affected side, and mediastinal shift; this is because air can enter during inspiration but gets trapped during expiration, creating a ball-valve effect.

Option C:  A foreign body lodged in the esophagus will present with symptoms of choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. When foreign bodies are lodged in the oesophagus, the flat surface of the object is seen in the anteroposterior view and the edge is seen in the lateral view. The reverse is true for objects in the trachea.
questions.learning: Trachea — A history of cough, respiratory distress, a palpable knob and on auscultation, an audible thud in a child suggests a foreign body lodged in the trachea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study involving radiographic evaluations, two physicians independently assessed 100 chest X-rays. They calculated a Kappa statistic of 0.71 to measure inter-rater agreement. What does this Kappa value indicate about the level of agreement between the two doctors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Substantial

The Kappa statistic measures inter-rater agreement beyond chance.

It is commonly used when:

• Two or more observers classify categorical data
• We want to evaluate reliability of diagnostic interpretation

Why Kappa is Needed? If two doctors read the same X-ray:

• Some agreement occurs by chance alone
• Simple percent agreement overestimates true reliability

Kappa adjusts for this chance agreement.

A Kappa value of 0.71 falls in the range of 0.61–0.80, which corresponds to substantial agreement.

Values above 0.80 indicate almost perfect agreement, while lower values reflect moderate to poor reliability.

Importance in Research

Kappa is used for:

• Diagnostic reliability studies
• Inter-observer variability analysis
• Questionnaire validation
• Clinical classification systems

Higher κ values indicate more reliable assessments.
questions.learning: Substantial — The Kappa statistic measures inter-rater agreement beyond chance. It is commonly used when: • Two or more observers classify categorical data • We want to evaluate reliability of diagnostic interpretation Why Kappa is Needed?

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with metastatic testicular cancer is planned for chemotherapy. Among the chemotherapeutic agents used in this setting, which drug is most commonly associated with renal tubular toxicity?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a foundational platinum-based chemotherapy drug used for many solid tumors, including testicular cancer. Its primary and dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, specifically causing renal tubular damage. This can lead to acute kidney injury or chronic renal insufficiency if not carefully managed. Streptozocin (Option B) is an alkylating agent used for pancreatic islet cell tumors and is also nephrotoxic, but it is not the standard treatment for metastatic testicular cancer. Methysergide (Option C) is a serotonin antagonist used for migraines, not a chemotherapeutic agent. Cyclophosphamide (Option D) is notoriously associated with hemorrhagic cystitis (bladder damage) rather than primary renal tubular necrosis. To prevent cisplatin-induced kidney damage, patients receive aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline before and after the infusion, often supplemented with mannitol to maintain high urine output. Regular monitoring of serum creatinine and electrolytes is mandatory for all patients on cisplatin therapy to ensure safe treatment delivery

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A medication is administered orally and has a 40% absorption rate. If the hepatic extraction ratio of the drug is 0.6, what would be its systemic bioavailability?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 16 percent

Systemic bioavailability depends on the fraction of drug absorbed and the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism. For an orally administered drug, the systemic bioavailability (F) is calculated as:

F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

In this case:

• Fractional absorption = 0.40 (40%)
• Hepatic extraction ratio = 0.60
• F = 0.40 × (1 - 0.60)
• F = 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16 or 16%

Other Options:

• Option B - 24% would result if we used 0.60 instead of 0.40 for the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism.
• Option C - 4% would result if we multiplied the absorption rate by the hepatic extraction ratio (0.40 × 0.10)\, which is the incorrect formula.
• Option D - 60% is simply the hepatic extraction ratio\, not the bioavailability.

Educational Objective:

• Systemic bioavailability of orally administered drugs depends on both the fraction absorbed from the GI tract and the fraction that escapes first-pass metabolism in the liver, calculated as: F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman attends the clinic for a routine follow-up. She has well-controlled mild hypertension and denies symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, or chest pain. An ECG recording is provided. Based on the ECG findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The ECG characteristically shows a prolonged PR interval exceeding 0.20 seconds (5 small squares). Crucially, every P wave is followed by a QRS complex, meaning there are no dropped beats. This consistent delay without conduction failure is diagnostic of First-Degree AV Block. Regarding the distractors, Second-Degree AV Block (Option A) would show intermittent dropped beats (e.g., Mobitz I or II). Third-Degree AV Block (Option C) would show complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes. Bundle Branch Block (Option D) is characterized by a widened QRS complex ( s), which is not present here. Since the patient is asymptomatic and the conduction is stable, First-Degree AV Block is the most likely finding, typically requiring only routine observation

The test is performed by heating a blood stain with glacial acetic acid and a halide (salt); a positive result is the formation of characteristic dark brown, rhombic, needle-like crystals of hemin chloride. The Barberio test (Option A) is used to identify semen (spermine). The Florence test (Option B) is also for semen (choline). Because the image specifically captures the dark, rhomboid hemin crystals, it definitively identifies the Teichmann test. This forensic tool is used to prove that a suspected stain is indeed biological blood

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Zellweger syndrome is due to defect in the biogenesis of _________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peroxisomes

Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes.

Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. It is caused by mutations in the PEX family of genes. This results in defective beta-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids, defective alpha oxidation, and impaired synthesis of bile acids and plasmalogens.

The child presents with

* Dysmorphic facial features.

* Weakness, hypotonia.

* Neonatal seizures

* Eye abnormalities.

Biochemical findings will show :

* Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid

* Abnormalities in the synthesis of bile acids

* Marked reduction of plasmalogens

There is no appropriate treatment for Zellweger syndrome. It is very severe and infants rarely survive beyond a few months.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which nerve is involved in Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Auriculotemporal nerve

The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Frey’s syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery. It is caused by an aberrant regeneration of post-ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers crossed along the sympathetic pathways to the sweat glands near the parotid region.

Clinical features are due to the result of salivary stimulation (by the smell or taste of food) leading to the sweating and flushing of the periauricular region on the involved side of the face. A starch iodine test is used for diagnosis.

Treatment ranges from antiperspirants (in mild cases) to tympanic neurectomy or botulinum toxin injection (in severe cases). It can be prevented by incorporating careful extracapsular dissection and closure of the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer during parotidectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve that supplies the muscles of the face, and results in facial paralysis if injured during parotidectomy

Option B: Oculomotor is the 3rd cranial nerve which supplies the extraocular muscles. If injured during ophthalmic surgeries, it results in ocular paralysis and the eye pointing down and out.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.
questions.learning: Auriculotemporal nerve — The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating). Frey’s syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome.

questions.text: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intracellular proteins

Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to intracellular proteins.

Donnan and Gibbs showed that "When an ion on one side of a membrane cannot diffuse through the membrane, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affected in a predictable way".

According to this, in the presence of intracellular proteins, which are negatively charged non-diffusable ions, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affected in a predictable way (Donnan Effect) so that at equilibrium their concentration ratios are equal.

questions.explanation: The image displays a Taylor brace (Option C), which is a thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO). It is characterized by two long vertical metal bars (paraspinal bars) connected to a pelvic band, along with shoulder straps. This brace is traditionally used to restrict spinal flexion and extension, particularly in the management of stable vertebral fractures, Pott's disease (spinal tuberculosis), or Scheuermann's kyphosis. The Milwaukee brace (Option B) is a cervico-thoraco-lumbosacral orthosis that includes a neck ring, used for high-thoracic scoliosis. The Boston brace (Option A) is a low-profile, rigid plastic shell used primarily for lumbar or thoracolumbar scoliosis. The ASHE brace (Option D) is another spinal support but lacks the specific Taylor vertical-bar structure. Understanding these orthoses is essential for pediatric and spinal care. questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Choose the correct statement regarding the telomerase theory of aging.
options: Telomere stability is associated with aging
Abnormal telomerase activation is associated with aging
Decreased telomere length is associated with aging
Increased telomere length is associated with aging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased telomere length is associated with aging

A decreased telomere length is associated with aging.

Telomeres are short TG-rich repeated sequences of DNA present at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes. Telomeres do not code for any proteins. They are important for ensuring the complete replication of chromosome ends and for protecting the ends from fusion and degradation.

Normally, with every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence.

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres. It is a specialized RNA-protein complex that uses its own RNA as a template for adding nucleotides to the ends of chromosomes.

This enzyme is usually present in germ cells but is absent in most somatic cells. Therefore most of the somatic cells age, their telomeres become shorter and they exit the cell cycle, resulting in an inability to generate new cells to replace damaged cells. Abnormal telomerase reactivation in somatic cells leads to evasion of senescence and apoptosis. It enables the cells to divide several times than usual.

In stem cells and cancer cells, telomerase is usually reactivated and telomere length is stabilized, allowing the cells to proliferate indefinitely.
questions.learning: Decreased telomere length is associated with aging — A decreased telomere length is associated with aging. Telomeres are short TG-rich repeated sequences of DNA present at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden vision loss and painful eye movements. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye, a normal-appearing optic disc, and a central scotoma on visual field testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of sudden vision loss, pain with eye movements, and a central scotoma (blind spot in the center of the field) is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms a lesion of the optic nerve. Crucially, the finding that the optic disk appears normal points specifically to retrobulbar neuritis, a form of optic neuritis where the inflammation occurs behind the globe, leaving the visible disk margin sharp and healthy. Optic nerve glioma (Option A) causes progressive, painless proptosis in children. Eale's disease (Option C) is a peripheral retinal vasculitis causing vitreous hemorrhage. Neuroretinitis (Option D) would show visible disk swelling accompanied by a macular star. Optic neuritis is frequently the presenting symptom of Multiple Sclerosis. Therefore, because the symptoms localize to the nerve without visible disk edema, Option B is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of sudden vision loss, pain with eye movements, and a central scotoma (blind spot in the center of the field) is highly characteristic of optic neuritis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension, tachycardia, and early renal involvement is prescribed Telmisartan. What is the most likely mechanism by which this medication improves heart rate and blood pressure?
options: Increases sodium excretion via loop diuresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreases peripheral vascular resistance

The most likely mechanism of action of telmisartan in this case is the decrease in peripheral vascular resistance.

Telmisartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), has shown evidence of having PPARγ agonist action. It is very useful in hypertensive patients with diabetes. PPARγ agonists are the thiazolidinedione group of drugs that act by inducing several insulin-sensitising genes, thereby reducing overall insulin resistance. Common side effects of telmisartan are hypotension, hyperkalaemia, teratogenicity, headache, gastrointestinal upset, and dizziness.

By acting as an agonist on the PPARγ receptor, telmisartan regulates the downstream glucose and lipid metabolism. It increases basal and insulin-stimulated uptake of glucose into the adipocytes via GLUT-4. It also decreases the amount of reactive oxygen species and increases serum adiponectin. By these mechanisms, it improves oxidative stress and insulin resistance in patients with type II diabetes mellitus. Furthermore, it has been shown to reduce cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy. Telmisartan can be given safely to a patient with chronic renal failure (CRF) because it is mainly cleared from the circulation by biliary excretion.

The drugs that reduce mortality in patients with HFrEF are

* Beta-blockers block β1 receptors and prevent ventricular remodelling promoted by the stimulated RAAS and sympathetic system. Metoprolol and bisoprolol are selective for the β1 receptor, whereas carvedilol also blocks the β2 and α1 receptors, resulting in vasodilation. Adverse effects include fluid retention, worsening HFrEF, fatigue, bradycardia or heart block, and hypotension.

* ACE inhibitors—enalapril and lisinopril—reduce mortality. ACE inhibitors decrease peripheral resistance and reduce the load on the failing myocardium by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Hereby, it prevents vasoconstriction and causes relaxation of the vasculature.

* Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) – They inhibit the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) by blocking the binding of angiotensin II to its receptor, which in turn leads to vasodilation and prevents the release of aldosterone. They are found to reduce mortality and morbidity in HFrEF cases.

* Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril/valsartan is a novel therapy that was approved in July 2015 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for patients with HFrEF. Sacubitril/valsartan consists of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the ARB valsartan.

* Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone are also known to decrease the mortality risk.

Diuretics like furosemide and torsemide are not found to reduce mortality or hospital readmission. They are the only agents that can adequately control the fluid retention associated with HFrEF.

Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, does not decrease mortality risk in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), unlike other neurohormonal antagonists such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors.

* C: Celiprolol ( III )

* B: Bisoprolol

* A: Acebutolol

* A: Atenolol

* N: Nebivolol ( III )

* B: Betaxolol ( III )

* M: Metoprolol

* E: Esmolol

( III ) - Third generation beta blockers. All the others are second generation beta blockers

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A gardener presents with multiple vesicles on the hands and multiple eruptions along the lymphatic distribution. The lesions are limited to cutaneous tissues. Which of the following will be observed on microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asteroid bodies

The presence of multiple vesicles on the hands and multiple eruptions along lymphatics in a gardener is suggestive of sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii, which is characterised by asteroid bodies.

Sporotrichosis is a type of subcutaneous mycosis caused by S. schenckii, a dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation such as grasses, trees, rose bushes, etc. It occurs in the yeast phase in tissues and in cultures at 37°C and in the mycelia phase in nature and cultures at 25°C. The septate hyphae appear very thin and carry flower-like clusters of small conidia borne on delicate sterigmata. Asteroid bodies seen in sporotrichosis consist of a central basophilic yeast cell surrounded by radiating extensions of eosinophilic material.

Following traumatic inoculation into the skin, as in a thorn prick, S. schenckii causes sporotrichosis, a chronic granulomatous infection. The initial lesion appears following a trauma or a thorn prick. The infection then spreads via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This results in secondary ulcers on the lymph nodes.

Treatment:

* Cutaneous form can be treated with oral or topical potassium iodide

* Lymphocutaneous form—Itraconazole is effective in over 90% of patients with lymphocutaneous infection

* For disseminated infection, amphotericin B is the drug of choice.

The image below shows the asteroid body and flower-like clusters of small conidia seen in sporotrichosis:

The given image shows the distribution of the nodules along lymphatics.

Other options:

Option B: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics. Histopathology shows sclerotic bodies or medlar bodies.

Option C: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are PAS-positive basophilic concretions due to iron and calcium deposits in lysosomes seen in malakoplakia. Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory reaction resulting from acquired defects in phagocyte function affecting the urinary bladder.

Option D: Henderson–Patterson bodies are seen in molluscum contagiosum, caused by poxvirus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is with pentosuria?
questions.explanation: Essential pentosuria is a rare, benign metabolic disorder characterized by the excessive excretion of L-xylulose in the urine. This condition is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme L-xylulose reductase, which normally converts L-xylulose to xylitol in the uronic acid pathway. Patients remain asymptomatic, but the presence of L-xylulose can lead to false-positive results in urine sugar tests for glucose. Regarding the distractors, D-Ribose (Option B) is an essential sugar for nucleotide synthesis and is not typically excreted in this condition. D-Ribulose (Option C) is an intermediate in the pentose phosphate pathway and is similarly not associated with pentosuria. D-Lactose (Option D) is a disaccharide found in milk; its presence in urine (lactosuria) occurs in different clinical contexts, such as late pregnancy or lactation, and is unrelated to pentose metabolism. Thus, L-xylulose is the specific pentose sugar associated with the diagnosis of pentosuria

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In fluorescein angiography, how do microaneurysms typically appear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperfluorescent dots

In fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), microaneurysms—the earliest clinically visible lesions in diabetic retinopathy—appear as multiple small hyperfluorescent dots.

Why they appear hyperfluorescent:

• Microaneurysms are outpouchings of capillary walls
• They fill with fluorescein dye → appear as bright pinpoint spots in early phases

Important distinction:

• Microaneurysms:

• Early hyperfluorescence (dots)
• May show late leakage

• Leakage (e.g., macular edema, neovascularization):

• Progressive increase in size and intensity over time

• Hypofluorescence (dark areas):

• Due to blockage (hemorrhage) or capillary non-perfusion

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: To study the dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, which sampling method would be most appropriate for obtaining a representative sample?
questions.explanation: To study dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, the population is highly heterogeneous with variations in income, education, occupation, culture, and locality. To ensure proper representation of all these subgroups, stratified random sampling is the most appropriate method. In this method, the population is divided into homogeneous strata (e.g., income groups, regions, age groups), and then random samples are taken from each stratum. This ensures that all important sections of the population are proportionally represented, leading to more accurate and reliable results. Why Other Options Are Less Suitable (A) Cluster sampling: May miss diversity if clusters are not representative (C) Simple random sampling: May underrepresent key subgroups (D) Systematic sampling: Can introduce bias if there is hidden pattern in population
questions.learning: To study dietary habits of the urban population of Delhi, the population is highly heterogeneous with variations in income, education, occupation, culture, and locality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of bony deformities. Physical examination revealed wrist widening, cupping. He is asymptomatic otherwise. Laboratory investigation revealed low plasma Vitamin D and serum ALP levels of 1500. What will be the most appropriate immediate management for this boy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin D supplementation

The above clinical scenario of an asymptomatic 8-year-old boy with wrist widening and cupping, with low plasma vitamin D on laboratory investigation, is consistent with Rickets. Treatment of nutritional Rickets includes Vitamin D Supplementation.

Radiograph of wrist showing cupping and fraying is given below

Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. A Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

Clinical features of rickets include:

* General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc.

* Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, and delayed closure of fontanelles.

* Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e., widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration.

* Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis

* In the distal extremities, widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), and anterior tibial bowing.

Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include:

* Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets in children

* Osteomalacia- in adults

Treatment:

Vitamin D–dependent rickets is treated long-term with active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcitriol). The typical starting dose ranges from 0.25 to 2 µg/day, which is gradually reduced after clinical and radiological healing of rickets. During early treatment, ensuring adequate calcium intake is essential to support proper bone mineralization and prevent hypocalcemia.

Option D: Vitamin C supplementation is recommended for children to prevent Scurvy.

Pearl PF2091: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets.

Pearl PF2079: Radiological Features of Scurvy

Radiological features of scurvy:

* Generalised osteopenia

* Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning

* Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage

* Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions

* Hemarthrosis

* Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding

* Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification

* Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line

* Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis
questions.learning: Vitamin D supplementation — The above clinical scenario of an asymptomatic 8-year-old boy with wrist widening and cupping, with low plasma vitamin D on laboratory investigation, is consistent with Rickets.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 42-year-old female who is on antitubercular therapy (ATT) experiences red-green color discrimination issues. Which of the following ATT drugs is most likely responsible for this side effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethambutol

The most likely ATT drug responsible for the red-green color discrimination issue in this case is ethambutol. It is important to monitor patients on this drug for visual side effects and, if necessary, consider dosage adjustments or discontinuation under medical supervision.

Ethambutol inhibits arabinose transferase III, thereby decreasing arabinogalactan biosynthesis. This results in, disruption in mycobacterial cell wall synthesis. It is primarily excreted unchanged by kidneys and accumulation occurs in renal failure. Ethambutol does not undergo hepatic metabolism and can be safely prescribed for the treatment of TB in patients with hepatitis.

Optic neuritis resulting in decreased visual acuity and loss of ability to differentiate red from green is the most serious adverse effect of ethambutol. It is a dose-dependent adverse effect that can be unilateral or bilateral.

Tests of visual acuity and red-green discrimination before the start of therapy and periodically thereafter are recommended.

Other options:

Option A:Isoniazid is known for causing peripheral neuropathy and hepatotoxicity as potential side effects.

Option C: Pyrazinamide is more commonly associated with hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia.

Option D: Rifampicinis known for causing orange discoloration of body fluids.

Pearl PF0763: Key points on the first line drugs used in the treatment of TB

Isoniazid
Rifamycins
Pyrazinamide
Ethambutol

Mechanism of action
Blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
Inhibition of RNA polymerase, leading to the inhibition of RNA synthesis.
Inhibition of fatty acid synthase-I, leading to the inhibition of the cell membrane.
Inhibition of arabinosyl transferase, leading to a reduction in arabinogalactan needed for the cell wall.

Unique side effects

Shoulder hand syndrome and CNS side effects.

Orange urine, sweat, and tears. Flu-like symptoms with intermittent dosing.

The most hepatotoxic drug. It also causes hyperuricemia.

Optic neuritis and hence, not preferred in children.

Mechanism of resistance

Kat G mutation- the most severe form of resistance.

Inh a gene overexpression-  confers cross-resistance with ethionamide.

Mutation in rpoB- the gene coding for the β subunit of RNA polymerase.

Mutation of the Pnca gene.

Mutations in the embB gene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A tall male patient, age 22, arrives at OPD for a standard physical examination. He has long legs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, a wide arm span, and a high-arched palate. Which of the following gene mutations is the most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fibrillin

The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of Marfan syndrome, which is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for an extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 (FBN1).

Marfan's syndrome is an inherited connective tissue disorder. The FBN1 locus is on the long arm of chromosome 15. It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. The Ghent criteria are used for diagnosing Marfan syndrome. The main features are tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilatation.

Features of Marfan's syndrome (Mnemonic: MARFAN’S)

* Mitral valve prolapse

* Myopia due to upward dislocation of the lens (bilateral ectopic lentis)

* Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation

* Retinal detachment

* Fibrillin 1 gene defect: Reduced fibrillin 1 production, causing joint laxity

* Fifteen (Chromosome 15 is involved)

* Flat feet

* Arachnodactyly, Astigmatism, Air in lungs (Pneumothorax)

* Nearsightedness

* Subluxation of lens, Scoliosis, Speech disorders, Sleep apnea

Skeletal manifestations:

* Overgrowth of long bones (dolichostenomelia) with an arm span to height ratio of more than 1.05

* Pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum

* Long and slender fingers (arachnodactyly) and contracture of fingers (camptodactyly)

* Malar hypoplasia

* Joint laxity

Cardiovascular manifestations:

* Thickened atrioventricular valves, valvular prolapse (mitral regurgitation)

* Aortic valve dysfunction due to an aortic root aneurysm

* Aortic dissection and rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta

Ocular manifestations:

* ectopia lentis

* myopia

* flat cornea

* retinal detachments

* early cataracts and glaucoma

Other systemic manifestations:

* thoracic scoliosis

* spontaneous pneumothorax

* striae atrophicae in the skin

Other options:

Option B: Elastin is a crucial protein found in connective tissue. Williams-Beuren syndrome is an associated developmental disorder (deletions of the elastin gene) affecting connective tissue and the central nervous system. Fragmentation or a decrease of elastin is found in conditions such as pulmonary emphysema, cutis laxa, and ageing of the skin. Copper deficiency can also affect the formation of crucial cross-linking in elastin.

Option C: Collagen is a connective tissue. Defects in collagen lead to conditions like osteogenesis imperfecta, Stickler syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Alport syndrome.

Option D: Laminin is a component of the basement membrane, providing structural support and anchoring the epidermis to the dermis. Mutations in its genes cause epidermolysis bullosa junctionale.
questions.learning: Fibrillin — The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of Marfan syndrome, which is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for an extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 (FBN1).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old man was found unresponsive at the scene of a RTA and intubated by paramedics. He received 2.5 L of normal saline over 20 minutes en route to the emergency department. At the emergency department, blood pressure is 70/30 mm Hg and pulse is 120/min. The patient responds to strong vocal and tactile stimuli by opening his eyes. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. There are multiple bruises over the anterior chest and upper abdomen. Neck veins are flat, trachea is midline, and extremities are cold. The abdomen is mildly distended. Cardiac monitoring shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Diastolic collapse with elevated right ventricular pressure
Dilated left ventricle with apical hypokinesis
Small left ventricular cavity volume with ejection fraction of 75%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small left ventricular cavity volume with ejection fraction of 75%

This patient has hemorrhagic hypovolemic shock following trauma.

• Severe hypotension (70/30 mm Hg)

• Tachycardia ,Cold extremities

• Flat neck veins → ↓ preload

• Trauma with abdominal distension → likely intra-abdominal bleeding

• Poor response despite large fluid bolus

These indicate ongoing blood loss → decreased circulating volume → low preload.

Option A: Diastolic collapse with elevated right ventricular pressure ❌

• Seen in cardiac tamponade.
• Typical findings:-

• Distended neck veins
• Beck’s triad (JVD, hypotension, muffled heart sounds)

• In question stem, neck veins are flat, so cardiac tamponade ❌

Option B: Dilated left ventricle with apical hypokinesis ❌

• Seen in cardiogenic shock or myocardial infarction.
• Associated with:

• Poor cardiac contractility
• Reduced ejection fraction

• Trauma patient with hemorrhage → not cardiogenic shock.

Option C: Inferior vena cava engorgement ❌

• Seen in obstructive shock :

• Tension pneumothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Massive pulmonary embolism

• These cause raised venous pressure → distended neck veins, not flat neck veins.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A young man with a paternal family history of bipolar disorder presents to the OPD with three documented manic episodes. Which mood stabilizer would be the most appropriate and effective treatment option for him?
questions.explanation: For a patient with recurrent episodes of classic mania and a strong family history of the disorder, Lithium remains the "gold standard" mood stabilizer (Option D). Lithium is highly effective at both treating acute manic episodes and preventing future recurrences of mania and depression. Valproate (Option A) is an excellent alternative, particularly for "mixed episodes" or rapid cycling, but Lithium is classically favored for pure manic presentations. Lamotrigine (Option B) is primarily effective for the maintenance phase of bipolar depression rather than acute mania. Olanzapine (Option C) is an atypical antipsychotic used for acute stabilization but is not the primary long-term mood stabilizer compared to the established efficacy of lithium. Therefore, given the specific recurrent manic history, Lithium is the most appropriate and historically validated choice for this patient. Monitoring of serum lithium levels and renal/thyroid function is mandatory
questions.learning: For a patient with recurrent episodes of classic mania and a strong family history of the disorder, Lithium remains the "gold standard" mood stabilizer (Option D).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with chronic back pain, frequent fatigue, and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections over the past three months. Laboratory tests show elevated ESR, and skull X-ray reveals abnormalities. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to further evaluate his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—elderly male with back pain, anemia (suggested by fatigue), and the provided skull radiograph showing multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions—is pathognomonic for Multiple Myeloma . Once this diagnosis is suspected, the most appropriate and essential next diagnostic test is Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) (Option D). This test will identify the presence of a monoclonal "M-spike," confirming the production of monoclonal proteins by malignant plasma cells. MRI of the brain (Option A) and CT scan (Option C) would show the structural lesions but do not provide the definitive biochemical evidence required for diagnosis. A PET scan (Option B) is useful for staging but is not the primary diagnostic investigation. Therefore, because SPEP (along with UPEP) is the gold standard for confirming the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia, it is the definitive next step. Early diagnosis is critical for managing potential renal failure and hypercalcemia
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—elderly male with back pain, anemia (suggested by fatigue), and the provided skull radiograph showing multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions—is pathognomonic for Multiple Myeloma .

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which muscle on the other supporting side is problematic when standing on one leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gluteus Medius

When a person stands on one leg: The opposite side of the pelvis tends to drop due to gravity

To prevent that: The gluteus medius of the stance leg contracts

Trendelenburg Mechanism

• Standing on right leg
• Right gluteus medius contracts
• Keeps pelvis level on left side

If weak: Pelvis drops on opposite side → Trendelenburg sign

Clinical Importance

Weak gluteus medius →

• Trendelenburg sign (positive)
• Waddling gait

Causes:

• Superior gluteal nerve injury
• Hip joint pathology
• Muscle weakness

| Muscle | Function | Clinical Role

| ------ | -------- | -------------

| Gluteus medius | Abduction | Pelvic stabilization (Trendelenburg)

| Gluteus maximus | Extension | Rising, climbing

| Iliacus | Flexion | Hip flexion

| Quadratus lumborum | Pelvic tilt | Accessory stabilization

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with diarrhoea, and a specific clinical sign is observed on examination. Based on this finding, which micronutrient deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a child with diarrhea and a characteristic periorificial or acral rash indicates acrodermatitis enteropathica, caused by zinc deficiency. This condition results in dry, scaly skin lesions primarily in the periorificial, buttocks, and acral areas. Zinc deficiency is also associated with growth retardation, alopecia, and impaired immune function. Copper deficiency (Option B) presents with anemia and neutropenia rather than this specific rash. Vitamin A deficiency (Option C) typically presents with visual disturbances like night blindness. Vitamin C deficiency (Option D) leads to scurvy, characterized by gum bleeding and subperiosteal hemorrhages. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is often due to a genetic defect in intestinal zinc absorption (ZIP4 protein) or can be acquired through malnutrition or chronic diarrhea. Treatment involves elemental oral zinc therapy, which usually leads to rapid skin improvement
questions.learning: The clinical picture of a child with diarrhea and a characteristic periorificial or acral rash indicates acrodermatitis enteropathica, caused by zinc deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops postoperative ileus after abdominal surgery. Which of the following is the drug used for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alvimopan

Postoperative ileus is worsened by opioid analgesics, which act on peripheral µ-opioid receptors in the gut myenteric plexus to suppress motility. Alvimopan is a peripherally-acting µ-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA) with negligible CNS penetration — it reverses opioid-induced gut stasis and accelerates return of bowel function without antagonizing central analgesia. It is FDA-approved specifically for accelerating GI recovery after bowel resection (short-term, in-hospital use only, due to MI risk with long-term use).

Other options:

• Atropine (B) and Glycopyrrolate (D) are antimuscarinics → block M₃ receptors → further ↓ motility; they would aggravate ileus.
• Loperamide (C) is a peripheral µ-opioid agonist → ↓ motility — used for diarrhea, exactly the wrong direction.
• Octreotide also ↓ GI secretions and motility → not useful.
questions.learning: Alvimopan Postoperative ileus is worsened by opioid analgesics, which act on peripheral µ-opioid receptors in the gut myenteric plexus to suppress motility.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a suitable method for free flow oxygen delivery to a newborn baby?
options: Oxygen tube kept close to the baby's nose and mouth
Oxygen mask placed firmly over the baby's mouth and nose
Self-inflating bag attached to an oxygen mask placed over baby's mouth and nose
A reservoir bag attached to oxygen mask kept over the baby's nose and mouth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Self-inflating bag attached to an oxygen mask placed over baby's mouth and nose

Self-inflating bag is not used for free flow oxygen delivery. It is used to provide positive pressure ventilation. Self-inflating bag and mask is used in neonatal resuscitation.

Bag and mask ventilation is used as the first step in airway management to provide positive pressure ventilation. It serves as a rescue technique to provide oxygenation and ventilation in patients with difficult airways until tracheal intubation is achieved.

The bag in this apparatus is a self-inflating bag. This allows for it to be used without a pressurized gas supply and is delivered to the patient when the bag is squeezed (compressed). A patent airway and a good seal are essential to facilitate bag and mask ventilation.

The rescuer should be positioned at the patient’s head. A one-person technique involves the "E-C seal" in which your first and second digits form a "C" over the mask with your thumb pressing down by the nasal bridge, your second digit over the bottom of the mask by the mouth, and your third through fifth digits forming an "E" and applying pressure to the mandible to hold the mask tight

Effective ventilation can be confirmed by:

• Chest rise on squeezing the bag
• Condensation in the clear mask
• Pulse oximetry shows improved saturation
• Capnography shows exhaled carbon dioxide

Mask ventilation is usually contraindicated in patients with an increased risk of regurgitation. It should be used with caution in patients with severe facial trauma.

The following image shows the parts of a self-inflating bag and mask apparatus with a reservoir bag.
questions.learning: Self-inflating bag attached to an oxygen mask placed over baby's mouth and nose Self-inflating bag is not used for free flow oxygen delivery. It is used to provide positive pressure ventilation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old smoker presents with high-grade fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral lower-lobe infiltrates, but sputum Gram stain shows no organisms. Laboratory findings include hyponatremia (Na 126 mEq/L), mildly elevated liver enzymes (AST 62, ALT 56), normal bilirubin, and a positive HIV test. Which microorganism is the most likely cause of these clinical features?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation strongly suggests Legionnaires’ disease, caused by Legionella pneumophila. Elderly age, history of smoking, and immunocompromise (positive HIV test) are important risk factors. The clinical picture shows high-grade fever, pneumonia, confusion, and diarrhea, indicating a multisystem illness, which is characteristic of Legionella infection. The laboratory findings further support this diagnosis. Hyponatremia (Na⁺ 126 mEq/L) is a classic biochemical clue in Legionella pneumonia, often due to SIADH. Elevated liver transaminases (AST and ALT) are another well-known association. Despite clear radiographic evidence of pneumonia, the sputum Gram stain is negative, which is typical because Legionella is a fastidious intracellular organism that does not stain well with routine Gram stain. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) usually presents with lobar pneumonia without diarrhea or hyponatremia. Pneumocystis jirovecii (Option C) causes subacute pneumonia with diffuse interstitial infiltrates and minimal systemic symptoms. Klebsiella (Option D) causes necrotizing pneumonia with currant-jelly sputum. Diagnosis is confirmed by urinary Legionella antigen testing, and treatment includes macrolides or fluoroquinolones
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation strongly suggests Legionnaires’ disease, caused by Legionella pneumophila. Elderly age, history of smoking, and immunocompromise (positive HIV test) are important risk factors.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old female presents to emergency following bleeding per vaginum, preceded by amenorrhea for 7 weeks. She's in hemodynamic shock with a positive serum beta hCG. On examination, a mass is palpable in the lower abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

The given clinical scenario of amenorrhea for 7 weeks with bleeding per vaginum and palpable mass on examination is indicative of ruptured ectopic pregnancy, as suggested by:

* A positive urine/serum beta hCG test: suggestive of pregnancy.

* Bleed per vaginum: The patient experienced amenorrhea for more than four weeks before the onset of the current vaginal bleeding.

* 6 - 8 weeks post last regular menstrual cycle

* Unstable vitals: suggestive of internal blood loss.

Unstable patients with these findings should undergo urgent surgery. It involves surgical exploration(laparotomy). It reduces haemorrhage and also gives a better view of the operating field to the surgeon.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenase utilises which of the following cofactors during the phase 1 reaction of detoxification of xenobiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NADPH

The microsomal cytochrome P450 system, located in the liver, facilitates the process of drug and foreign substance detoxification through hydroxylation processes that rely on the availability of NADPH.

Phase 1 reactions include oxidation, reduction, or hydrolytic reaction. CYPs- Cytochrome P family of enzymes play a major role in phase 1 reactions. Reactions carried out by phase 1 enzymes usually lead to the inactivation of a drug. The addition of functional groups does little to increase the water solubility of the drug but alters its biological properties.

The importance of NADPH is enumerated as follows:

• NADPH is needed for the reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and steroids, hence HMP shunt is more active in lipogenesis tissues like adipose tissue and the liver.
• Along with Glutamate dehydrogenase helps in the synthesis of various amino acids.
• Maintaining reduced glutathione is critical for RBC membrane integrity. NADPH keeps haemoglobin's ferrous iron (Fe2+) lowered to prevent methemoglobin (Fe3+) buildup.
• High concentrations of NADPH are also required to maintain the transparency of the lens.

The cytochromes are a class of proteins that possess a conjugated heme group. The latter is comprised of a porphyrin ring containing an iron atom. The heme group present in cytochromes exhibits distinct characteristics when compared to the heme group observed in the structures of haemoglobin and myoglobin. The heme iron within cytochromes undergoes a cyclic process of oxidation (Fe3+) and reduction (Fe2+), playing a crucial role in facilitating electron movement throughout the electron transport chain (ETC). This stands in opposition to the heme iron found in haemoglobin and myoglobin, which remains in the ferrous (Fe2+) form. The cytochromes were initially assigned the designations of a, b, and c based on the specific heme type they contained and their corresponding absorption spectra. Subsequent discoveries led to the identification of additional cytochromes, including c1, b1, b2, a3, among others.

Other options

Option A: Flavin adenine mononucleotide (FMN) is a phosphorylated form of riboflavin which functions as a cofactor for various enzymes. Some of these include as a cofactor for blue-light photoreceptors and oxidoreductases.

Option C:  Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is nothing but phosphorylated riboflavin and is used in the electron transport chain and also is a cofactor for various enzymes. Some of these include oxidative phosphorylation, DNA repair, beta-oxidation of fatty acids as well as amino acid catabolism.

Option D: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) consists of the vitamin B3 (niacin) and also serves as a coenzyme for various enzymatic reactions in the body. Some of these include oxidative phosphorylation (ATP production), DNA repair and intracellular calcium signalling.
questions.learning: NADPH — The microsomal cytochrome P450 system, located in the liver, facilitates the process of drug and foreign substance detoxification through hydroxylation processes that rely on the availability of NADPH.

questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with acute onset pain and swelling of the knee joint. Synovial fluid analysis reveals rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals. X-ray of the knee shows chondrocalcinosis. Which of the following underlying conditions is most commonly associated with this disorder?

Correct answer: D. All of the above

• Acute monoarthritis
• Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals
• Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray

CPPD is associated with several metabolic disorders, classically remembered as:

“Pseudo-Gout = 5 H’s”

• Hemochromatosis
• Hyperparathyroidism
• Hypomagnesemia
• Hypothyroidism
• Hypophosphatasia

Therefore, all of the listed conditions are recognized associations.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: On conducting the autopsy on a victim of hanging, the ligature mark is seen at the lower 1/3rd of the neck. The victim is seen to have a protruded tongue. He was found with his head hanging to his left side with saliva dribbling from the left angle of his mouth. Both the pupils are dilated and the right eye is open. Compression of which of the following structures is the probable reason for an open right eye in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cervical sympathetic chain

Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain is the probable reason for an open right eye in this case.

Dilated pupils are seen when the ligature knot presses on the cervical sympathetic chain, the eye on the same side may remain open and its pupil dilated termed as le facie sympathique. It indicates antemortem hanging.

Dribbling of saliva is the surest sign of antemortem hanging. This occurs due to the increased salivation before death due to the stimulation of the salivary glands by the ligature or by congestive hypoxia. Stimulation of pterygopalatine ganglion also causes increased salivation.

Dribbling of saliva occurs from the angle of the mouth opposite to the side of the knot. When the knot is on the nape of the neck, it occurs across the middle of the lower lip.

The ligature mark is usually above the hyoid bone. It runs obliquely, backward, upwards, is non continuous, and towards the point of suspension. The mark is noncontinuous because of a gap at the nape of the neck. When the knot is in an inverted V shape when it is in contact with the skin, because the ligature material extends downward on both sides. The skin is usually depressed/grooved, yellowish-brown, dry, hard, with small abrasions called rope burns at its edges.

Protrusion of tongue results from the pressure on floor of the mouth by ligature. It is usually swollen and blue. Injuries include bite marks with or without underlying small hemorrhages (‘marginal’ hemorrhages).

Tardieu’s spots may be present on the forehead, over the eyelids, under the conjunctiva, and near the temple.

Other options:

Option A- In partial hanging, internal jugular veins are compressed, but vertebral arteries continue to supply blood to the head, resulting in congestion of the face and petechiae. When suspension is complete, face is pale and petechial haemorrhages are relatively uncommon due to the complete obstruction of the arterial system.

Option C- Vagus nerve compression leads to a sudden halt of the progression of the pure asphyxial process due to the superimposition of vagal inhibition. In these cases, the face remains pale.

Option D- Right internal carotid artery compression can cause transverse tears of carotid artery intima, known as the Amussat's sign. It is seen with antemortem hanging. These are usually seen in obese victims and in posteriorly placed knots.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In the case of anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, where is the anterior ethmoidal nerve most commonly compressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle meatus

The middle meatus is the most common site of compression of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, causing neuralgia.

Anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, also known as Sluder's neuralgia is caused when the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the nasociliary nerve (which is itself a branch of the ophthalmic nerve, CN V1), is compressed. The most common site of compression is at the middle meatus, where the nerve may be impinged by anatomical variations, inflammation, or other pathologies affecting the paranasal sinuses.

The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the nasal cavity by descending through the cribriform plate near the crista galli. Once in the nasal cavity, the nerve descends along the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. It runs above the superior border of the middle meatus and provides sensory innervation to the mucosa of the anterior part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity

The patient typically presents with severe, sharp, and stabbing pain localized to the forehead and the root of the nose, often radiating to the periocular region. The pain is usually unilateral but can occasionally be bilateral. Associated symptoms may include tenderness over the affected area and occasionally nasal congestion or discharge if there is concurrent sinusitis.

Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the paranasal sinuses can be employed to identify anatomical variations, mucosal thickening, or other potential sources of nerve compression.

Management involves analgesics (such as NSAIDs or acetaminophen), and in more severe cases, neuropathic pain medications like gabapentin or pregabalin can be used to alleviate pain.
Nasal corticosteroids or saline nasal irrigation may be prescribed to reduce inflammation and relieve associated nasal symptoms.
Surgical intervention is considered in cases where conservative treatments are ineffective and anatomical abnormalities are identified.

questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During a spinal cord electrophysiology experiment, stimulation of an α-motor neuron produces a brief burst of activity followed by suppression of firing in the same motor neuron pool. This inhibitory effect is mediated by an interneuron that is excited by acetylcholine released from recurrent axon collaterals of the motor neuron. Which neurotransmitter released from this interneuron is primarily responsible for the inhibition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycine

• The interneuron described is the Renshaw cell.
• Mechanism:

• α-motor neuron releases acetylcholine
• Activates Renshaw cell via nicotinic receptors
• Renshaw cell releases glycine
• Produces recurrent inhibition of α-motor neurons

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with joint pain which increases in the early morning when he wakes up and decreases with activity. Examination reveals the following picture (given below) along with inflammation of the wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriathic arthritis

The condition depicted in the above image with nail pitting and yellowing of the nails and inflammation of the DIP joints, point to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Psoriasis is a papulosquamous disease with joint and nail manifestations apart from the skin. It has silvery scales.

The joint manifestations in psoriasis are referred to as psoriatic arthritis. It is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy and hence it is associated with HLA-B27. It is seen in 5-30% of patients with cutaneous manifestations. Nail involvement increases the risk of concomitant joint involvement.

Other features:

* Psoriatic nail changes like yellowing and hypertrophy

* Inflammation of the toes- dactylitis

* Shortening of toes- telescoping (because of osteolysis)

* Severe deformity- suggestive of arthritis mutilans

* Associated heel pain- suggestive of enthesitis (pain at the sites of ligament/tendon attachment)

The x-ray shows 'pencil in cup' deformity due to tapering of phalanges with cupping of proximal parts. Also all the bones of a single digit maybe involved refered to as ray deformity.

The drug of choice for different types of psoriasis is shown in the pearl below.

The most likely diagnosis for this patient's joint pain, which worsens in the early morning and improves with activity, along with the given picture showing nail changes and inflammation of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, is Psoriatic Arthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. It is categorized under the seronegative spondyloarthropathies and is often linked to the presence of HLA-B27. It is seen in 5-30% of patients with cutaneous manifestations. Nail involvement increases the risk of concomitant joint involvement.

Some key features associated with psoriatic arthritis:

* Psoriatic nail changes like yellowing and hypertrophy

* Inflammation of the toes - dactylitis (sausage appearance).

* Shortening of toes - telescoping (because of osteolysis)

* Severe deformity - suggestive of arthritis mutilans

* Associated heel pain - suggestive of enthesitis (pain at the sites of ligament/tendon attachment)

* Radiographic findings, including the "pencil-in-cup" deformity, which results from the tapering of phalanges and cupping of proximal parts.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

Pearl PF1460: Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

I. In Mild Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* Coal tar

* Dithranol

* Potent topical steroid

* Vitamin D analogue

Second line

* Local NB-UVB or PUVA

* Excimer laser

II. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* NB-UVB or PUVA

Second line

* Acitretin

* Apremilast

* Ciclosporin

* Fumaric acid esters (where available)

* Methotrexate

Third line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Secukinumab

* Ustekinumab

III. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis with Psoriatic Arthritis

First line

* Apremilast

* Methotrexate

Second line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Ustekinumab

Third line

* Combination therapy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in a pregnant woman diagnosed with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB)?
questions.explanation: Managing drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in pregnancy is challenging due to the fetal toxicity of several second-line agents. Kanamycin (Option C), an aminoglycoside, is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy. Like other aminoglycosides (e.g., Streptomycin), it is known to cross the placenta and cause permanent ototoxicity (eighth cranial nerve damage) and potential nephrotoxicity in the developing fetus. Amoxicillin (Option A) is generally safe in pregnancy. Clofazimine (Option B) and Linezolid (Option D) are second-line agents that are often utilized in extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB cases; while they carry their own risks, they are considered "safer" alternatives or are used when the benefit outweighs the risk compared to the known teratogenicity of aminoglycosides. Therefore, because of its documented ability to cause fetal deafness, Kanamycin is the definitive "not safe" choice among the options provided
questions.learning: Managing drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in pregnancy is challenging due to the fetal toxicity of several second-line agents. Kanamycin (Option C), an aminoglycoside, is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is associated with untoward side effect of renal tubular damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cisplatin

Nephrotoxicity is one of the dose-limiting toxicity of cisplatin therapy. Cisplatin achieves a high concentration in nephrons. Both direct toxicity and inflammation are responsible for nephrotoxicity. A high concentration of chloride stabilizes cisplatin and reduces nephrotoxicity. Therefore, chloride diuresis is used to reduce nephrotoxicity.

Option B: streptozotocin use can result in diabetes mellitus due to the destruction of beta cells of the pancreas.

Option C: methysergide use is associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Option D: cyclophosphamide causes hemorrhagic cystitis as one of its characteristic side effect.
questions.learning: Cisplatin Nephrotoxicity is one of the dose-limiting toxicity of cisplatin therapy. Cisplatin achieves a high concentration in nephrons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal, located below the pectinate line, presents with palpable, tender, enlarged lymph nodes. What is the anatomical basis for this pattern of lymphatic spread?
options: Below the pectinate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes
Below the pectinate line drains to internal iliac nodes
Both above and below the pectinate line drain exclusively to internal iliac nodes
Lymphatic drainage is determined solely by arterial supply
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Below the pectinate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes

• The pectinate (dentate) line marks the embryological junction where hindgut (endoderm) meets ectoderm, and this origin dictates the distinct neurovascular and lymphatic supply above versus below the line.
• Above the pectinate line (endoderm-derived, visceral structures):

• Arterial supply: Superior rectal artery (branch of IMA)
• Venous drainage: Superior rectal vein → IMV → splenic vein → portal vein
• Innervation: Visceral (inferior hypogastric plexus, T12–L3) → painless pathology (e.g., internal hemorrhoids)
• Lymphatics: Drain to internal iliac lymph nodes
• Malignancy here is typically adenocarcinoma

• Below the pectinate line (ectoderm-derived, somatic structures):

• Arterial supply: Inferior rectal artery (branch of internal pudendal artery)
• Venous drainage: Inferior rectal vein → internal pudendal vein → internal iliac vein → common iliac vein → IVC (systemic, bypassing the portal system)
• Innervation: Somatic (pudendal nerve, S2–S4) → painful pathology (e.g., external hemorrhoids, anal fissures)
• Lymphatics: Drain to superficial inguinal lymph nodes
• Malignancy here is typically squamous cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with an ankle injury following excessive eversion of the foot. Which of the following ligaments is most commonly injured in this type of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deltoid ligament

The correct answer is Deltoid ligament.

Excessive eversion stresses the medial collateral (deltoid) ligament, making it the ligament most commonly injured in eversion ankle trauma.

ATFL, PTFL, and calcaneofibular ligaments are lateral ligaments typically injured in inversion injuries, not eversion.
questions.learning: Deltoid ligament — The correct answer is Deltoid ligament. Excessive eversion stresses the medial collateral (deltoid) ligament, making it the ligament most commonly injured in eversion ankle trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a branch of posterior division of internal iliac artery ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior gluteal artery

The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

Branches of the anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery:

1. Obturator artery
2. Superior vesical artery
3. Inferior vesical artery
4. Inferior gluteal artery
5. Middle rectal artery
6. Vaginal artery (in females)
7. Uterine artery (in females)
8. Internal pudendal artery

Branches of the posterior trunk of the internal iliac artery:

• Iliolumbar artery
• Lateral sacral arteries
• Superior gluteal artery
