questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with complaints of skin lesions and joint pain. Cutaneous examination reveals erythematous, scaly plaques, while musculoskeletal examination shows a painful, swollen, and tender finger joint with signs of inflammation. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a chronic skin condition (red, scaly patches characteristic of psoriasis) and inflammatory joint pain involving a specific digit is diagnostic for Psoriatic Arthritis. This seronegative spondyloarthropathy often presents with "dactylitis" (sausage digit) and can involve the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, which is less common in rheumatoid arthritis. The provided image further supports the diagnosis by showing pathognomonic psoriatic nail changes, such as pitting, onycholysis, and oil spots. Reactive arthritis (Option A) typically follows a GI/GU infection and presents with a classic triad including uveitis and urethritis. Pseudogout (Option B) is a crystal-induced arthropathy characterized by chondrocalcinosis on X-ray. Osteoarthritis (Option C) is a degenerative "wear and tear" disease that lacks the primary scaly skin rash of psoriasis. Up to 30% of patients with psoriasis will eventually develop psoriatic arthritis. Management involves a combination of NSAIDs, conventional DMARDs like methotrexate, and modern biologic therapies (TNF inhibitors) to control both skin and joint inflammation
questions.learning: The combination of a chronic skin condition (red, scaly patches characteristic of psoriasis) and inflammatory joint pain involving a specific digit is diagnostic for Psoriatic Arthritis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following beta-adrenergic blockers are beneficial for patients with reduced ejection fraction and can reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing exacerbations over a few years?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bisoprolol

The beta-adrenergic blocker that is useful in patients with reduced ejection fraction and can reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing exacerbations over a few years is bisoprolol.

Bisoprolol is preferred for use in patients having heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

The exacerbation mentioned in the context of beta-blockers for heart failure refers to the potential worsening of heart failure symptoms in some patients, despite the overall benefits of these medications. They can sometimes lead to a decline in left ventricular function, particularly in individuals with limited cardiac reserve who rely heavily on adrenergic stimulation. This deterioration can manifest as increased heart failure symptoms or a decrease in cardiac function. The only beta-blockers that have been proven to improve the survival of patients with HFrEF or chronic HF are -

• Bisoprolol
• Metoprolol
• Carvedilol

HFrEF is a complex clinical syndrome where the ventricle fails to adequately fill with or eject blood, typically defined by an ejection fraction (EF) less than or equal to 40%. Key etiologies include coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, congenital heart diseases, and autoimmune diseases like giant cell myocarditis. Patients with HFrEF commonly experience symptoms like dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and may present with pedal edema, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), ascites, and hepatomegaly on examination.

The pharmacological management of HFrEF involves drugs with both symptomatic and mortality benefits, including Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) such as sacubitril/valsartan, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors like ramipril and enalapril, β-blockers such as metoprolol and carvedilol, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors like dapagliflozin, and hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate (noting a mortality benefit specifically in African-American patients). Drugs used primarily for symptomatic relief, such as loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), and digoxin, are reserved for specific indications or during decompensation. Non-pharmacological therapies for HFrEF include implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICD) and cardiac resynchronization therapy.
questions.learning: Bisoprolol — The beta-adrenergic blocker that is useful in patients with reduced ejection fraction and can reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing exacerbations over a few years is bisoprolol.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is intubated with a high-volume, low-pressure cuffed endotracheal tube for a prolonged surgical procedure. The anesthesiologist periodically measures cuff pressure to prevent tracheal mucosal ischemia. What is the maximum recommended cuff pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 25 cm H₂O

Endotracheal cuff pressure should be maintained ≤25 cm H₂O to avoid tracheal mucosal ischemia, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and post-intubation tracheal stenosis. The cuff should be inflated only until an adequate seal is achieved.

Educational Objective:

Maintain cuff pressure below 25 cm H₂O and monitor it periodically, especially when nitrous oxide is used, as it diffuses into the cuff and increases cuff pressure.
questions.learning: 25 cm H₂O Endotracheal cuff pressure should be maintained ≤25 cm H₂O to avoid tracheal mucosal ischemia, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and post-intubation tracheal stenosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What are the characteristic laboratory findings in primary hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing to produce adequate hormones. Because of the negative feedback loop, the pituitary gland compensates by increasing its secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH). Therefore, the hallmark laboratory finding is an elevated TSH level coupled with low free T4 (thyroxine) levels. While T3 levels (Option B) also eventually drop, T4 is the primary hormone measured for diagnosis because T3 levels can remain within the normal range for a longer period. Elevated TSH with elevated T4 (Option C) is rare and could indicate TSH-producing pituitary tumors or thyroid hormone resistance. Low TSH with low T4 (Option D) is characteristic of "secondary" or "central" hypothyroidism, where the problem lies in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus. Patients with primary hypothyroidism typically present with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and bradycardia. Standard treatment involves lifelong replacement therapy with levothyroxine
questions.learning: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing to produce adequate hormones. Because of the negative feedback loop, the pituitary gland compensates by increasing its secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female with breast cancer undergoes investigation which reveals the presence of ER positivity. Presence of ER is important as it is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prognostic marker

• ER positivity tells you how well the tumour will respond to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), making it a prognostic > predictive marker (remains controversial)
• Although ER status correlates with a better prognosis, its clinical value also lies in predicting the benefit of hormonal treatment; it is not diagnostic, nor a surrogate molecular subtype marker on its own.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-week neonate presents with ambiguous genitalia with Na+ - 127; K+ - 6 meq/L with a BP of 50/22 mm Hg. Along with IV fluids, what specific management is done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrocortisone

The given clinical case of a neonate presenting with ambiguous genitalia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension points towards a diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Hydrocortisone must be administered along with IV fluids for the management of this baby.

The most common enzyme deficiency in CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Babies with 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically present around 10-14 days of age with the subset of symptoms due to aldosterone deficiency, cortisol deficiency, and androgen excess.

Aldosterone deficiency leads to salt-wasting crises marked by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis.

Cortisol deficiency causes manifestations like hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and shock.

Androgen excess in 21-hydroxylase deficiency results in virilization of females, leading to female pseudohermaphroditism, and precocious puberty in males. Virilization is usually apparent at birth in females and within 2 to 3 years of life in males.

Without treatment, shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks.

Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels or by genetic testing.

Glucocorticoid replacement therapy is the primary treatment for cortisol deficiency, aiming to suppress androgen production and prevent complications associated with androgen excess. Fludrocortisone is given to control mineralocorticoid deficiency.

If the condition is diagnosed prenatally, dexamethasone may be administered to the mother.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with high-frequency hearing loss that worsens in noisy surroundings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Presbycusis

Presbycusis is an age-related sensorineural hearing loss characterized by bilateral high-frequency loss with difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments.

·     Pathology: Degeneration of hair cells in the basal turn of cochlea

·    Hearing loss:

o    High frequency first

o    Gradually progressive, bilateral and symmetric

·   Hallmark complaint:

o    “I can hear but cannot understand,” especially in noisy settings (poor speech discrimination)

Why not other options:

·     Meniere disease: Fluctuating low-frequency loss, vertigo, tinnitus

·     Acoustic neuroma: Unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus

·    Otosclerosis: Conductive hearing loss, not high-frequency SNHL

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is typically not seen in allergic rhinitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otto Veraguth folds

Otto Veraguth folds are not seen in allergic rhinitis.

Otto Veraguth fold is a physical sign of depression wherein there is a triangular fold in the nasal corner of upper eyelid.

Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated immunological response of the nasal mucosa to allergens in the environment.

Patients typically present with recurrent bouts of sneezing, nasal obstruction, watery nasal discharge, and itching.

Clinical signs include:

• Allergic shiners: dark circles around the eyes.
• Allergic salute: black transverse nasal crease on the dorsum of the nose due to repeated upward rubbing.
• Dennie-Morgan lines - transverse skin creases in the infraorbital area.

Allergic rhinitis can be classified into intermittent and persistent, based on the duration of the disease:

• Intermittent- Symptoms are present for less than 4 days a week, or less than 4 weeks
• Persistent- Symptoms are present for more than 4 days a week, or more than 4 weeks

It can be classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on the severity of the disease:

• Mild- None of the following symptoms are present- sleep impairment, impairment of daily activities, school, or work, troublesome symptoms.
• Moderate- severe: If at least one of the symptoms mentioned above are present.

A step-care approach is recommended for allergic rhinitis and its impact on asthma (ARIA) for the treatment of allergic rhinitis includes the following:

• Oral antihistamines or intranasal cromolyn sodium are recommended for mild, intermittent disease. (option A).
• Intranasal corticosteroids are used for moderate disease as monotherapy. (option B).
• Oral antihistamines and intranasal steroids can be used in combination to treat severe diseases. (option C).
• A short course of oral corticosteroids and immunotherapy can be used for severe, persistent disease in case the above intervention fails

In the given image, Otto Veraguth's sign or Veraguth's fold is shown, a diagonal palpebral fold running from the lateral corners of the eyes, medially upward to the medial end of the eyebrows. It is a physical sign of depression.

Another physical sign of depression is the Omega sign. In this, there is vertical wrinkling between the eyebrows joined at the top by a horizontal crease.
questions.learning: Otto Veraguth folds Otto Veraguth folds are not seen in allergic rhinitis. Otto Veraguth fold is a physical sign of depression wherein there is a triangular fold in the nasal corner of upper eyelid.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with complaints of long-standing dacrocystitis. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dacrocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for long-standing chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery. it involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus.

Chronic dacryocystitis is a multifactorial disease affecting the lacrimal sac.

Clinical features can be divided into 4 stages.

* Stage of chronic catarrhal dacryocystitis: inflammation of lacrimal sac and blockage of nasolacrimal duct

* Stage of lacrimal mucocele: chronic stagnation and distension of the lacrimal sac forming a swelling

* Stage of chronic suppurative dacryocystitis: purulent discharge from punctum

* Stage of chronic fibrotic sac: thickening of mucosa to form a fibrous sac

Treatment

Dacrocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the treatment of choice once local infection if present is controlled with topical antibiotics. it re-establishes the drainage

Dacrocystecomy is considered if DCR is contraindicated like in advanced age, TB or syphilitic infection of the sac
questions.learning: Dacrocystorhinostomy — The treatment of choice for long-standing chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery. it involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old was brought to the ER after falling off his bicycle. His vitals were stable, but he had a bruise over the perineum and he had not passed urine yet. Blood was seen at the meatus and the bladder was not palpable. How do you manage him?
options: Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate

The clinical features of a perineal bruise and blood at the urethral meatus following a fall from a bicycle are suggestive of a bulbar urethral injury. In this case, since the bladder is not palpable, the best option would be to wait for the bladder to fill and for the urge to urinate to occur. Once the bladder is full, the urine should be drained using a suprapubic catheter.

The image given below shows the various parts of the urethra:

Urethral injuries can be classified into:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Loose manhole covering
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma
• Injury to the membranous urethra leads to accumulation of urine in the deep perineal pouch.

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (Butterfly hematoma)

A retrograde urethrogram with water-soluble contrast is used for confirmation of the diagnosis.
questions.learning: Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate — The clinical features of a perineal bruise and blood at the urethral meatus following a fall from a bicycle are suggestive of a bulbar urethral injury.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which nerve results in absent gag reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IX & X

The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the posterior pharynx.

The efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) supplying the pharyngeal muscles.

Injury to either nerve can abolish the gag reflex.
questions.learning: IX & X — The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the posterior pharynx. The efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) supplying the pharyngeal muscles.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 26-year-old patient presents with a history of headache, fever, and neck stiffness for several days. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals the following parameters: protein 62, glucose 20 mg/dl (plasma glucose 140 mg/dl), and white blood cells composed of lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tubercular meningitis

The lymphocytic predominance and low CSF glucose points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis.

Note: CSF glucose/Serum glucose < 0.4 -> Hypoglycorrhachia; Secondary to glycolysis by bacteria or leukocytes, and/or by altered glucose transport.

Tuberculous meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is caused by the formation of tubercles in the brain parenchyma. This happens during the hematogenous spread of the bacilli during primary infection. It can also be due to the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space.

Tuberculous meningitis presents as a subacute infection and has a longer course than bacterial meningitis. Ocular nerve palsy is a common association as there is marked meningeal involvement at the base of the brain. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus.

The CSF sample shows a pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils.

Important features of TB meningitis:

• Common between 6 months and 4 years of age
• Usually spread by hematogenous route
• Gelatinous exudate infiltrates corticomeningeal blood vessels leading to hydrocephalus.
• Three stages

• Prodromal stage
• stage of meningitis
• stage of coma

• CSF study shows reduced sugar level, increased protein level, and lymphocytosis.
• Treatment includes antitubercular drugs for 12 months and corticosteroids (to reduce neurologic sequelae).

Other options:

Coxsackie meningitis is a viral meningitis. (aseptic meningitis) The CSF findings in Coxsackie meningitis are typically normal-elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis. The glucose level in the CSF is usually normal.

The CSF findings in HSV encephalitis are typically normal-elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis, and RBCs due to hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe. CSF Glucose levels would be normal.

The CSF findings in bacterial meningitis are typically elevated protein, neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose level.
questions.learning: Tubercular meningitis — The lymphocytic predominance and low CSF glucose points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis. Note: CSF glucose/Serum glucose Hypoglycorrhachia; Secondary to glycolysis by bacteria or leukocytes, and/or by altered glucose transport.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained? (NEET PG 2018)
options: Asking the patient to void and see if the pessary is in place
Seeing if the patient feels any discomfort, which means that the pessary is retained
Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manuever and see if the pessary is in place
Being able to admit two fingers between the ring and the pessary.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manuever and see if the pessary is in place

A pessary is a vaginal support device used for pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence. After pessary insertion, the first step to check adequate retention is Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva maneuver

This increases intra-abdominal pressure and helps determine whether:

• The pessary remains properly positioned
• It slips, rotates, or is expelled

Additional assessment after proper retention:

• Patient comfort
• Ability to void normally
• Ability to walk and perform routine activities

A properly fitted pessary should stay in place during straining but should not cause pain or excessive pressure.
questions.learning: Asking the patient to perform the Valsalva manuever and see if the pessary is in place A pessary is a vaginal support device used for pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, weight loss, and early satiety over several months. On examination, he has pallor, hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly. Laboratory and molecular evaluation reveal a gain-of-function mutation in a non-receptor tyrosine kinase (JAK2) leading to constitutive activation of the JAK–STAT signaling pathway in hematopoietic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Primary myelofibrosis

Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 mutation, leading to constitutive JAK–STAT activation, abnormal megakaryocyte proliferation, and release of fibrogenic cytokines (e.g., TGF-β), resulting in bone marrow fibrosis.

• Extramedullary hematopoiesis → massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly
• Bone marrow failure → anemia, fatigue
• Peripheral smear → teardrop (dacrocyte) RBCs

Conceptual Highlights:

• JAK2 mutation → hallmark of myeloproliferative disorders
• Fibrosis → “dry tap” on marrow aspiration
• Spleen enlarges due to compensatory hematopoiesis

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

A. APL → t(15;17), DIC

B. CLL → lymphocytosis, smudge cells

C. NHL / Mantle cell → lymphoid malignancies, not JAK2-driven

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented to the hospital with a history of increased frequency of micturition. On cystoscopy, a pale ureteric orifice was seen. The patient's KUB X-ray is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bladder tuberculosis

The given clinical scenario and KUB X-ray point to the diagnosis of bladder tuberculosis.

The earliest sign of tuberculosis of the bladder observed by cystoscopy is the pallor of the mucosa around the ureteric orifice due to submucous edema. Subsequently, tubercles may be seen.

A thimble bladder is a small contracted bladder due to fibrosis of the bladder walls. It is seen in bladder tuberculosis and is appreciated in a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU). The X-ray KUB given above shows a thimble bladder.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)? 1. Use of contraceptive pills 2. IUD use 3. Genetic predisposition 4. Sexually active teenagers Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract. It is most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Several behavioral and gynecological factors increase the risk of acquiring PID.

• 1. Use of contraceptive pills ✗

• Combined oral contraceptive pills are not a risk factor for PID. They may even reduce the risk of ascending infection by thickening cervical mucus.

• 2. IUD use ✓

• There is a slightly increased risk of PID during the first 3 weeks after IUCD insertion. Long-term IUCD use itself does not significantly increase the risk if no STI is present, but for examination purposes it is considered a risk factor.

• 3. Genetic predisposition ✓

• Host genetic factors affecting immune response may increase susceptibility to PID and its complications.

• 4. Sexually active teenagers ✓

• Adolescents are at increased risk because of:

• Higher prevalence of STIs
• Cervical ectopy, facilitating infection
• High-risk sexual behavior
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract. It is most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Correct answer: A. Oligospermia

The given scenario of decreased sperm concentration with normal range of motility and morphology points to the diagnosis of oligospermia.

Oligospermia is defined as sperm concentration of <15 million/ml.
It is further subdivided into mild-moderate oligospermia when the concentration is 10-15 million sperms /ml & severe oligospermia when the concentration is <5 million sperms/ml.

Teratozoospermia or teratospermia (option B) is defined as Increased proportion of morphologically abnormal sperms.

Asthenozoospermia or asthenospermia (option C) is used to define sperms with diminished motility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clearance x plasma concentration

The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration.

The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration. When a drug is given repeatedly at short intervals it will accumulate in the body until the elimination of the drug matches its input. So steady-state concentration is the plasma concentration at which the drug elimination and drug input balance each other.

Steady-state concentration(Cpss) = Dose rate / Clearance

From this equation dose rate for a target steady-state plasma concentration is calculated as

Dose rate = Clearance(CL) x target plasma concentration(Cpss)
questions.learning: Clearance x plasma concentration — The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration. The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth, which has now become acutely painful, erythematous, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The infant has a congenital scrotal mass (likely an inguinal hernia) that has suddenly become painful, erythematous, and irreducible, indicating that the blood supply to the trapped tissue is compromised. This is the definition of a strangulated hernia, a surgical emergency where delayed treatment leads to bowel necrosis. Acute epididymo-orchitis (Option A) is rare in infants and would not involve an irreducible groin mass. Testicular torsion (Option B) presents with acute pain but would not have been present from birth. An incarcerated hernia (Option D) is irreducible but does not yet have vascular compromise; therefore, it lacks the severe redness and systemic tenderness seen in strangulation. Physical examination shows a tense, extremely tender mass with no cough impulse. Immediate resuscitation followed by surgical exploration is mandatory

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzymes that convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA are given in the diagram. What are the enzymes marked as E1 and E2 respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and dihydrolipoyl transacetylase

E1 is pyruvate dehydrogenase and E2 is dihydrolipoyl transacetylase in the image showing oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate. This is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex where E1, E2, and E3 are the three enzyme components of the complex.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a multienzyme complex that is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. It catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA which enters the citric acid/Kreb’s cycle.

Enzyme components of PDH complex
Co-factors

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)

Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2)

Lipoic acid

Coenzyme A

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3)

Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)

Steps of pyruvate decarboxylation:

• Pyruvate is transported into the mitochondria by a proton symporter.
• Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1). TPP is required for this step. The decarboxylated pyruvate remains bound to the enzyme, as hydroxyethyl thiamine pyrophosphate.
• The hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to form an acetyl group. It is then transferred from TPP to lipoamide to form acetyl lipoamide. This step is catalyzed by dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2).
• Acetyl lipoamide reacts with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA and reduced lipoamide.
• The reduced lipoamide is reoxidized by FAD-dependent dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).

The overall reaction is : Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2

Clinical significance:

1. Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits PDH. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis. Lactic acidosis is a common presentation in patients with inherited pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency too.
2. In arsenic and mercury poisoning, the heavy metal ions react with -SH groups of lipoic acid and inhibit pyruvate dehydrogenase.

Other multienzyme complexes include alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. All the five coenzymes of PDH are common to these two complexes too.
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and dihydrolipoyl transacetylase E1 is pyruvate dehydrogenase and E2 is dihydrolipoyl transacetylase in the image showing oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with a history of multiple sexual partners presents with lower abdominal pain for 1 month. She experiences minimal discharge and complaints of intermenstrual bleeding. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neisseria gonorrhoea

This clinical scenario indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which has led to pelvic inflammatory disease.

Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by N. gonorrhoeae. It uses pili in adhesion to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. The cocci penetrate the intracellular spaces to reach the subepithelial tissue by the third day of infection. The incubation period is 2-8 days.

The major symptoms include vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency. The specific symptoms seen in males and females are as follows:

In females:

About half the female patients remain asymptomatic. But, patients typically present with urethritis, cervical discharge, pruritus, dysuria, and intermenstrual bleeding.

The ectocervix and vagina are not usually affected in adults as the stratified squamous epithelium is resistant to infection by the cocci. The acidic pH of vaginal secretions is also protective. The principal sites of invasion for gonococcal infection are the columnar and transitional epithelium.

The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, skene glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Unilateral pain and swelling over the labia may be caused by the inflammation of the Bartholin glands.

Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Other complications are tubo-ovarian abscesses and ectopic pregnancies. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). The patient presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness with abnormal liver function tests.

In males:

• Acute urethritis: This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis.
• Genital discharge: It is mucopurulent that can be described as that resembling the 'flow of seed' (semen).
• Strictures: Chronic urethritis may lead to stricture formation.
• Water-can perineum: The infection may spread to the periurethral tissues causing abscesses and multiple discharging sinuses.

Other options:

Option A: Herpes simplex presents as painful genital ulcers.

Option B:  While genital tuberculosis may present as menstrual irregularity, it is usually accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and weight loss. Often with concurrent pulmonary disease. It may also present as infertility or may remain asymptomatic.

Option C: Vaginal candidiasis presents as intense pruritus and copious cottage cheese vaginal discharge.
questions.learning: Neisseria gonorrhoea — This clinical scenario indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which has led to pelvic inflammatory disease. Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by N. gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A 10-year-old boy presented with fatigue. Investigations revealed: Hemoglobin, 9 g/dL; MCV, 60 fL; MCH, 20 pg; and serum ferritin, 185 μg/L. The TLC was elevated and showed predominant lymphocytes and neutrophils. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?

Normal values:

• Serum Ferritin: 50-150 μg/L
• Mean cell volume (MCV)-  80-100 fL
• Mean cell Hb (MCH)- 27–31 pg

TLC- Total leukocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anemia of chronic disorder

The given clinical scenario and the investigation findings are suggestive of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is anemia of chronic disorder.

Anemia of chronic disorders more commonly presents as normochromic normocytic anemia that later develops into microcytic hypochromic anemia rarely. It is caused due to production of erythrocytes.

Anemia of chronic disease is anemia resulting due to chronic diseases which produce systemic inflammation. During chronic inflammation, inflammatory mediators like interleukin - 6 (IL-6) stimulate the production of hepcidin from the liver. Hepcidin is an acute phase reactant that inhibits ferroportin on macrophages and also decreases transport of iron from stores to developing RBC precursors. This results in decreased proliferation of erythroid progenitors due to impaired iron utilization.

Other options:

Option B: Thalassemia also presents as iron deficiency anemia but it does not have elevated luekocytosis.

Option C: Iron deficiency anemia also presents as microcytic hypochromic anemia. But since there is deficient iron, the serum ferritin level will also be low. This patient has normal serum ferritin and hence does not have iron deficiency anemia.

Note:

MCV/RBC count (Mentzer index) can also be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio.

Option D: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation in β-globin that creates sickle hemoglobin (HbS). It does not present as microcytic hypochromic anemia.
questions.learning: Anemia of chronic disorder — The given clinical scenario and the investigation findings are suggestive of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is anemia of chronic disorder.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with an enlarged inguinal lymph node. The most likely primary cause is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anal cancer

The most likely primary cause of an enlarged inguinal lymph node is anal cancer.

Lymphatics from the anal canal distal to the dentate line (anal margin) drains into the inguinal lymph nodes. Hence, anal cancer arising distal to dentate line can cause enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Lymphatics proximal to the dentate line (anal canal) drains into internal iliac lymph nodes through superior rectal lymphatics.

Option A: In testicular cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the paraaortic lymph nodes.

Option C: In sigmoid colon cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the regional lymph node and then to the central lymph node.

Option D: In prostate cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the:

• Lymph nodes beside the internal iliac vein and in the hollow of the sacrum
• External iliac lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Assertion: RMP is dependent on proteins and phosphate ions.
Reason: Diffusion potential can be calculated using Nernst Equation.

RMP- Resting membrane potential
options: The assertion is independently a true statement, but the reasons is independently a false statement.
The assertion is independently a false statement, but the reasons is independently a true statement.
Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion
Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion

Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion.

Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in the electrical potentials between the cytoplasm of the cell and the extracellular space. It represents an equilibrium situation where the concentration gradient of ions across the membrane is equal and opposite to the electrical gradients.

Resting membrane potential is primarily influenced by sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions, along with negatively charged intracellular proteins and organic phosphates. In neurons, the concentration of potassium is higher inside the cell, while sodium ions exhibit the opposite distribution. The establishment of this concentration difference is facilitated by the Na, K ATPase pump. Potassium ions passively move out of the cell, while sodium ions move into the cell.

The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation is utilized to calculate the resting membrane potential since multiple ions are involved. Among these ions, potassium, which has the greatest conductance across the membrane at rest, becomes the primary contributor to the resting membrane potential.

Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation

The Nernst equation establishes a connection between the diffusion potential and the ion concentration difference across a membrane. The magnitude of the Nernst potential is determined by the ratio of the ion concentrations on the two sides of the membrane.

Nernst equation :

EMF(millivolts) = [61/z] X log [Co / Ci]

• EMF = electromotive force (Nernst potential)
• z = charge of ion
• Co = concentration outside
• Ci = concentration inside

questions.text: How muscle spindle able to detect the length while muscle is contracting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nuclear bag fibers

The muscle spindle is a proprioceptive receptor that detects muscle length and the rate of change in length (stretch reflex).

Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers of two types:

• Nuclear bag fibers → detect dynamic changes in muscle length, especially during active contraction or rapid stretch.
• Nuclear chain fibers → detect static muscle length.

Mechanism during contraction:

• Gamma motor neurons stimulate intrafusal fibers to maintain spindle sensitivity while the muscle shortens.
• Nuclear bag fibers help the spindle continue sensing changes in muscle length even during contraction.

Other receptors:

• Golgi tendon organ senses muscle tension, not muscle length.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes memantine’s mechanism of action in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NMDA receptor antagonist

Memantine improves symptoms in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease by acting as a non-competitive NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist. It reduces excessive glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, which contributes to neuronal injury and cognitive decline, while preserving normal synaptic transmission.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition: Mechanism of donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which increase acetylcholine levels in the brain and are primarily used for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease.
• C. Blockade of A-beta amyloid: Mechanism of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab and donanemab, which target amyloid plaques.
• D. Dopamine D₂ receptor antagonism: Mechanism of antipsychotic drugs (e.g., haloperidol, risperidone); not used to treat the cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease.
questions.learning: NMDA receptor antagonist Memantine improves symptoms in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease by acting as a non-competitive NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about radiotherapy?
options: Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance
Vomiting is a late adverse reaction
Rapidly proliferating cells are most radioresistant
Radiation-induced skin changes is a reversible adverse effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance

The intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This is known as the inverse square law in radiotherapy.

Inverse square law - the intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This principle is unsuitable for large tumors and has potential risks of radiation exposure to medical staff.

Other options:

Option B: Vomiting can be an acute (early) adverse reaction to radiation therapy, occurring shortly after treatment.

Option C: Permanent non-dividing cells are more radioresistant than rapidly proliferating cells.

Option D: Not all the adverse effects of radiation therapy are reversible. Some of the adverse effects of radiation therapy, such as fibrosis, radiation-induced skin changes, late radiation enteritis, etc are irreversible.

questions.text: Which of the following methods of cervical ripening is a type of hygroscopic dilator?
options: Foley catheter at internal os of cervix
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracervical laminaria tent

Among the given methods of cervical ripening, the one which is a type of hygroscopic dilator is an intracervical laminaria tent.

Hygroscopic osmotic dilators are devices that draw water from cervical tissues and expand to gradually dilate the cervix. They expand to an ultimate diameter 3-4 times that of its dry state.

Laminaria tent is derived from various species of Laminaria algae that are harvested from the ocean floor. Synthetic dilators include Dilapan and Lamicel.

The image below shows Dilapan on the left and Laminaria tent on the right:

Pharmacological methods of cervical ripening:

Misoprostol at a dose of 25 μg is placed in the posterior fornix. Although it has increased efficacy, it is associated with a higher incidence of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) and uterine tachysystole, especially when used in higher doses.

Dinoprostone is the synthetic analog of PGE2, available in three forms, as a gel, as a time-release vaginal insert, and as a suppository. Of these, the first two forms are used in cervical ripening whereas suppository is used only in abortion

The gel form is available in a prefilled syringe for local application in the cervical canal. The dosage used per procedure is 0.5 mg. This procedure can be repeated for a maximum of 3 doses in 24 hours with a time interval of 6 hours between each administration. The vaginal insert has a dose of 10 mg of dinoprostone. 0.3 mg of the drug is released per hour. It is placed horizontally in the posterior fornix.

Monitoring uterine contraction and fetal heart rate is a must after each dose. Adverse effects of dinoprostone include uterine tachysystole (especially when the gel is used in labour that has started spontaneously).

Cervidil (Dinoprostone) vaginal insert:

Note: Dinoprostone, which is a synthetic analogue of PGE2, not to be confused with Dinoprost, is a natural PGF2-α preparation.

questions.text: Two weeks after undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplant for multiple myeloma, a 55- year-old man develops a severely pruritic rash, abdominal cramps, and profuse diarrhea. He appears lethargic. Physical examination shows yellow sclerae. There is a generalized maculopapular rash on his face, trunk, and lower extremities, and desquamation of both soles. Correct answer: A. Donor T cells in the graft

This patient has acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

• Immunocompetent donor T cells present in the graft recognize recipient (host) tissues as foreign.
• These donor T cells become activated and attack host organs.

Common target organs:

• Skin: maculopapular rash, desquamation
• Gastrointestinal tract: abdominal pain, diarrhea
• Liver: elevated liver enzymes, jaundice

Typically occurs within weeks after transplantation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought for a routine health check-up. Which developmental milestone is most commonly expected to be achieved at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.explanation: By 9 months of age, most infants have achieved the gross motor milestone of creeping well on their hands and knees. They are also beginning to pull themselves up to stand and typically demonstrate an immature pincer grasp. A mature grasp (Option A), specifically the ability to pick up small objects with precision, is typically achieved closer to 12 months. Hopping on one foot (Option C) is a complex gross motor skill that does not develop until approximately 4 years of age. Running steadily (Option D) is a milestone reached around 18 to 24 months as the child gains better coordination. Therefore, at the 9-month check-up, creeping is the most developmentally appropriate skill to expect. Other typical findings at this age include "waving bye-bye" and expressing stranger anxiety

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A lady presents with recurrent bluing of her hand and stretching of her skin. She also has difficulty in swallowing and lung lesions. What is the pattern of ANA and the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti-centromere pattern: Systemic sclerosis

Clinical and immunofluorescence patterns are suggestive of a diagnosis of Systemic sclerosis and Anti-centromere pattern in ANA.

The given clinical scenario featuring the recurrent bluing of hands(Raynaud phenomenon), difficulty swallowing (GERD), and tightening of the skin in the hands is suggestive of CREST syndrome/ limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, and anti-centromere antibodies are most specific for this disease.

CREST syndrome consists of the following:

• Calcinosis cutis
• Raynaud’s phenomenon
• Esophageal dysmotility
• Sclerodactyly
• Telangiectasia

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic autoimmune disease. Progressive fibrosis due to the deposition of extracellular matrix components in different tissues and organs is the prominent feature of SSc.

The characteristic features of SSc are vascular damage, inflammation, and the presence of specific autoantibodies.

SSc is classified into two based on the extent of skin involvement.

• Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis / CREST syndrome
• Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis

In limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), fibrosis in the skin of acral parts of the body, like the face and limbs (distal to elbow and knee), takes place. Skin fibrosis in limited type has a slow progression, but microcirculation disturbances like Raynaud's phenomenon start long before the skin symptoms and are associated with the involvement of the lungs and esophagus.

Since it has late and slow organ involvement, it is associated with a good prognosis with a 10-year survival of over 90%.

Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are present in 90 - 95% of cases with SSc.

Autoantibodies specific to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis include:

• Anti-centromere
• Anti-Th/To
• Anti-U1-RNP
• Anti-hUBF

Other options:

Option A: A speckled/granular pattern of staining is seen in systemic sclerosis due to antibodies against Scl-70, SLE, and Sjogren's syndrome. The image given below shows the speckled pattern of immunofluorescence.

Options C and D: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness. Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and lupus nephritis.ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, and anti-smith antibodies are positive in SLE. Homogenous or diffuse staining and peripheral staining patterns are most commonly seen in SLE.
questions.learning: Anti-centromere pattern: Systemic sclerosis Clinical and immunofluorescence patterns are suggestive of a diagnosis of Systemic sclerosis and Anti-centromere pattern in ANA.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with hearing loss in the left ear and episodic pulsatile tinnitus. On examination, there was a mass in the middle ear behind the tympanic membrane. A CT performed is as shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glomus jugulare

The given clinical vignette of a woman with hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus and examination suggesting a mass behind the tympanic membrane and CT image showing a mass in the region of jugular foramen makes Glomus Jugulare the likely diagnosis.

Glomus tumors are the most common benign tumors of the middle ear. The tumors comprise paraganglionic cells and arise from glomus bodies which resemble carotid bodies. Glomus bodies are present in the dome of the jugular bulb and on the promontory along the course of the tympanic branch of the IX cranial nerve.

They are most commonly seen in females between the ages of 40-50 years. They are very slow-growing, thus it may take years before changes in symptoms are appreciated. It follows the rule of 10s - 10% are familial, 10% are multicentric, and 10% are functional (secrete catecholamines).

Depending on the area from which it arises, glomus tumors are classified into two types:

• Glomus jugulare, arising from the dome of the jugular bulb
• Glomus tympanicum, arising from the promontory of the middle ear

The presentation of glomus tumors is as follows:

• Intratympanic presentation

• Progressive hearing loss
• Pulsatile tinnitus is synchronous with pulse and can be stopped by carotid pressure
• Otoscopy: red reflex through the intact tympanic membrane
• Rising sign when a tumor arises from the floor of the middle ear
• Pulsation or Brown sign: when the ear canal pressure is raised with Siegel's speculum the tumor pulsates and blanches. This reverses when pressure is released.

• Polyp presentation

• Profuse bleeding
• Otorrhea if there is a secondary infection
• Red vascular polyp filling the meatus that bleeds easily

• Cranial nerve palsies

• Dysphagia and hoarseness with unilateral paralysis of the soft palate, and pharynx due to IX and X
• Vocal cord paralysis due to X
• Weakness of the trapezius and sternomastoid muscles XI
• Atrophy of half of the tongue XII

• Audible bruit over the mastoid

They can be diagnosed by CT scan, MRI, four-vessel angiography, brain perfusion and flow studies, embolization, and biopsy. It is treated by surgery, radiation, embolization, or a combination of them. Phlep sign is seen in a CT scan of the glomus jugulare tumor. It is erosion of the normal crest of bone between the carotid canal and jugular foramen.

The following image shows the rising sun sign in the case of glomus jugulare.

Other options:

Option A: Glomus tympanicum is a close differential to the jugular tumor, however, it commonly arises from the promontory of the middle ear rather than the jugular bulb and does not show the Phlep sign and it is also found in relation to the temporal bone on CT.

Option B: Giant cell reparative granuloma accounts for 1–7% of all benign lesions of the jaw. It often arises in the maxilla followed by the mandible and affects children and young adults. It is usually a slow-growing lesion. The fast-growing lesions are rare and despite the innocent histological appearance, have an aggressive behavior mimicking a malignant lesion. The following image shows the CT of the reparative granuloma of the maxilla showing the extension of tumor mass over the pterygoid plates and infratemporal fossa.

Option D: Acoustic neuromas are noncancerous, usually slow-growing tumors that form along the vestibulocochlear nerve. They arise from Schwann cells. Schwannomas can occur on any cranial or peripheral nerve in the body, but in the brain, acoustic neuromas are the most common schwannomas. The following image depicts the classical ice cream cone appearance of acoustic neuroma on MRI.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During intercostal drain insertion, which anatomical location is considered the most appropriate for placing the chest tube?
options: Upper border of the lower rib
Lower border of the lower rib
Lower border of the upper rib
questions.explanation: The most critical anatomical consideration during the insertion of an intercostal tube drain is the location of the neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, and nerve). This bundle runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Therefore, to avoid catastrophic hemorrhage or nerve injury, the tube must be inserted by sliding over the upper border of the lower rib in the chosen intercostal space. Placing the tube near the lower border of the upper rib (Option C) would directly risk damaging these structures. The middle of the space (Option D) and the lower border of the lower rib (Option B) are less anatomically precise and do not offer the same safety margin. The standard insertion site is within the "safe triangle" bounded by the pectoralis major, the latissimus dorsi, and the 5th intercostal space. Adhering to this "upper border" rule is a fundamental surgical safety principle to minimize procedural morbidity
questions.learning: The most critical anatomical consideration during the insertion of an intercostal tube drain is the location of the neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, and nerve).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child with B/L sensorineural hearing loss was given hearing aids, which have not been beneficial. Which of the following is the next treatment option for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cochlear implant

The next treatment option for this child is a cochlear implant.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from hearing aid.

The principle of the surgery is to place the electrode array within the Scala Tympani Of Cochlea. Intact 8th nerve and the higher auditory pathway is a prerequisite for surgery. The facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach is the preferred surgical approach. Auditory brainstem implant is placed in the lateral recess of 4th ventricle

Pearl PF1581: Cochlear implant

A cochlear implant replaces the organ of Corti i.e. when hair cells of the organ of Corti are severely damaged these implants bypass it and directly stimulate the auditory nerve.

Indication: Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss i.e. > 70 dB.

Components:

Preoperative investigation: Complete audiological evaluation and HRCT and MRI (to detect the structure of cochlea, cochlear nerve and CNS abnormalities).

Surgical approach: Two surgical techniques to approach the cochlea for implantation are the facial recess approach (via facial recess) and the pericanal technique (via EAC).

Postoperatively: Activation of the device after 3-4 weeks and evaluation is by HRCT (MRI is contraindicated).

Contraindications:

* Absence of cochlea (Michel aplasia)

* Deafness due to absent cochlear nerve, lesions of cochlear nerve or lesions of the central auditory pathway
questions.learning: Cochlear implant — The next treatment option for this child is a cochlear implant. A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from hearing aid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The given image is of a person with a history of minor trauma with a piece of wood, 20 days back. His face is affected on the left side with facial swelling and orbital edema. CT scan revealed clear sinuses and the presence of subcutaneous nodules. Microscopy of the tissue sections was PAS-positive and stained positive with Grocott's methenamine silver stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phycomycosis

The history of facial swelling and orbital edema following trauma with wood and positive fungal stain (Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver) points toward phycomycosis (mucormycosis), a potentially invasive fungal infection.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis caused by various molds in the Mucorales order which are ubiquitous thermotolerant saprobes. These molds, including Rhizopus, Mucor, and Absidia, are common in the environment. The spores can be found in air and dust.

Mucormycosis can manifest as a localized cutaneous or subcutaneous infection in immunologically normal individuals after traumatic exposure to soil or vegetation. It is a fatal condition due to its angio-invasive nature. Lung involvement is common, and the infection primarily affects immunocompromised patients.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is frequently seen in individuals with diabetic ketoacidosis. It typically starts with eye and facial pain and may progress to orbital cellulitis, proptosis, and vision loss. A characteristic finding is a black necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity.

Diagnosis involves testing specimens and cultures. In exudate samples, wet preparations with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) reveal broad, ribbon-like hyphae. Tissue biopsy confirms the diagnosis by observing non-septate hyphae branching at right angles, characteristic of Mucorales like Rhizopus delemar.

Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick cottony, and fluffy surface.

Treatment is primarily with liposomal amphotericin B. Surgical debridement of the affected tissues and control of underlying predisposing cause is equally important.

Other options:

Option D: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibodies, which is the hallmark of the disease. IgG4-RD leads to fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Patients may present with Riedel's thyroiditis, autoimmune pancreatitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation, but not with ptosis. Diagnosis is confirmed through positive fibrosis and the presence of plasma cells on biopsy. Treatment with Rituximab is done.

Option C: Foreign body granulomas are due to inflammation induced by inert foreign bodies. These granulomas develop without T-cell-mediated immune responses. Sutures are a common site for their formation. The foreign material is at the center of the granuloma, surrounded by epithelioid cells and specific giant cells opposing the surface.

Option B: Midline lethal granuloma is characterized by necrotizing destruction and damage to the nose and other respiratory structures. It is rare and usually a diagnosis of exclusion. CT scans can detect the lesions associated with this condition. Negative c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) and fungal stain results contribute to the diagnosis.
questions.learning: Phycomycosis — The history of facial swelling and orbital edema following trauma with wood and positive fungal stain (Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver) points toward phycomycosis (mucormycosis), a potentially invasive fungal infection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient with a reduced food intake over the past few months now presents with hypoglycemia. What is the most likely cause of hypoglycemia in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired gluconeogenesis

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic presenting with hypoglycemia is suggestive of alcohol (ethanol) intoxication that inhibits the process of gluconeogenesis.

Alcohol is metabolized in the liver via the enzymes alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase. These reactions convert ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetate, using NAD⁺ as a cofactor and producing NADH. The excess NADH shifts the balance of metabolic processes, diverting key substrates (like pyruvate and oxaloacetate) away from gluconeogenesis, thus impairing the liver's ability to produce glucose.

The patient had decreased food intake over the past few months, leading to reduced dietary glucose consumption and increased reliance on the liver for blood glucose maintenance through gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. However, since alcohol inhibits these processes, it would further worsen hypoglycemia.

Other options:

Option A: Decreased glycogenolysis reduces the breakdown of glycogen into glucose, leading to impaired blood sugar regulation and potential hypoglycemia. This can result from enzyme deficiencies, liver dysfunction, or hormonal imbalances affecting glycogen metabolism.

Option C: Increased glycolysis accelerates the breakdown of glucose into pyruvate, leading to higher energy production in the form of ATP. This process can be upregulated in conditions like hypoxia, cancer, or insulin stimulation.

Option D: The HMP shunt is an alternative pathway to glycolysis and is used to produce ribose-5-phosphate and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH). It doesn't cause hypoglycemia.

Pearl PF1737: Reducing Equivalents and Their Uses

Reducing agents

Uses

NADPH

Lipid synthesis

Cholesterol synthesis

Fatty acid chain elongation

Cytochrome P450 hydroxylation of aromatic compounds, steroids, alcohols, and drugs

NADH

Metabolizes alcohol

Oxidative phosphorylation

β- Oxidation of fatty acid

Catalyzes reactions in muscle and liver cells

Electron Transport Chain

FADH2

Krebs cycle

Electron Transport Chain

Oxidative Phosphorylation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is seen in rickets?
questions.explanation: Rickets is a childhood skeletal disorder characterized by soft, weak bones, typically caused by a profound and prolonged deficiency of Vitamin D. Vitamin D is essential for the absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the gut; without it, these minerals cannot be properly deposited into the growing bone (mineralization). Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia. Vitamin B (Option B) is a complex of many vitamins, whose deficiencies cause various diseases like beriberi (B1) or pellagra (B3). Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, which affects collagen synthesis and leads to bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Children with rickets often present with "bow-legs," "knock-knees," and a "rachitic rosary" (swelling of the rib-cartilage junctions). Prevention involves adequate sunlight exposure and Vitamin D supplementation, which is now routinely recommended for breastfed infants

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient who has taken the first COVID vaccine comes for the second dose. An astute nurse noticed that the shoulder was flabby, flat, and was asymmetrical. There was an associated loss of contour of the shoulder joint. Injury to which of the structures might have resulted and was avoidable?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Axillary nerve

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of injury to axillary nerve which leads to deltoid muscle palsy.

The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid muscle. Iatrogenic injuries of the axillary nerve can occur due to incorrectly administered IM injection or while performing transaxillary operations on the shoulder with lateral deltoid-splitting incisions. But, note that this nerve is commonly injured during shoulder dislocation (most commonly anterior type) or fractures of the humeral neck as both the nerve and the posterior circumflex vessels (Option-B) pass horizontally and posterior to the neck of the humerus.

Injury to the axillary nerve can lead to:

• Weakness of abduction and lateral rotation of the arm
• Retropulsion (extension of the shoulder with the arm abducted to 90 degrees) is impossible.
• Atrophy of the Deltoid muscle leading to the loss of muscle contours of the shoulder
• Loss of sensation in the Regimental badge area

Note:

Upper (superior) lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (Option-C) that innervates the skin over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area). Thus, this is not the best of the given four options.

The images below show the Seargent/regimental badge sign and the various anatomical structures that can be appreciated in the transverse section of the shoulder joint respectively.

Vaccine administration in the deltoid can sometimes injure the axillary and the radial nerve.
questions.learning: Axillary nerve — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of injury to axillary nerve which leads to deltoid muscle palsy. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid muscle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old girl who is not attending school presents for a health checkup, and her hemoglobin level is low. Which government program is most likely to provide significant health benefits for her condition?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is a comprehensive child health initiative of the Government of India aimed at the early identification and management of the “4 Ds”: Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays (including disabilities). The program covers all children from birth to 18 years of age, including out-of-school children, making it especially relevant for vulnerable populations. In this case, the 10-year-old girl with anemia falls under the category of “Deficiencies”, one of the core components of RBSK. Therefore, she would be screened and managed by RBSK mobile health teams, with referral to District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs) when required, ensuring free treatment and follow-up care. Janani Suraksha Yojana (Option B) focuses on maternal health and institutional deliveries. The Mid-Day Meal Scheme (Option C) benefits only school-going children and does not cover out-of-school children. Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (Option D) is limited to newborn care and resuscitation. Thus, RBSK is the most appropriate program, as it ensures universal child health screening and management, particularly for nutritional deficiencies like anemia, regardless of school enrollment status

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not the mechanism of action of progesterone only pills?
options: Kills the sperms in the cervical canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kills the sperms in the cervical canal

Minipills or progesterone-only pills (POP) do not kill sperm in the cervical canal. Progesterone-only pills act by thickening the cervical mucus (the main mechanism of all POPs except cerazette) that inhibits penetration of sperms, inhibiting tubal motility, and suppressing ovulation.

Other advantages of POPs include a reduction in the incidence of pelvic inflammatory diseases and sexually transmitted diseases (due to thickened cervical mucus).

Due to the inhibition of tubal motility, the absolute risk of all pregnancies including ectopic pregnancy decreases, while the relative risk of ectopic pregnancy increases. But a previous history of ectopic pregnancy is not a contraindication for POP.

POPs do not affect clotting, lipid metabolism, and carbohydrate metabolism. So they can safely be used by women who are obese, breastfeeding, hypertensive, have SLE or a history of thromboembolism, diabetic with vascular disease. Significant adverse effects of POPs are irregular bleeding (mostly scanty), and secondary amenorrhea after longtime usage as it causes endometrial atrophy.

Contraindications for POPs include undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, pregnancy, known or suspected breast cancer, and benign or malignant liver tumors.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), how is maternal death defined?
options: Death from full-term pregnancy within 24 hours of delivery
Death during pregnancy and within 1 year after delivery
Death during pregnancy and within 6 weeks of delivery
questions.explanation: The WHO defines maternal death as the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days (6 weeks) of termination of pregnancy. This death can be from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes. Option A is too non-specific regarding the time frame. Option B incorrectly limits the definition to 24 hours post-delivery. Option C describes "late maternal death," which occurs between 42 days and one year after delivery, but this is a separate statistical category. The 42-day window (6 weeks) is critical for public health monitoring, as it covers the puerperium period where pregnancy-related complications like sepsis or hemorrhage are most likely to occur. Accurately classifying these deaths allows countries to measure their Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) and evaluate the quality of their obstetric care systems

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient undergoing anticancer therapy is found to have neutropenia on blood examination, increasing the risk of infection. Which drug is most effective for managing this complication?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia is a common and dangerous side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy, leaving patients vulnerable to life-threatening infections. To manage neutropenia and stimulate the production of white blood cells, the drug of choice is Filgrastim. Filgrastim is a recombinant human Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor (G-CSF). It works by binding to specific receptors on hematopoietic progenitor cells in the bone marrow, stimulating their proliferation and differentiation into functional neutrophils. Romiplostim (Option A) is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist used to increase platelet counts in ITP. Oprelvekin (Option B) is a recombinant IL-11 also used to stimulate platelets. Epoetin alfa (Option D) is recombinant erythropoietin used to stimulate red blood cell production to treat anemia. In clinical practice, prophylactic Filgrastim is often given to patients receiving high-risk chemotherapy to reduce the duration of neutropenia and the incidence of febrile neutropenia episodes. Understanding these specific growth factors is essential for managing the hematological toxicities associated with modern cancer treatment
questions.learning: Neutropenia is a common and dangerous side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy, leaving patients vulnerable to life-threatening infections. To manage neutropenia and stimulate the production of white blood cells, the drug of choice is Filgrastim.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Allopurinol and vitamin C are used to reduce uric acid levels and prevent gout-like symptoms. Which of the following factors plays a key role in the maturation of collagen?
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is essential for the maturation of collagen. It acts as a vital cofactor for the enzymes prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the procollagen chain. This post-translational modification is necessary for the formation of stable hydrogen bonds that hold the collagen triple helix together. A deficiency in Vitamin C leads to scurvy, characterized by fragile connective tissue, bleeding gums, and poor wound healing. Proline (Option A) is an amino acid component of collagen, but not the "maturing" agent. Copper and zinc (Option B) are cofactors for other enzymes (like lysyl oxidase for cross-linking), but the primary "maturation" step of hydroxylation is Vitamin C-dependent. Phenylalanine (Option D) is unrelated to collagen synthesis. In the context of the question, Vitamin C serves dual roles: aiding collagen health and facilitating the excretion of uric acid. Thus, ascorbic acid is the indispensable factor for collagen structural integrity
questions.learning: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is essential for the maturation of collagen. It acts as a vital cofactor for the enzymes prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the procollagen chain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vasculitis does not involve medium-sized arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis

Vasculitides are classified according to the predominant size of the blood vessels involved. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis, whereas Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) and Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) primarily involve medium-sized arteries, and Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) predominantly affects small vessels but may occasionally involve medium-sized arteries.

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is an immune complex– mediated small-vessel vasculitis involving postcapillary venules, characterized histologically by neutrophilic infiltration with leukocytoclasia (nuclear debris) and palpable purpura.

Key vessel involvement:

• PAN → Medium-sized muscular arteries (spares pulmonary arteries)
• Buerger disease → Small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities
• GPA → Predominantly small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), but medium arteries may also be involved
• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis → Small vessels only

| Vessel size | Entities

| ----------- | --------

| Large | Takayasu, GCA

| Medium | PAN, Kawasaki

| Small — ANCA-associated | GPA, MPA, EGPA

| Small — immune complex | Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, IgA vasculitis (HSP), cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM, hypocomplementaemic urticarial

| Variable vessel | Behçet, Cogan
