questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy visits a fish farming area and accidentally ingests a white, odorless substance. Soon afterward, he develops an exaggerated adverse reaction to a medication he is taking. Which compound is most likely responsible for enhancing the toxic effects of the drug?
questions.explanation: Rotenone is a naturally occurring, white, odorless compound derived from the roots of several tropical plants and is commonly used as a broad-spectrum insecticide and piscicide (fish poison) in fish farming areas. Mechanistically, rotenone is a potent and specific inhibitor of Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. By blocking the transfer of electrons from iron-sulfur centers to ubiquinone, it halts ATP production and generates reactive oxygen species, leading to severe cellular oxidative stress and potentially enhancing the toxicity of other medications metabolized through similar pathways. Antimycin A (Option C) is a piscicide that inhibits Complex III, but it is less commonly described in this clinical accidental ingestion context. BAL (Option B) is a heavy metal chelator. Alkyl guanidines (Option A) can also inhibit Complex I but are not standard environmental toxins found in fish farms. Rotenone exposure is also a significant concern in neurological research as it is used to induce parkinsonian-like symptoms in animal models due to its high toxicity to dopaminergic neurons
questions.learning: Rotenone is a naturally occurring, white, odorless compound derived from the roots of several tropical plants and is commonly used as a broad-spectrum insecticide and piscicide (fish poison) in fish farming areas.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a 12-year-old girl who has reached Tanner stage 4 for breast development and pubic hair growth, which of the following pubertal changes is not exclusively dependent on estrogen?
questions.explanation: Puberty involves two distinct hormonal events: gonadarche (gonadal activation) and adrenarche (adrenal activation). Breast development and the menstrual cycle are primarily driven by ovarian estrogen. Estrogen is responsible for the maturation of the reproductive tract, including vaginal cornification (Option A), cervical mucus production (Option C), and the proliferation of the endometrium leading to menstruation (Option D). However, pubic and axillary hair growth (Option B) is NOT dependent on estrogen; it is driven by androgens secreted by the adrenal glands and ovaries. This process is known as adrenarche and can occur independently of the estrogen-driven thelarche (breast development). Therefore, in a girl with clinical signs of both pathways (breast and hair development), the hair growth is the only component listed that is strictly androgen-mediated rather than estrogen-mediated
questions.learning: Puberty involves two distinct hormonal events: gonadarche (gonadal activation) and adrenarche (adrenal activation). Breast development and the menstrual cycle are primarily driven by ovarian estrogen.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with non-blanching rashes over the legs and buttocks, joint pain, abdominal pain with vomiting, and blood in the stools. Investigations reveal a normal platelet count, while urinalysis shows marked hematuria (+++) with mild proteinuria (+). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a palpable (non-blanching) purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia (joint pain), and gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, bloody stool) in a young child is pathognomonic for Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP). HSP is an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. A critical diagnostic clue provided is the normal platelet count, which distinguishes the purpura of HSP from thrombocytopenic conditions like ITP (Option C). The presence of hematuria and proteinuria confirms the associated renal involvement, known as HSP nephritis. SLE (Option A) and PAN (Option D) can cause vasculitis but are much rarer in children and typically present with a different constellation of multi-organ findings and laboratory markers (like ANA or ANCA). Therefore, the classic clinical tetrad of rash, joints, gut, and kidney in a pediatric patient definitively identifies HSP
questions.learning: The combination of a palpable (non-blanching) purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia (joint pain), and gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, bloody stool) in a young child is pathognomonic for Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In ocular surface examination and dry eye staining, which of the following order of dyes is used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorescein ->Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green

Amongst the given options, the better order of dyes to pick for use in ocular surface examination and dry eye staining is Fluorescein -> Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green.

Fluorescein staining of the cornea is carried out with a disposable autoclaved filter paper strip impregnated with the dye. The denuded epithelial area seen in corneal abrasions or ulcers appears brilliant green when stained with fluorescein. Under a cobalt blue light, the stained area appears opaque green.

A corneal abrasion highlighted with fluorescein staining is shown below.

Rose Bengal stains dead and devitalized cells including mucous strands on ocular surface. The dye causes a stinging and burning sensation soon after instillation.

Lissamine green stains dead and degenerate cells, but does not stain healthy epithelial cells. It is used to diagnose ocular surface disease. It stains the conjunctiva. It does not cause stinging like Rose Bengal. The Green staining is best observed two minutes after instillation.

The image below shows the lissamine staining of the eye.

Note: The answer to this question is controversial and there is no clearcut evidence based information on the sequence. The above mentioned answer is the best amongst the given options based on consensus.
questions.learning: Fluorescein ->Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green Amongst the given options, the better order of dyes to pick for use in ocular surface examination and dry eye staining is Fluorescein -> Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever, lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge 3 days after undergoing an abortion by an unlicensed practitioner. On examination, she is febrile, tachycardic, and has marked uterine tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Septic abortion

Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and/or surrounding tissues, most commonly following an unsafe abortion performed under unsterile conditions. It is a gynecological emergency that requires prompt recognition and treatment.

• Risk factors: Unsafe abortion, retained products of conception, instrumentation by an untrained person.
• Clinical features:

• Fever
• Lower abdominal pain
• Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
• Vaginal bleeding
• Uterine tenderness
• Tachycardia ± hypotension/septic shock

• Common organisms: Polymicrobial infection (E. coli, anaerobes, Streptococci, Staphylococci, Clostridium).

Management

• Immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

• e.g., Clindamycin + Gentamicin ± Ampicillin (or equivalent broad-spectrum regimen)

• IV fluids and hemodynamic stabilization
• Evacuation of retained products after antibiotics are initiated and the patient is stabilized
• Monitor for complications such as septic shock, DIC, and pelvic abscess.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Incomplete abortion: Vaginal bleeding with retained products but no signs of systemic infection.
• C. Threatened abortion: Bleeding with a closed cervix and a viable pregnancy.
• D. Missed abortion: Retained nonviable fetus with minimal symptoms, typically no fever or foul-smelling discharge.
questions.learning: Septic abortion Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and/or surrounding tissues, most commonly following an unsafe abortion performed under unsterile conditions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a household survey, a family includes a 35-year-old man, his wife who is 6 weeks pregnant, and their 3-year-old child, along with the temporary stay of the man’s brother and sister-in-law during winter vacation. How should this household be classified?
questions.explanation: In sociology and public health demography, a Nuclear family is strictly defined as a household consisting of a married couple and their own unmarried children living together. This household includes the man, his wife, and their 3-year-old child. The temporary presence of the man’s brother and his wife for a winter vacation does not change the core classification, as they are not permanent residents of the household. A Joint family (Option A) consists of multiple generations and/or multiple married siblings and their families living together as a single permanent unit. An Extended family (Option C) includes other relatives beyond the nuclear core who live permanently in the household. A Third generation family (Option D) specifically includes grandparents, parents, and children. Categorizing family types is essential for assessing social support networks and health risks. Because the brother's family is only visiting, the primary sociological structure remains that of a nuclear unit, focusing on the parental pair and their child
questions.learning: In sociology and public health demography, a Nuclear family is strictly defined as a household consisting of a married couple and their own unmarried children living together.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is ECG change associated with the use of anti-tubercular drug bedaquiline?
questions.explanation: Bedaquiline is a critical newer drug used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its most significant and life-threatening adverse effect is QT interval prolongation on the ECG. This prolongation increases the risk of Torsades de Pointes, a potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmia. PR interval prolongation (Option B) relates to AV block. QRS widening (Option C) occurs with bundle branch blocks or hyperkalemia. ST-segment elevation (Option D) is the hallmark of acute myocardial infarction. Because of this risk, patients on bedaquiline must undergo regular ECG monitoring, especially if they are also taking other QT-prolonging drugs like moxifloxacin or clofazimine. Clinicians must be prepared to stop the medication if the QTc exceeds . This pharmacological safety requirement is a major focus in MDR-TB clinics to ensure that the benefits of treatment outweigh the cardiac risks
questions.learning: Bedaquiline is a critical newer drug used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its most significant and life-threatening adverse effect is QT interval prolongation on the ECG.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Koebner's phenomenon is seen in all of the following, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpes

Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in herpes.

Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma. If the same response is seen from the spread of an infective agent ( like molluscum contagiosum, viral warts), it's called pseudo-Koebner’s phenomenon.

Any of the following can elicit an isomorphic response: physical trauma, including friction, pressure, incision and laceration, skin grafting, bites, vaccination skin tests, burns, freezing, and ultraviolet (UV) and ionizing radiation.

It is seen commonly associated with psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Other associated disorders include Darrier’s disease, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen nitidus, DLE, necrobiosis lipoidica, and Grzybowski syndrome.
questions.learning: Herpes Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in herpes. Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old hypertensive male patient was prescribed hydrochlorothiazide and he developed fatigue and hypokalemia. Which of the following medications could be introduced instead of thiazide diuretics to prevent potassium depletion in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amiloride

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic and can causes hypokalemia. Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that can be used in this patient to prevent further potassium loss.

Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in collecting tubules. Therefore, it reduces sodium retention and potassium wasting.

Other options:

Furosemide is a loop diuretic and acts by inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl- transporter in the ascending loop of Henle. Used in cases of acute pulmonary edema, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, and hypertension.

Adenosine is used for its antiarrhythmic properties, particularly in the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). It is fast-acting and has a short half-life. Adenosine does not directly influence potassium levels or diuresis.

Acetazolamide: Acetazolamide belongs to the class of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and functions as a diuretic by inhibiting bicarbonate ion reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron. While acetazolamide may induce mild potassium depletion as a potential side effect, it is not typically utilized to counteract the potassium-depleting effects associated with thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide.
questions.learning: Amiloride Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic and can causes hypokalemia. Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that can be used in this patient to prevent further potassium loss.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Match the following :

Section A
Section B

1. Yolk sac tumor
A. LDH

2. Dysgerminoma
B. Beta-hCG

3. Choriocarcinoma
C. AFP

4. Epithelial cell tumor
D. CA-125

LDH - Lactate dehydrogenase

HCG - Human chorionic gonadotropin

AFP - Alpha fetoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D

Option B represents the correct answer. 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D

Ovarian tumors
Tumor marker

1. Yolk sac tumor
C. AFP

2. Dysgerminoma
A. LDH

3. Choriocarcinoma
B. Beta-HCG

4. Epithelial cell tumor
D. Ca-125

Endodermal sinus tumor/yolk sac tumor is a type of ovarian germ cell tumor that is seen in premenarchal girls. Schiller-Duval bodies are pathognomonic on histopathology. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is commonly produced by this tumor and is used as a tumor marker.

Dysgerminona is a type of germ cell tumor and it corresponds to the seminoma of the testis. It does not secrete either male or female sex hormones. It secretes placental alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and β-hCG. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is usually used in monitoring individuals or disease recurrence.

Choriocarcinoma is a type of mixed germ cell tumor. It is highly vascular. Histologically, the tumor shows syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts. It secretes large quantities of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) hormone, which is used as a tumor marker in the diagnosis and management of the tumor.

Malignant epithelial cell tumors of the ovary secrete CA-125. It is a glycoprotein and surface cell antigen which is secreted by malignant epithelial tumors of the ovary. A level of more than 35 U/mL suggests a malignant and residual tumor and indicates the need for chemotherapy. CA-125 is also raised in abdominal tuberculosis and endometriosis.
questions.learning: 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D Option B represents the correct answer. 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D Ovarian tumors Tumor marker 1.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the deformity depicted in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Boutonnière deformity

The image shows flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. This deformity is known as Boutonnière deformity seen in rheumatoid arthritis.

Rheumatoid Arthritis :

It is a chronic inflammatory disease. Its incidence increases between 25 and 55 years of age.

Signs and symptoms -

* Swelling and pain of the small joints of the hands initially(spares DIP joint)

* Morning stiffness

* Swan-neck deformity(hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint), Boutonnière deformity(flexion of the PIP joint with hyperextension of the DIP joint), or Z-line deformity(subluxation of the first MCP joint with hyperextension of the first interphalangeal (IP) joint )

* Ulnar deviation of fingers

* Constitutional findings such as fever, weight loss, etc

* Monoarthritis of large joints can occur later

* Tenosynovitis of palm(trigger finger0

* Atlantoaxial joint involvement

Joints commonly affected in Rheumatoid Arthritis: (bilateral and symmetrically involved)

* MCP joints

* Wrists

* PIP joints

* MTP joints

* Atlantoaxial joint

Diagnosis is made with clinical signs and symptoms with corroboration from lab and imaging findings.

* Anti-CCP, RF, and synovial fluid analysis are important lab investigations.

* X-ray findings show - soft tissue swelling, joint space narrowing, periarticular osteopenia, and bony erosions

Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

* DMARDs (Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs) are the mainstay of treatment.

* Methotrexate is the drug of choice in patients with RA. It can be used alone (in low disease activity) or with a 3-drug combination (in high disease activity) with other DMARDs such as hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide (reserve drug).

* It is a folic acid analong, Inhibits dihydrofolate reductas. Causes reversible myelosuppression

* Leucovorin is used to manage myelosuppression

* Can cause pulmonary fibrosis

* Escalation with triple therapy involves - methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine

* Glucocorticoids

Other extra-articular manifestations are:

* Sjogren's syndrome

* Pericarditis, Mitral regurgitation

* Pleuritis, Interstitial Lung disease

* Vasculitis

* Felty's syndrome

* Diffuse large B cell lymphoma

The image below shows extraarticular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis -

Pearl PF0401: Deformities in rheumatoid arthritis

Boutonnière deformity: Flexion of the PIP joint with hyperextension of the DIP joint.

Swan-neck deformity: Hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint.

Z line deformity: Subluxation of the 1st MCP joint with hyperextension of the 1st IP joint.

Piano-key movement of the ulnar styloid.

Trigger finger due to flexor tendon synovitis.

Pearl PF0403: Most commons conditions in Rheumatoid Arthritis

M/C extra-articular manifestation
Subcutaneous nodules

M/C pulmonary manifestation
Pleuritis

M/C cardiac involvement
Pericarditis

M/C valvular lesion
Mitral regurgitation

M/C hematologic abnormality
Normochromic, normocytic anemia

M/C part of the spine involved
Cervical spine

M/C type of lymphoma
Diffuse large B cell lymphoma

M/C cause of death
Cardiovascular disease

Pearl PF0404: Important drugs for rheumatoid arthritis

NSAIDs - Analgesic and anti-inflammatory, used as adjunctive agents for the management of uncontrollable symptoms and useful in an acute flare.

Glucocorticoids - Used during an acute flare for rapid disease control and as initial therapy before the onset of the effect of DMARDs. Chronic administration of low doses is needed to control disease in patients with inadequate response to DMARDs.

* Prednisolone- oral

* Triamcinolone - intraarticular

DMARDs - disease-modifying anti-rheumatoid drugs

Conventional DMARDs:

* Methotrexate (MTX): It is an antifolate drug. The DMARD of choice and the anchor drug for combination therapy. Regular LFT monitoring is required.

* Hydroxychloroquine: It used as monotherapy for early and mild disease and in combination with other DMARDs for severe cases.

* Sulfasalazine: A salicylate. It reduces the radiographic progression of the disease.

* Leflunomide: A pyrimidine synthase inhibitor used as an alternative to MTX.

Biologicals:

* TNF-α antagonists: Used in combination with MTX. Has a risk of serious bacterial infections, opportunistic fungal infection & reactivation of latent TB. The TNF-α inhibitors are adalimumab, golimumab, etanercept, infliximab, and certolizumab.

* Abatacept: A T-cell costimulation inhibitor, used in combination with MTX, leflunomide, etc.

* Rituximab: An anti-CD20 antibody. Used in refractory disease in combination with MTX.

* Anakinra: An IL-1 receptor antagonist. It should not be combined with an anti-TNF alpha.

* IL-6 receptor antagonists: Tocilizumab and sarilumab are used as monotherapy or combination therapy in moderate to severe disease.

Small molecules: Janus kinase inhibitors: Tofacitinib, barcitinib, and upadacitinib are used as monotherapy or combination therapy.
questions.learning: Boutonnière deformity — The image shows flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: About two-thirds of stroke cases in a community are due to hypertension and could be prevented if hypertension were controlled. This is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Population Attributable Risk

Population Attributable Risk (PAR) estimates the proportion of disease in the entire population that is attributable to a specific risk factor. It represents the potential reduction in disease burden if the risk factor were completely eliminated, making it a valuable measure for public health planning and preventive strategies.

• The statement refers to all stroke cases in the community and indicates that two-thirds could be prevented if hypertension were controlled.
• This describes the impact of eliminating a risk factor at the population level, which is the definition of Population Attributable Risk (PAR).

Why not the other options?

• A. Relative Risk (RR): Measures the strength of association between exposure and disease in exposed versus unexposed individuals.
• B. Attributable Risk (AR): Measures the excess risk among exposed individuals attributable to the exposure.
• C. Odds Ratio (OR): Measures the association between exposure and disease, mainly in case-control studies.
questions.learning: Population Attributable Risk Population Attributable Risk (PAR) estimates the proportion of disease in the entire population that is attributable to a specific risk factor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Congenital lactic acidosis is seen due to a defect in which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Congenital lactic acidosis is seen due to a defect in pyruvate dehydrogenase.

The major source of acetyl CoA for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA)cycle is the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by the multienzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC). The PDHC is a protein aggregate of multiple copies of three enzymes, pyruvate decarboxylase (E1), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3). Each catalyzes a part of the overall reaction.

A deficiency of the E1 component of the PDHC is the most common biochemical cause of congenital lactic acidosis. The deficiency results in a decreased ability to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA, causing pyruvate to be shunted to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase. This creates particular problems for the brain, which relies on the TCA cycle for most of its energy and is particularly sensitive to acidosis. Symptoms include neurodegeneration, muscle spasticity, and, in the neonatal-onset form, early death. The inheritance pattern is X- linked dominant, with both males and females affected. Although there is no proven treatment for PDHC deficiency, dietary restriction of carbohydrates and supplementation with thiamine may reduce symptoms in select patients.

Other options :

Option B - Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency results in maple syrup urine disease. There is defective oxidative decarboxylation of leucine, isoleucine and valine. The disease is characterized by feeding problems, ketoacidosis, changes in muscle tone, and coma.

Option C -  Defective transketolase is a rare disorder of pentose phosphate metabolism with symptoms apparent in infancy including developmental delay and intellectual disability, delayed or absent speech, short stature, and congenital heart defects.

Option D -  Isocitrate dehydrogenase is an enzyme of the TCA cycle which converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. Defects in this enzyme are linked to carcinogenesis.
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase Congenital lactic acidosis is seen due to a defect in pyruvate dehydrogenase. The major source of acetyl CoA for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA)cycle is the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by the multienzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with malignancy develops humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. Arrange the following steps in the appropriate sequence of management. 1. IV saline hydration to promote calciuresis 2. Bisphosphonate therapy 3. Loop diuretics after hydration 4. Find the source of exogenous ca
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4, 1, 3, 2

Hypercalcemia of malignancy is a medical emergency. Initial management focuses on eliminating factors that worsen hypercalcemia, restoring intravascular volume, promoting renal calcium excretion, and inhibiting bone resorption.

The correct sequence of management is:

1. Stop external calcium intake and discontinue drugs that aggravate hypercalcemia (e.g., thiazides, vitamin D supplements, lithium).
2. IV normal saline hydration to correct dehydration and enhance urinary calcium excretion.
3. Loop diuretics (only after adequate hydration and if clinically indicated) to further increase calciuresis.
4. IV bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid, pamidronate) to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and provide sustained calcium reduction.

Why not the other options?

• Hydration must precede loop diuretics to avoid worsening volume depletion.
• Bisphosphonates are not immediate-acting and should be administered after initial stabilization with hydration.
questions.learning: 4, 1, 3, 2 Hypercalcemia of malignancy is a medical emergency. Initial management focuses on eliminating factors that worsen hypercalcemia, restoring intravascular volume, promoting renal calcium excretion, and inhibiting bone resorption.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What joint is present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synchondrosis

The joint present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone is called synchondrosis.

Synchondrosis refers to the primary cartilaginous joints in which the advancing areas of ossification are separated by hyaline cartilage. They are temporary joints and are associated with growth. Hyaline cartilage has the ability to ossify with age, thus making these joints undergo synostosis (fusion) once the growth is complete. An example of this type of joint is the epiphyseal plate between the epiphysis and diaphysis of long bones

Structurally, joints are classified as fibrous joints, cartilaginous joints, and synovial joints (see the table). Sutures, syndesmosis, and gomphosis are fibrous joints. Symphysis and synchondrosis are types of cartilaginous joints.

Type
Subtypes

Fibrous joints
Sutures
Syndesmosis
Gomphosis

Cartilaginous joints
Primary cartilaginous joints (or synchondrosis)
Secondary cartilaginous joints (or symphysis)

Synovial joints
Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints
Sellar or saddle joints
Condylar or bicondylar joints
Ellipsoid joints
Hinge joints
Pivot or trochoid joints
Plane joints
questions.learning: Synchondrosis — The joint present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone is called synchondrosis. Synchondrosis refers to the primary cartilaginous joints in which the advancing areas of ossification are separated by hyaline cartilage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents to OPD with low backache. His PSA level are 100ng/ml. Which of the following drug is indicated for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goserelin

The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA levels are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

Androgen deprivation therapy is the primary medical therapy for prostate cancer. The drugs approved for this indication include leuprolide, goserelin, histrelin, buserelin, and triptorelin.

The agonist action of the GnRH analogues causes increased testosterone production, causing a tumour flare. It can be prevented by concomitant administration of an androgen receptor antagonist such as flutamide, bicalutamide, or nilutamide until downregulation of testosterone is complete.

The combined androgen deprivation therapy with continuous GnRH agonist and an androgen receptor antagonist is as effective as surgical castration in reducing the levels of serum testosterone and its effects.

Other options:

Option A: Somatostatin analogs acts as growth hormone antagonist and are used in the treatment of acromegaly, gigantism, acute control of bleeding from esophageal varices.

Option B: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analog used in the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome.

Option D: Anabolic steroids like testosterone are used to treat osteoporotic bone pain and counteract the effects of long-term corticosteroid use.
questions.learning: Goserelin — The clinical features and investigations showing elevated PSA levels are suggestive of prostate cancer. Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In which condition is excessive urinary excretion of 5- hydroxy indole acetic acid seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carcinoid syndrome

Excessive urinary excretion of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is seen in carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is marked by symptoms of bronchospasm, cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. It occurs due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism by tumors commonly in the small intestine, liver and lungs. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA.
questions.learning: Carcinoid syndrome Excessive urinary excretion of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is seen in carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome is marked by symptoms of bronchospasm, cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which type of graph is used to illustrate studies on healthcare and disease prevalence in a population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ishikawa diagram/Fish bone diagram

The Kaoru Ishikawa (fish-bone) diagram is used to systematically analyse and illustrate the multiple determinants and contributing factors affecting health outcomes and disease prevalence in a population.

The structure resembles a fish skeleton:

• Head of fish → problem or outcome
• Bones → major categories of causes
• Smaller branches → contributing factors

In public health research, it helps map biological, environmental, social, and health-system factors influencing disease burden.

Bar diagrams and histograms display data distribution, while regression models are analytical tools rather than illustrative diagrams.

A. Bar diagram- Bar diagrams show comparisons between categories, such as disease rates across regions.

B. Histogram- Histograms display frequency distribution of continuous variables.

Example: age distribution of patients.

C. Multiple regression model- This is a statistical analysis technique, not a graphical representation.
questions.learning: Ishikawa diagram/Fish bone diagram — The Kaoru Ishikawa (fish-bone) diagram is used to systematically analyse and illustrate the multiple determinants and contributing factors affecting health outcomes and disease prevalence in a population.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common side effect she is likely to experience following the insertion?
questions.explanation: The Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. However, users frequently experience specific side effects. The most common side effect leading to the removal of the device is abnormal vaginal bleeding (Option D), which can manifest as heavier or longer menstrual periods (menorrhagia) or intermenstrual spotting. Pain (Option C), such as pelvic cramps, is the second most common side effect . While pelvic infection (Option B) (PID) and ectopic pregnancy (Option A) are serious potential complications, their overall incidence is significantly lower than the occurrence of bleeding. Most bleeding issues are mild and resolve within the first few months after insertion, but they remain the primary reason for patient dissatisfaction. Clinicians should counsel patients about these expected changes to improve compliance. Therefore, increased menstrual bleeding is the most frequent adverse outcome of IUCD use
questions.learning: The Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. However, users frequently experience specific side effects.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn, born to a diabetic mother, presents after 24 hours of life with a blood glucose level of 35 mg/dL. The baby is asymptomatic. What is the next best step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose

In an asymptomatic newborn with hypoglycemia (<45 mg/dL), the first-line management is to initiate breastfeeding or provide expressed breast milk, followed by reassessment of glucose levels.

Infants of diabetic mothers are at a high risk of developing neonatal hypoglycemia. This is particularly applicable after the initial 2–3 hours of life. Blood sample is collected by heel prick. Babies showing plasma glucose <40 mg/dL on a reagent strip should be treated for hypoglycemia. Since reagent strips have high false-positive rates, a confirmation of hypoglycemia by a lab test is recommended.

Stepwise Management of Neonatal Hypoglycemia

* Initial Screening & Feeding

*

* All infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) and other at-risk babies should be screened within 30 minutes of the first feed.

* Feeding should begin within 1 hour after birth.

* The target blood glucose is ≥40 mg/dL before feeds during the first 48 hours of life.

* Treatment is indicated if glucose <47 mg/dL in asymptomatic infants.

* First-Line Therapy for Asymptomatic Hypoglycemia

* Feeding is the initial treatment for asymptomatic hypoglycemia.

* Options include breastfeeding, formula, or oral gavage feeds.

* Dextrose gel can be used as a prophylactic alternative, but early oral feeds are equally effective.

* Recurrent or Persistent Hypoglycemia

* If hypoglycemia persists despite feeding, repeat feeds or IV glucose may be required.

* Infants with glucose <25 mg/dL in the first 4 hours after birth or <35 mg/dL between 4–24 hours should be started on IV glucose therapy, especially if symptomatic.

* IV Glucose Therapy

* Give a 200 mg/kg dextrose bolus (approximately 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose).

* To avoid a recurrence, administer glucose continuously via intravenous infusion (IV) at a rate of 4–8 mg/kg/min.

* Hypertonic (25%) glucose bolus injections should be avoided as they can result in rebound hypoglycemia from hyperinsulinemia.

questions.text: A newborn presents with proteinuria, low–molecular-weight proteins in urine, and vitamin D deficiency despite normal intake. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in the LRP2 gene. Which of the following proteins is most likely dysfunctional in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Megalin

The LRP2 gene encodes megalin, a multiligand endocytic receptor located on the apical membrane of proximal convoluted tubule (PCT).

Megalin is responsible for reabsorption of:

• Low–molecular-weight proteins
• Vitamin D–binding protein (25-OH vitamin D complex)
• Other filtered proteins
• Retinol-binding protein

Mutation leads to impaired proximal tubular protein reabsorption → low–molecular-weight proteinuria and vitamin D deficiency despite adequate intake.

Why not other options:

A. Cubilin: Different gene (CUBN), not LRP2.

B. Aquaporin-2: Water channel defect → DI, not proteinuria.

D. Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase: General ion pump, not specific for protein reabsorption.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing modified radical neck dissection (MRND) for laryngeal malignancy. While ligating the internal jugular vein, his etCO2 dropped from 40 mmHg to 14 mmHg, and the patient developed hypotension along with cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous air embolism

A drastic fall in etCO2 with hypotension during neck surgery is most likely due to venous air embolism (VAE).

In modified radical neck dissection (MRND), a head-up position is given to provide a bloodless surgical field. VAE into severed vessels is likely to occur when the surgical site is above the right atrium and venous pressure at the incision site is below the atmospheric pressure. Pulmonary artery pressure will rise and etCO2 will fall after a venous air embolism.

In sympathetic overactivity and carotid body stimulation, blood pressure will rise.

In vagal stimulation, a drastic drop in etCO2 is unlikely.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to the clinic for cervical cancer screening. HPV testing is positive for HPV type 18. What is the next best step in management?
options: Acyclovir and review after 6 weeks with repeat testing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Colposcopy and biopsy

Detection of high-risk HPV types (especially HPV 16 or 18) during cervical cancer screening requires immediate colposcopic evaluation, even if cytology is normal.

• HPV 16 and HPV 18 are the highest-risk oncogenic HPV types associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer.
• A positive result for these types warrants colposcopy with directed biopsy to identify any precancerous lesions or early malignancy.

Why other options are incorrect:

• LLETZ: performed only after biopsy confirms high-grade lesions (CIN 2/3).
• Acyclovir: ineffective because HPV is not treated with antivirals.
• HPV vaccination: preventive, not used as treatment for existing infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen in pregnancy?
options: Increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks
Peripheral resistance to insulin leading to hyperinsuliemia
Increased plasma volume and RBC mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks

Increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks is not a physiological change seen in pregnancy.

During early pregnancy, systemic vascular resistance decreases, leading to a drop in blood pressure (both systolic and diastolic), which typically reaches its lowest point in the second trimester. Blood pressure gradually returns to pre-pregnancy levels in the third trimester.

An increase in blood pressure during early pregnancy is not physiological and could indicate an underlying pathology (e.g., chronic hypertension or gestational hypertension later in pregnancy).

Cardiovascular parameters that increase in pregnancy are:

• Cardiac output
• Stroke volume
• Heart rate

Cardiovascular parameters that decrease in pregnancy are:

• Peripheral vascular resistance (due to smooth muscle relaxation by progesterone)
• Both diastolic BP and systolic BP (decrease in DBP > SBP)
• Mean arterial BP
• Artery venous O2 gradient

Other Options:

Option B: Peripheral resistance to insulin leading to hyperinsuliemia: During pregnancy, placental hormones like human placental lactogen (hPL), cortisol, and progesterone induce insulin resistance to ensure adequate glucose availability for the fetus. This leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

Option C: Fasting hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperglycemia: Fasting hypoglycemia occurs due to increased maternal glucose utilization by the fetus. Postprandial hyperglycemia is a result of insulin resistance and slower glucose uptake.

Option D: Increased plasma volume and RBC mass: Plasma volume increases by about 40-50%, and red blood cell (RBC) mass increases by 20-30%, leading to hemodilution and the physiological anemia of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Composition of Lente insulin is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 70% crystalline 30% amorphous

Lente insulin is an intermediate-acting insulin and is a combination of Ultralente and Semilente in the ratio of 7:3

Two types of insulin zinc suspensions have been produced. The one with large particles is crystalline and practically insoluble in water (Ultralente). It is long-acting. The other has smaller particles and is amorphous (Semilente), is short-acting. Their 7:3 ratio mixture is called ‘Lente insulin’ and is intermediate-acting.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presented with progressive blurred vision, photophobia, and eye pain. On examination, there was conjunctival redness, a mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber in the right eye. He has been treated both medically and surgically for the condition but showed no improvement. The following procedure incorporates a device to aid drainage. Identify the device.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ex-Press™ implant

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of glaucoma not responsive to medical treatment and trabeculectomy and the device used is an ex-Press™ glaucoma implant (mini shunt).

It is a form of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) to increase aqueous drainage.

Ex-PRESS glaucoma implant is a small stainless steel device. It is inserted under a scleral flap during a modified trabeculectomy. Complications such as hypotony are lower than with standard trabeculectomy.

Glaucoma drainage devices are devices that allow aqueous outflow by establishing communication between the anterior chamber and sub-Tennon's space/sub-conjunctival space. While these devices were traditionally reserved for high-risk patients, or after trabeculectomy had failed, they are becoming increasingly popular.

The commonly used devices are as follows:

1. Shunts using episcleral explants

• Ahmed glaucoma valve: Silicone
• Molteno implant - Polypropylene plate and silicone plate
• Baerveldt implant - Silicone

2. Mini-shunts

• Ex-Press™ Mini-Shunt: Stainless steel
• iStent® - Titanium

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What clinical test is depicted in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cottle’s test

The image representing a clinical test where the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly is Cottle’s test.

This test is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve in patients with a deviated nasal septum. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive and indicates an abnormality of the vestibular component of the nasal valve on that side.

Option A: Epley’s maneuver is used in the treatment of BPPV.

Option B: Heimlich manoeuvre is used in the treatment of accidental inhalation of foreign body.

Procedure: Stand behind the person and place your arms around his lower chest and give four abdominal thrusts. The residual air in the lungs can dislodge the foreign body providing some airway.

Option D: Trotter’s method is used in the treatment of epistaxis. In Trotter’s method, the patient is made to sit, leaning a little forward over a basin to spit any blood. He should pinch the nose firmly for 5 to 10 mins and breathe quietly from the mouth.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient has a history of a road traffic accident 2 years back, and has developed pain and swelling now at the same site. His X-ray image is shown in the image given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic osteomyelitis

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of an accident 2 years ago, experiencing symptoms of pain and swelling at the site of injury, and an X-ray of the lower limb revealing sequestrum and involucrum in the tibia, strongly suggests a diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis.

Chronic osteomyelitis may occur by direct inoculation of the infective organism during trauma (like road traffic accidents). The infection continues to thrive within the bone leading to alternating quiescent and flare-up stages of chronic osteomyelitis.

Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone. It is formed when a fragment of bone gets separated from the healthy bone due to necrosis. It varies in size from a spicule to a large fragment and acts as a nidus for infection. It leads to abscess and persistent pus discharge in the bone. Sinus tracts are formed when the abscess from the infected bone drains out through the skin.

The involucrum is the dense new sclerotic bone surrounding the sequestrum. It is formed from deep layers of stripped periosteum. Cloacae are the perforations in the involucrum. Pus and tiny spicules of bone may be discharged through them.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma shows an onion-skin appearance of the periosteum, as shown below.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the amount of milk given to a term baby in the first 24 hours after delivery?
questions.explanation: According to standard pediatric guidelines, the fluid and nutritional requirements for a healthy term baby in the first 24 hours of life are approximately of body weight. This volume accounts for the infant's limited stomach capacity and the physiological weight loss (primarily water) that occurs immediately after birth. This requirement is gradually increased each day, typically reaching by the end of the first week. Option A (40 ml/kg) and Option B (50 ml/kg) are below the standard initial target. Option D (80 ml/kg) is the requirement for Day 2. While early and frequent exclusive breastfeeding is the gold standard, this value serves as the clinical guide for calculating intake if supplementation or IV fluids are medically necessary. Monitoring the baby’s hydration status through urine output and weight tracking is critical during this transitional period

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a bomb blast explosion, a person suffered a crush injury as a building fell on top of him. Which type of bomb blast injury is most commonly observed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Quaternary

A building crushing a person classifies as a quarternary blast injury.

Blast injuries are classified as:

* Primary injuries – effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterised by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this.

* Secondary injuries – injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries.

* Tertiary injuries – caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects.

* Quaternary injuries – all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. e.g., flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.

Mechanism of injury

Health impact

Secondary

MARSHAL’s triad (triad of abrasions, contuisions, lacerations)

Tertiary

Blast wind

Victim is thrown in air and strikes other objects leading to fracture and blunt trauma

Quaternary

Any complicating factor not in the other three categories

Burns, histotoxic anoxia, and crush injuries

* The specific pulmonary injury of air blast is known as blast lung.

* When the explosion is in the water the pressure changes are called underwater blast. Intestinal damage is very common in underwater blast injuries.

* Solid blast refers to the wave of energy that spreads through the rigid structure when an explosive is detonated near it and people in contact with its structure can be injured.

* Caecum is most sensitive to intestinal blast injury.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is noted to have a right transverse palmar crease, an associated cardiac defect, survival beyond infancy, and mild intellectual disability. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The features described, including a transverse palmar crease, cardiac defect, and intellectual impairment, are classic for Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21). In this case, the survival into childhood with only "mild" impairment suggests Mosaicism, which occurs in about 1% of cases. Mosaicism results from a post-zygotic mitotic error, leading to a mixture of normal and trisomy 21 cells; this often results in a milder clinical phenotype than full meiotic nondisjunction. Tetralogy (Option A) likely refers to Tetralogy of Fallot, a heart defect that can occur in syndromes but is not a chromosomal abnormality itself. Haploid (Option B) refers to a single set of chromosomes (23), which is incompatible with human life. Monosomy (Option C) is the loss of a chromosome, such as in Turner syndrome (45,X). Mosaicism allows for a broad range of developmental outcomes
questions.learning: The features described, including a transverse palmar crease, cardiac defect, and intellectual impairment, are classic for Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The radiograph shown below is done for better assessment of the frontal sinus. What is the common name of this view?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Caldwell view

The frontal sinus is best seen in Caldwell's view (occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position).

The structures seen in Caldwell's view include:

• Frontal sinuses (seen best)
• Ethmoid sinuses
• Maxillary sinuses
• Frontal process of the zygoma and the zygomatic process of the frontal bone
• Superior margin of the orbit and lamina papyracea
• Superior orbital fissure
• Foramen rotundum (inferolateral to superior orbital fissure)

The nose and forehead are touching the X-ray film and the X-ray beam is projected 15 degrees caudally in Caldwell's view.

Other options:

Option A: Water's view (occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view where an X-ray beam is angled at 45 degrees to the orbitomeatal line. Structures seen are the maxillary sinus (best seen), sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with an open mouth), frontal sinus, zygoma, zygomatic arch, nasal bone, and infratemporal fossa.

Option C: Pierre's view is the occipitomental with an open mouth. It helps in visualizing the sphenoid sinus as well, in addition to the sinuses that can be seen in water's view.

Option D: Towne's view is an angled anteroposterior radiograph of the skull. Structures seen are the petrous part of the pyramids, arcuate eminence, superior semicircular canal, mastoid antrum, internal auditory canal, tympanic cavity, cochlea, and external auditory canal. This view is taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In fetal circulation, which vessel carries deoxygenated blood back to the placenta?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Umbilical artery

Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta during the fetal period. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood away from the placenta.

Arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart, except for the pulmonary and umbilical arteries which carry deoxygenated blood.

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein (pO2 30 to 35mmHg). From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava (IVC) (pO2: 26 - 28mmHg) through ductus venosus.

The right atrium receives the oxygenated blood from the IVC and superior vena cava (less oxygenated). The right atrial pressure is more than the left atrial pressure resulting in the major flow of blood from the right atrium to the left atrium via the foramen ovale. The blood from the left atrium flows to the left ventricle. The upper part of the fetal body (coronaries, cerebral arteries, and upper extremities) is exclusively perfused by the left ventricle via the ascending aorta.

The major portion of this blood bypasses the lung and flows from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta via the ductus arteriosus. Finally, some of this blood from the aorta and the lower parts of the body is pumped back to the placenta via umbilical arteries.

The concept of fetal circulation and the various embryological remnants of the vascular entities of fetal circulation is a high-yield frequently tested topic in NEET-PG examination.  The concepts are summarized in the pearl attached below.
questions.learning: Umbilical artery Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta during the fetal period. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood away from the placenta.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What marker is regularly monitored in the management of ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. β-hCG

The marker used in the monitoring of ectopic pregnancy is β-hCG

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a glycoprotein. It can be detected in the maternal serum or urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization. Maximum levels in blood and urine are found between 60 - 70 days of pregnancy. It disappears from circulation within 2 weeks following delivery.

Ectopic pregnancy has decreased levels of hCG as compared to normal pregnancy hCG, and it is used as a marker for medical management of ectopic pregnancy. Following conservative surgery or medical treatment, estimation of serum β-hCG level should be done weekly until the β-HCG values go down.

Medical management is indicated when the patient is asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. It involves the systemic or local use of chemotherapeutic drugs:

* Drugs used: Methotrexate (50 mg/m2, single dose intramuscularly)

* Regular monitoring of serum β-hCG

Medical management is likely to be successful when

* Initial serum hCG level is <3,000 IU/L.

* Ectopic mass is less than 4 cm.

* Fetal cardiac activity is absent.

* Intra-abdominal hemorrhage is absent.

Surgical management of ectopic pregnancy includes laparoscopic salpingostomy, salpingectomy, and microsurgical laparotomy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Beta hCG is structurally similar to which biochemical moiety?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LH

Beta hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) has biological activity similar to that of luteinizing hormone (LH).

hCG is a glycoprotein produced by syncytiotrophoblasts. It is made up of α and β subunits. Though the α subunit of hCG is similar to the α subunits of LH, FSH, and TSH, the β subunit has structural similarity to LH only. Hence, LH is a better answer than FSH.

hCG is primarily luteinizing and luteotrophic. It appears to act on the same receptor as that of LH. The function of hCG is to prevent regression of the corpus luteum. It can be detected in blood as early as 6 days after conception and forms the basis of various tests used to identify pregnancy.

Its level peaks at gestational week 9 and then declines gradually but is present in lower concentration till the end of pregnancy. But hCG is not specific for pregnancy as it is secreted in a variety of gastrointestinal and genital tumors in both males and females.
questions.learning: LH Beta hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) has biological activity similar to that of luteinizing hormone (LH). hCG is a glycoprotein produced by syncytiotrophoblasts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a known history of DM and HTN on regular medications presents with a history of progressively worsening dyspnoea on exertion. The given symptoms and signs are suggestive of heart failure (Option A).

Portal hypertension (Option D) can be a result of right-sided heart failure, however, the presence of worsening dyspnea along with the other symptoms implies a primary cardiac condition.

Heart failure is a common endpoint for most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary heart disease.
The symptoms of heart failure are commonly due to volume overload with pulmonary and/or systemic venous pressures.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 9-month-old child is admitted to the ICU with a history of recurrent sinusitis and otitis media caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Lab results shows low levels of Immunoglobulins (G,A,M,E) and low quantity of plasma B cells. There is a normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bruton's agammaglobulinemia

This child's presentation suggests X-linked or Bruton's agammaglobulinemia.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia) is an immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the failure of B-cell precursors (pro-B and pre-B cells) to develop into mature B-cells. It is caused by a mutation in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase called Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq21.22). The features of the disease are -

* B cells are absent or markedly reduced.

* Decreased levels of all classes of Immunoglobulins.

* Germinal centres are underdeveloped in lymph nodes, peyer's patches, and tonsils.

* T-cell mediated reactions are normal. (normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin.)

* The disease usually becomes apparent after 6 months of age since it is masked by the presence of maternal antibodies until 6 months of age.

The patient has recurrent pharyngitis, otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, and pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, and Hemophilus influenzae. Gastrointestinal infections can occur by viruses or Giardia lamblia due to reduced IgA secretion.
The treatment is replacement therapy with immunoglobulins in the form of prophylactic intravenous IgG therapy.

Other Options:

Option A: Ataxia telangiectasia is caused due to mutation of the ATM gene. This gene is involved in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to impaired Ig isotype switching and the formation of antigen receptors. As a result, the patient is immunodeficient with partial T cell deficiency, and hence live vaccines are avoided.

Option C: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is a rare primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by defects in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex, which is essential for the respiratory burst in phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages). This defect impairs the ability of phagocytes to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to ineffective intracellular killing of certain bacteria and fungi.

Option D: DiGeorge syndrome is caused due to deletion of chromosome 22q11.2. The characteristic features are (Mnemonic CATCH-22) - Cardiac abnormality, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia.

Pearl PF0295: Primary immunodeficiency disorders

Affected component of the immune system

Disorder

Humoral immunity:

Problems with B cells (lymphocytes) and their antibody production

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
A woman has vomiting whenever she eats spicy food. Arrange the sequence of events during vomiting.

1. LES is open and UES is closed.
2. Strong contractions in the stomach.
3. Inspiration against a closed glottis.
4. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter.
5. LES opens and UES opens.
6. Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine.

LES: Lower esophageal sphincter

UES: Upper esophageal sphincter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5

The correct sequence of vomiting is 6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5.

6. Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine.
4. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter.
2. Strong contractions in the stomach.
3. Inspiration against a closed glottis.
1. LES is open and UES is closed.
5. LES opens and UES opens.

The sensory signals that initiate vomiting are located in the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and upper portions of the small intestines. Excessive distention or irritation of the duodenum provides a strong stimulus for vomiting. Area postrema constitutes the vomiting centre.

In the early stage, reverse peristalsis begins often minutes before vomiting. It begins far down in the ileum and travels up the intestine. This process pushes a large share of lower small intestine contents to the duodenum and stomach. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter occurs during this process.

At the onset of vomiting, strong intrinsic contractions are seen in the duodenum and stomach. Once the vomiting centre has been stimulated, inspiration occurs against the closed glottis. It prevents the flow of vomitus into the lungs. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is open and the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) is closed at this stage.

The muscles of the abdominal wall contract, building intra-gastric pressure. Finally LES relaxes completely and UES also relaxes allowing the expulsion of the gastric contents.

Note: The esophageal smooth muscle functions as LES at the gastro-esophageal junction. It normally remains tonically constricted. Receptive relaxation of LES occurs when the peristaltic wave passes down the esophagus.
questions.learning: 6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5 The correct sequence of vomiting is 6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5. Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At a crime scene, blood stains are detected during forensic examination. Which of the following tests is not used for the identification of blood stains?
questions.explanation: In forensic science, the identification of blood involves presumptive and confirmatory tests. Takayama's test (Option B) and Teichman's test (Option C) are standard confirmatory tests that form characteristic hemochromogen and hemin crystals, respectively, when blood is present. Spectroscopy (Option D) is an advanced method used to identify the absorption bands of hemoglobin derivatives. Barberio's test (Option A), however, is not applicable for identifying blood stains; it is a specialized chemical test used specifically for the identification of semen by forming yellow needle-like crystals of spermine picrate. Accurately distinguishing between these biological fluid tests is a foundational skill in forensic medicine. Confirmatory tests for blood are essential to rule out other red substances (like rust or paint) and to provide definitive evidence for criminal investigations. Following these "presumptive-to-confirmatory" protocols ensures that the forensic evidence presented in a court of law is scientifically robust. Therefore, Barberio’s remains the correct outlier in the context of bloodstain identification

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with pain and redness in the right eye following an injury during welding. On examination, the image as seen below is observed. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Removal by 26G needle

A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye. Removal of the foreign body using a 26G needle is the next step in the management of this patient.

Foreign bodies, which are usually small particles of dust, iron, steel, etc., may impinge upon the conjunctiva or cornea and cause sudden discomfort and reflex blinking. The foreign body sticks to the palpebral conjunctiva and is liable to be dragged across the cornea, causing excoriation. Particles of steel and iron fly straight onto the cornea and penetrate the epithelium or substantia propria.

Fluorescein or oblique illumination of the anesthetized eye with a slit lamp can be used to determine the position of a foreign body. If not removed, they expose the cornea to organisms in the conjunctival sac causing ulceration and extrusion of the foreign body in the slough. The ulcer thus formed may heal, but if virulent organisms are present, a spreading ulcer, with or without hypopyon, may develop.

Foreign bodies are managed by removal as soon as possible.

* If the foreign body is found lying loose in either fornix, it can be removed with a clean swab after everting the eyelids.

* Double-eversion of the upper eyelid with a Desmarres retractor can be done if required.

* If embedded in the bulbar conjunctiva or cornea, it can be removed by a foreign body spud or fine forceps under topical anesthesia.

* A disposable hypodermic (26 or 27 gauge) needle can be used.

Following removal in all cases, an antibiotic ointment should be applied and the eye kept bandaged for a day. Foreign bodies in the eye are extremely common in industrial workers, especially in those working with grinding tools, lathe work, or hammering on a chisel, and thus eye must be protected by educative notices, lectures, and the provision of comfortable goggles.

Cases of ferruginous intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) may give rise to anterior capsular cataracts and reddish-brown staining of the iris leading to heterochromia iridis. MRI is contraindicated here and instead, CT with axial and coronal cuts is used to localize a metallic IOFB. Magnetic removal is done for the removal of ferrous foreign bodies.
questions.learning: Removal by 26G needle — A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He gives a history of having consumed shellfish and raw seafood a day before. The causative agent showed the Kanagawa phenomenon on Wagatsuma agar. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Kanagawa Phenomenon is shown by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. The Kanagawa phenomenon is hemolysis on wagatsuma agar.

On Wagatsuma agar (High salt blood agar), pathogenic strains of V. parahaemolyticus are hemolytic, while non-pathogenic strains are non-hemolytic. This is due to a heat-stable hemolysin.

V. parahaemolyticus causes food poisoning due to the consumption of contaminated seafood, after an incubation period of 12–24 hours. The common sources of infection are raw seafood like mollusks and crustaceans. No enterotoxin like cholera toxin has been identified, it causes enteritis by invasion of the intestinal epithelium.

Clinically, patients present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, fever, and watery or bloody diarrhea. Fecal leukocytes are often seen in stool samples. Enteritis subsides spontaneously in 1–3 days with no specific treatment. Adequate hydration and electrolyte balance should be restored.

V. parahaemolyticus is a capsulated bacterium. It shows bipolar staining and has a tendency to pleomorphism. It is characterized by peritrichous flagella on solid media and polar flagella on liquid media and it gives a negative string test.

Pathogenic strains of V. parahemolyticus are hemolytic on Wagatsuma agar, while non-pathogenic strains are non-hemolytic. This is called the Kanagawa phenomenon and is due to a heat-stable hemolysin.
questions.learning: Vibrio parahaemolyticus Kanagawa Phenomenon is shown by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. The Kanagawa phenomenon is hemolysis on wagatsuma agar.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with excessive tearing (epiphora). On probing, a soft obstruction is encountered at 7 mm. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: A child with epiphora (excessive tearing) and a "soft block" at 7 mm on probing indicates a canalicular obstruction rather than a nasolacrimal duct (NLD) blockage. For proximal obstructions in the canaliculi, the preferred treatment is Conjunctival DCR, also known as Lester Jones tube placement. This procedure bypasses the blocked canaliculi by placing a permanent drainage tube from the conjunctival sac directly into the nasal cavity. Endonasal DCR (Option A) and External DCR (Option C) are used for distal obstructions in the nasolacrimal duct where a "hard block" is felt against the lacrimal bone. Dacryocystectomy (Option D) involves the complete removal of the lacrimal sac and is usually a last-resort procedure for chronic infection or malignancy, not for restoring functional drainage. Correct diagnosis of the site of obstruction is essential for selecting the appropriate surgical approach
questions.learning: A child with epiphora (excessive tearing) and a "soft block" at 7 mm on probing indicates a canalicular obstruction rather than a nasolacrimal duct (NLD) blockage.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presents with a lump in her breast. All the following can be used to rule out malignancy, except _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PET scan

In a patient presenting with breast lump or other suspicions of breast carcinoma a triple assessment method is used to rule out malignancy. PET scan is used to assess the spread and sites of distant metastasis, it is not used to rule out malignancy. It is also not a part of the triple assessment.

The triple assessment in the examination of breast lump includes:

• Clinical assessment - Clinical history and physical examination of the lump.
• Radiological examination - USG/ mammography/ both.
• Cytological or histological examination - FNAC (Fine needle aspiration cytology)/ core biopsy of the lump.

Features of malignancy seen on clinical examination can be enlarged axillary lymph nodes, circumferential retraction of the nipple, peau'd orange appearance of the skin and ulcerations over the breast. Benign features include non-progressive, smooth, circumscribed, soft, mobile lumps without skin changes.

Microcalcifications seen on breast radiography are also highly suggestive of breast carcinoma.

FNAC and biopsy can detect malignant and atypical cells, suggestive of malignancy.

The triple assessment method has a positive predictive value of about 99.99%. In other words, if all three modalities give negative results, breast cancer can be excluded.
questions.learning: PET scan — In a patient presenting with breast lump or other suspicions of breast carcinoma a triple assessment method is used to rule out malignancy. PET scan is used to assess the spread and sites of distant metastasis, it is not used to rule out malignancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with the following arterial blood gas (ABG) results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 32 mEq/L What is the most probable cause for these findings?
questions.explanation: The ABG interpretation begins with the pH; a value of 7.55 (normal 7.35–7.45) indicates alkalosis. Next, the is 40 mmHg (normal range), which indicates that the primary problem is not respiratory in nature. The (bicarbonate) is 32 mEq/L (normal 22–26 mEq/L), which is elevated. An elevated bicarbonate level leading to an alkaline pH is the hallmark of metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) would show a low pH and low bicarbonate. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) would show a low pH and high . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) would show a high pH and low . Common causes of metabolic alkalosis include severe vomiting (loss of acid), diuretic use, or excessive alkali ingestion. In this case, the lack of respiratory compensation (normal ) suggests either an acute presentation or a mixed disorder
questions.learning: The ABG interpretation begins with the pH; a value of 7.55 (normal 7.35–7.45) indicates alkalosis. Next, the is 40 mmHg (normal range), which indicates that the primary problem is not respiratory in nature.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient involved in a severe road traffic accident is declared dead on arrival at the emergency department. Within minutes, the examining doctor observes marked stiffness of the neck, upper limbs, and lower limbs, with no preceding phase of muscle relaxation. This immediate onset of rigidity is noted during the initial examination. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm, also known as instantaneous rigor, is a rare form of post-mortem stiffening that occurs at the exact moment of death. It bypasses the stage of primary muscular relaxation that normally precedes rigor mortis. It is typically seen in deaths involving intense physical emotion, extreme nervous tension, or violent struggle (such as a severe road accident). In this condition, the muscles that were in a state of contraction at the time of death remain rigid. Rigor mortis (Option A) typically takes 2 to 3 hours to begin and 12 hours to become fully established. Heat stiffness (Option B) occurs due to coagulation of muscle proteins at high temperatures (e.g., in fires). Cold stiffness (Option D) occurs in freezing temperatures due to the solidification of body fats. Because the rigidity was "instantaneous" and "without preceding relaxation" following a violent event, Cadaveric spasm is the most accurate forensic diagnosis
questions.learning: Cadaveric spasm, also known as instantaneous rigor, is a rare form of post-mortem stiffening that occurs at the exact moment of death. It bypasses the stage of primary muscular relaxation that normally precedes rigor mortis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are features of umbilical hernia in adults? 1. Patients are commonly overweight with a thinned and attenuated midline raphe. 2. Most patients complain of pain due to tissue tension. 3. Men are affected more commonly than women. 4. Hernia repair can be done by the technique described by Mayo. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Adult umbilical hernia is an acquired hernia resulting from weakness of the umbilical ring due to raised intra-abdominal pressure and attenuation of the linea alba. It is commonly seen in obese individuals and multiparous women and usually requires mesh repair because of a high recurrence rate with simple suture repair.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Patients are commonly overweight with a thinned and attenuated midline raphe. ✅

• Obesity causes stretching and weakening of the linea alba, predisposing to umbilical hernia.

• 2. Most patients complain of pain due to tissue tension. ✅

• Adults commonly present with pain or discomfort, especially during coughing or exertion, due to tension on the hernia defect.

• 3. Men are affected more commonly than women. ❌

• Adult umbilical hernias are more common in women, particularly multiparous and obese women.

• 4. Hernia repair can be done by the technique described by Mayo. ✅

• Mayo’s repair (double-breasting technique) is the classic tissue repair for umbilical hernia, although mesh repair is preferred today for larger defects due to lower recurrence.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Adult umbilical hernia is an acquired hernia resulting from weakness of the umbilical ring due to raised intra-abdominal pressure and attenuation of the linea alba.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The murmur of Mitral Stenosis corresponds to which of the following component of the ECG?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. P wave

Mitral stenosis produces a diastolic murmur.

The murmur occurs when: Blood flows from Left Atrium → Left Ventricle during diastole through a narrow mitral valve.

However, the loudest part of the murmur occurs just before ventricular systole, during atrial contraction.

This is called: Presystolic accentuation

Atrial contraction corresponds to the P wave of ECG.

Remember the sequence:
