questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pituitary gland

Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the options given above except the pituitary gland.

Sodium iodide symporter is expressed mainly in the thyroid gland and is responsible for iodine uptake in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland.

Sodium iodide symporter (NIS)

The NIS is mainly present in the basolateral membranes of the thyrocytes. The NIS transports two Na+ ions and one I- ion into the cell against the concentration gradient. The energy for this transport is derived from the Na+-K+ ATPase pump. Na+-K+ ATPase pumps sodium outside the cell and causes low intracellular sodium concentration. This causes sodium to enter the cell by facilitated diffusion. Along with sodium, iodide ions also enter the cell. Since the energy to transport sodium and iodide ions in NIS is derived from Na+-K+ ATPase pump, this is called secondary active transport.

The NIS is also expressed in:

• Salivary glands
• Gastric mucosa
• Placenta
• Ciliary body of the eye
• Choroid plexus
• Mammary glands
• Certain cancers are derived from these tissues.

The significance of these extrathyroidal NIS is not known.
questions.learning: Pituitary gland Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the options given above except the pituitary gland. Sodium iodide symporter is expressed mainly in the thyroid gland and is responsible for iodine uptake in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought to the emergency department with respiratory distress. On evaluation, imaging reveals a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect as shown in the X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms and X-ray findings indicate a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), specifically a Bochdalek hernia. This is the most common type of CDH, accounting for 90% of cases, and typically presents through a posterolateral defect, occurring predominantly on the left side (80–90%). Morgagni hernia (Option B) is a retrosternal defect occurring through the foramen of Morgagni and accounts for only 2–6% of cases. Hiatal hernia (Option C) occurs specifically at the esophageal hiatus and does not present with the massive herniation of abdominal organs seen here. Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia (Option D) is not the diagnosis in this newborn scenario because there is no history of significant trauma. Pathologically, CDH leads to lung compression and pulmonary hypoplasia, causing respiratory distress, cyanosis, and a scaphoid abdomen. Immediate management requires neonatal stabilization with intubation and gastric decompression before surgical repair is performed, usually after 48 hours

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient presented with a fever and a positive filarial antigen test, what is the next best step of management?
options: Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear

This question tests the diagnostic approach to filariasis, especially how to proceed after a positive circulating filarial antigen (CFA) test.

• Filarial antigen test (CFA):

• Detects adult worm antigen (commonly Wuchereria bancrofti)
• Can be positive even when microfilariae are not yet demonstrated

• Next step after positive antigen test:

• Confirm infection by demonstrating microfilariae in peripheral blood smear
• Blood should ideally be collected at night (nocturnal periodicity)

This Confirms active infection and parasitemia and Helps in:

• Disease staging
• Monitoring treatment response

Why other options are incorrect:

• DEC provocation test → outdated, rarely used now
• Scrotal ultrasound → useful for detecting “filarial dance sign” but not first confirmatory step

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with dilated, tortuous veins of the leg and is diagnosed with grade C4a varicose veins. What is the most appropriate preferred treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Grade C4a varicose veins, according to the CEAP classification, indicate chronic venous insufficiency with skin changes like pigmentation or eczema. Endothermal ablation, which uses radiofrequency or laser energy to close the refluxing vein, is the first-line preferred treatment. It is minimally invasive, highly effective, and allows for faster recovery. Compression stockings (Option A) are used for symptomatic relief but do not address the underlying venous reflux. Non-endothermal methods like cyanoacrylate glue (Option C) are alternatives but not the primary gold standard. Open surgery (Option D), involving vein stripping, is now largely reserved for cases where endothermal techniques are technically unfeasible. Treatment aims to eliminate the source of venous hypertension to prevent progression to venous ulcers (C6). Therefore, thermal closure is the current standard of care for symptomatic C4a disease

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the investigation shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammography

The image shown above is of mammography.

The mammogram is an X-ray picture of the breast. The anode in the X-ray tube is made up of molybdenum. The X-ray film used is a single-sided coated film.

The views used are two types: Craniocaudal and Mediolateral oblique

Uses of the mammogram:

* Routine screening for (ductal carcinoma in situ) DCIS.

* The most important sign of malignancy in a mammogram is clustered microcalcification (more than 5 particles in 1 cm², 3 particles of less than 0.5 mm size)

Radiological findings in other diseases of the breast:

* Popcorn calcification is seen in fibroadenoma.

* Broken-needle type of calcification is seen in duct ectasia.

* Tea-cup calcification is seen in fibrocystic disease.

Differences between mammography and conventional radiography:

* Mammography involves the use of low-energy and high-amperage waves.

* The target anode is made of a tungsten disc in conventional X-ray tubes and molybdenum in mammography X-ray tubes.

* Most mammography tubes use beryllium exit windows between the evacuated tube and the atmosphere.

* The conventional X-ray tube has an aluminum filter, but in mammography, a molybdenum filter is used.

Some indications for mammography:

* Evaluation of breast signs and symptoms like masses, skin changes, deformities, nipple retraction, discharge, and eczema

* Breast cancer screening

* Follow-up for patients treated for breast cancer

* Localization of lesions not visible on ultrasound

Pearl PF1991: Breast Cancer Screening

Breast Cancer Screening*

Individuals are encouraged to conduct a risk assessment by 25 years of age. This helps classify them into average risk or increased risk groups.

Recommendations:

* Average-risk (no known genetic or family history of breast cancer)

* 25-39 years of age: clinical breast examination every 1-3 years;

* ≥ 40 years of age: clinical breast examination and mammogram annually

* Increased risk (positive family or genetic history of breast cancer)

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months after 21 years of age

* Annual mammogram or MRI from 25 years of age or 10 years prior to the age at which the youngest family member was diagnosed with breast cancer (whichever is earliest)

* Asymptomatic women with previously treated breast cancer

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months

* Annual mammogram

* Annual MRI to be considered

* Mammogram and USG are not contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women

High-risk patients for breast cancer:

* Women (or a first-degree relative) with a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation or TP53 or PTEN genes

* Two first-degree relatives with breast cancers with or without gene mutations

* Women with a history of chest irradiation between the ages of 10 and 30

* Women with previously biopsy-proven breast cancer

* Women with ≥ 20% lifetime risk for breast cancer based on breast cancer risk models

*According to NCCN 2022 guidelines

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Tzanck smear prepared from a vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells with "ground-glass" chromatin is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infections. These "Tzanck cells" result from the virus-induced fusion of infected keratinocytes. HIV (Option A) is primarily diagnosed via serological tests like ELISA or PCR and does not produce these specific cellular changes on a smear. HPV (Option C) is associated with koilocytes—epithelial cells with perinuclear halos—rather than multinucleated giant cells. EBV (Option D) is associated with "Downey cells" (atypical lymphocytes) on a peripheral blood smear, not a Tzanck smear. The Tzanck smear is a rapid bedside diagnostic tool for vesicular viral rashes, though definitive identification of the specific herpes virus may require further testing like PCR or viral culture
questions.learning: A Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells with "ground-glass" chromatin is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infections.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary use of this imaging modality?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), a high-resolution modality that combines endoscopy with ultrasonography to visualize the gastrointestinal wall layers. Its primary and most critical use is the clinical staging of esophageal cancer. It allows for the precise assessment of the depth of tumor invasion (T stage) and the identification of regional lymph node involvement (N stage). GERD (Option B) is typically evaluated using pH monitoring or manometry rather than EUS. Dysphagia (Option C) is initially investigated with a barium swallow or standard endoscopy; EUS is reserved for assessing specific submucosal lesions identified thereafter. Cardiac and aortic pathologies (Option D) are better assessed using Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE). EUS provides unique detail for staging malignancies and guiding fine-needle aspiration of adjacent structures, making it indispensable for oncology

questions.text: A patient undergoes worth's four-dot test . The results are as shown in the image below. Identify the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right suppression

The given image with 3 green dots likely suggests that the patient is suffering from right suppression.

Worth's four-dot test

• Sensory function test
• Patient wears goggles with

• Red lens: Right eye
• Green lens: Left eye

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a seminar on cervical cancer epidemiology, high-risk HPV serotypes linked to malignancy are discussed. Which combination of HPV serotypes is most strongly associated with the development of cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: Cervical cancer is definitively caused by persistent infection with high-risk serotypes of the human papillomavirus (HPV). Globally, HPV 16 and 18 are the two most oncogenic types, responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancer cases. Other recognized high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. Option D (16, 18, 31, 33) accurately identifies a grouping of the most significant high-risk serotypes . Options A, B, and C include serotypes 19 or 32, which are not standard members of the primary "high-risk" oncogenic group for cervical cancer. The integration of high-risk HPV DNA into the host genome leads to the overexpression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which disrupt tumor suppressor genes p53 and Rb, respectively. Therefore, this specific combination represents the most critical viral etiologies for cervical malignancy. Modern HPV vaccines target these types to effectively reduce the incidence of cervical cancer

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following tissues are dependent on insulin for glucose uptake?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adipose tissue

Adipose tissue is dependent on insulin for glucose uptake.

The uptake of glucose in skeletal muscles is also dependent on insulin but may be mediated via non-insulin-dependent mechanisms as well (such as muscle contractions). Therefore the best answer out of the given options is adipose tissue.

Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent. In the presence of insulin, GLUT-4 receptors translocate to the cell membrane and hence, glucose uptake by the cell occurs.

Most of the other GLUT transporters are not insulin sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. Ex: GLUT-1 in RBCs, brain and kidneys. (GLUT-3 is also present in the brain and kidneys)
questions.learning: Adipose tissue Adipose tissue is dependent on insulin for glucose uptake. The uptake of glucose in skeletal muscles is also dependent on insulin but may be mediated via non-insulin-dependent mechanisms as well (such as muscle contractions).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: According to myogenic hypothesis of renal autoregulation the afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch-induced by______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Opening of calcium channels

The afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch induced by the opening of calcium channels. The mechanism is called myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR.

The stretch of the vascular wall allows increased movement of calcium ions from the extracellular fluid into the cells, causing them to contract. This contraction prevents excessive stretch of the vessel. This prevents excessive increase of renal blood flow and GFR by raising vascular resistance.

This mechanism may be more important in protecting the kidney from hypertension-induced injury.

Autoregulation has two main mechanisms:

• Metabolic mechanism: Tissues produce vasodilatory metabolites that regulate flow e.g. prostaglandins, NO, CO2, H+ and K+
• Myogenic mechanism
questions.learning: Opening of calcium channels — The afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch induced by the opening of calcium channels. The mechanism is called myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment which of the following is incorrect about the reach in approach?
options: People with cataract are treated in a makeshift operation centre
IOL placement by small incision cataract surgery is preferred
Reach in approach has lesser post operative complications
People with cataract are identified and sent to higher centre
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. People with cataract are treated in a makeshift operation centre

Patients with cataract are not operated in makeshift operation centres but are rather shifted to base hospitals (reach-in approach) as the visual acuity results indicate that the Base Hospital had significantly higher final corrected visual acuity compared to the Peripheral Eye Camps.

The Base Hospital approach, also known as the reach-in approach, and the Peripheral Eye Camp approach, also known as the reach-out approach, are two community-oriented strategies implemented within the framework of the National Programme for the Control of Blindness. These techniques aim to address the existing backlog of cataract-related blindness. Both methods have demonstrated efficacy and possess distinct advantages and disadvantages. Both community participation and intersectoral coordination, together with the utilization of suitable technology at an affordable price, are essential components for both endeavours.

Based on recent developments, there is a shift in emphasis from the 'Reach-out' approach to the 'Reach-in' approach. The Reach-in Approach involves the organization of screening camps in rural and remote locations that lack access to eye-care institutions. Comprehensive eye care treatments, including refraction, are offered to patients. Subsequently, those requiring cataract surgery are conveyed to the nearest hospitals that possess adequate resources and facilities, following the base hospital strategy. To conduct ocular surgery, it is imperative to comply with the guidelines established by the Government of India.

• It is imperative to have at least one anesthesiologist who is well prepared to address typical crises to ensure patient safety and optimal care.
• It is recommended that a minimum of one, ideally two, operating surgeons be present, with each surgeon limiting their daily caseload to no more than 30 procedures.
• Currently, the preferred approach for cataract extraction is extracapsular surgery, with a preference for manual small incision cataract surgery (SICS) or phacoemulsification, together with the implantation of a posterior chamber intraocular lens.
• It is ideal to limit the number of surgical procedures conducted in a day to no more than 50.
• Simultaneous surgery on both eyes should be avoided.
• Patients who have a high surgical risk due to conditions such as severe diabetes, severe hypertension, and cardiac issues should not undergo surgery in camp settings. Cases related to such issues should be appropriately referred to the base hospitals.

National Programme for the Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). The levels of eye care, according to NPCBVI are:

Primary level: Sub-district level hospitals, community health centres, mobile ophthalmic units, upgraded PHCs, link workers, and Panchayats.
Secondary level: District hospitals, NGO eye hospitals
Tertiary levels: Regional institutes of Ophthalmology, medical colleges.
The goal is to reduce the prevalence of blindness to 0.3% by 2020.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Paris green dust is used to eliminate the larval form of _________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anopheles

Paris green is a commonly used larvicide agent against surface feeders like Anopheles larvae.

Paris green (Copper acetoarsenite) is an insecticide, which is a green powder that has 50% arsenious oxide. It is a stomach poison and to be effective, it must be ingested by the larvae.

The larvae of Anopheles are surface feeders as they lie parallel to the surface of the water due to the absence of a siphon tube. In contrast, Culicine larvae like Aedes, Culex, and Mansonia have a siphon tube that helps them to suspend in water with their head downwards and therefore not affected by pair green.

The image below shows Laraval forms of different mosquitoes.

Other commonly used larvicides include:

* Mineral oils - diesel oil, kerosene, fractions of crude oils, mosquito larvicidal oil

* Synthetic insecticides - Fenthion, Chlorpyrifos, and Abat

Larvicides that are not recommended include organochlorine compounds like DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane)and HCH (hexachlorocyclohexane). This is because they have a long residual effect, and contaminate water. Vector mosquitoes may also develop resistance to these compounds.

Pearl PF1010: Mosquito Control Measures

Mosquito Control Measures

* Anti-larval measures

* Environmental control

* This is done by source reduction by eliminating breeding places through appropriate methods for the different species.

* Intermittent irrigation is also a method of environmental control

* Chemical control

* Mineral oils: Oldest known larvicidal method. Oils that are used are diesel oil, kerosene, crude oil fractions. Disadvantage is that it kills fish.

* Paris green: Copper acetoarsenite is an emerald green, micro-crystalline powder and is insoluble in water. It is a stomach poison to larvae. It is not harmful to man or animals. Very effective against Anopheles as they are surface feeders.

* Synthetic insecticides: Organo-phosphorous compounds like fenthion, chlorpyrifos and abate are larvicidal. Abate is least toxic.

* Biological control

* The fish species Gambusia affinis and Lebister reticulatus (Barbados millions) feed on mosquito larvae.

* These are used in conjunction with other methods.

* Anti-adult measures

* Residual sprays

* Adult mosquitoes can be controlled by spraying with residual insecticides like DDT, Malathion, propoxur and gamma-HCH (lindane)

* Resistance to DDT has been shown by mosquitoes

* Space sprays

* Space sprays are those in which insecticides are sprayed into the atmosphere in the form of a mist or fog.

* Pyrethrum is a contact, nerve poison and is the most common insecticide used as a space spray. Its active principle is pyrethrin.

* Ultra-low volume space spraying (ULV) is done with Malathion and fenitrothion.

* Genetic control by sterile male technique, cytoplasmic incompatibility, sex distortion, etc.

* Protection against bites

* Usage of mosquito nets, building screens and repellants like diethyltoluamide (deet), indalone, dimethylphthalate, dimethyl carbate, etc.

Pearl PF1014: Insecticides

Contact poisons

* Natural: Pyrethrum, rotenone, derris, nicotine, mineral oils

* Synthetic:

* Organo-chlorine compounds: DDT, methoxychlor, HCH, lindane, chlordane, heptachlor, dieldrin, aldrin, toxaphene, kepone, mirex.

* Repellants: Benzyl benzoate, indalone, meta-diethyltoluamide, dimethyl phthalate, ethyl hexanediol.

* Organo-phosphorus compounds: Chlorthion (aryl), diazinon (aryl), demethoate, malathion (alkyl), fenthion, parathion (aryl), trichlorfon (alkyl), runnel, abale, naled, chlorpyrifos, fenitrothion, dicapthon.

* Carbamates: Carbaryl, dimetilan, propoxur, pyrolan.

* Synthetic pyrethroids: Prothrin, resmethrin, bioresmethrin, permethrin, proparthin, tetramethrin

* Stomach poisons: Paris green, sodium fluoride.

* Fumigants: Hydrogen cyanide, methyl bromide, sulphur dioxide, carbon disulphide.

Specific Insecticides
Comments

DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-thrichloroethane)
Insecticidal properties were discovered by Swiss scientist, Paul Muller. Most widely used insecticide. Attacks nerves of insects but doesn’t cause immediate death. White amorphous powder. Contains 70 – 80% of para-para isomers, which is the most active fraction of DDT. Has residual action up to 18 months. Used as a residual spray.Least toxic organo-chlorine compound.

HCH (hexachlorocyclo-hexane)
Synthesized by Michael Faraday. Normal HCH contains 13 – 16% of gamma isomer. Gamma-HCH or lindane has 99% gamma isomer.Short residual action – 3 months.

Malathion
Least toxicity of all organophosphorus compounds. Used as an ultra-low volume spray.

Fenthion
Also called baytex. Used as a residual spray.

Pyrethrum
Vegetable origin – Chrysanthemum cinerariafolium. Nerve poison and is excellent as a space spray.No residual action.Synergistic action with DDT as space spray.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Hooch tragedy is related to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Methanol

Hooch tragedy is due to the consumption of cheap illicit liquor containing methanol, particularly by the lower socio-economic classes.

The central organ for metabolism is the liver. Methanol or methyl alcohol is first oxidized to formaldehyde with the help of alcohol dehydrogenase. It is further metabolized to formic acid via aldehyde dehydrogenase. These metabolites are responsible for the adverse effects of intoxication.

Features seen are ophthalmological complications such as blindness, and optic neuropathy. Brain edema, acute renal failure, and severe metabolic derangement are also seen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Gold standard investigation before Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT scan

The gold standard investigation before FESS is a CT scan to rule out other pathologies and for confirmation of diagnosis. CT scan is better than MRI for visualizing bones and their anatomy.

Even while doing surgery, decisions on whether to open the mastoid antrum are based on CT findings and intraoperative findings. FESS is done for failed medical management of rhinosinusitis.

Other indications of FESS:

* Chronic bacterial sinusitis that is unresponsive to adequate medical treatment.

* Recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis

* Polypoid rhinosinusitis (diffuse nasal polyposis)

* Fungal sinusitis with a fungal ball or nasal polypi

* Antrochoanal polyp

* Mucocele of frontoethmoid or sphenoid sinus

* Control of epistaxis by endoscopic cautery.

* Removal of foreign body from the nose or sinus

* Endoscopic septoplasty

Advanced nasal endoscopic techniques

* Removal of benign tumors, e.g. inverted papillomas or angiofibromas.

* Orbital abscess or cellulitis management.

* Dacryocystorhinostomy

* Repair of CSF leak

* Pituitary surgery

* Optic nerve decompression

* Orbital decompression for Graves’ disease

* Control of posterior epistaxis (endoscopic clipping of sphenopalatine artery)

* Choanal atresia.

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet and exercise undergoes treadmill stress testing for complaints of intermittent fatigue. He reports no chest pain during the test, but stops after 6 minutes due to exertional Vitals: o Resting heart rate: 72/min; peak stress heart rate: 138/min o Resting blood pressure: 120/75 mm Hg; peak stress: 135/82 mm Hg. • ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. • Physical exam and echocardiogram at rest are unremarkable. During exercise, which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely to be decreased compared to the resting state?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total systemic vascular resistance

During dynamic exercise, cardiac output rises due to ↑ heart rate and stroke volume, while arterioles in exercising skeletal muscle dilate to increase blood flow. This widespread vasodilation leads to a decrease in total systemic vascular resistance (SVR).

A. Cardiac output – Increases significantly with exercise.

B. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure – Usually unchanged or mildly increased due to enhanced venous return and ventricular compliance.

C. Systemic systolic blood pressure – Increases due to increased cardiac output despite lower SVR.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a correct match for ABCD according to paediatrics advanced life support?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dehydration

According to paediatrics advanced life support (PALS), the incorrectly matched one is D-dehydration.

The American Heart Association, in its Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) curriculum, supports the structured format of the airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure- ABCDE for primary assessment.

Airway- The primary survey's first and most important portion is the patient’s airway. A simple chin-lift or jaw thrust manoeuvre re-aligns the airway. An artificial airway that is appropriate for the patient’s situation like oropharyngeal airways (OPA), and nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be used.

Breathing-Assessment of breathing includes respiratory rate, effort, abnormal sounds, and pulse oximetry. Central cyanosis is a sign of severe hypoxia and indicates an emergent need for oxygen supplementation and respiratory support.

Circulation- Cardiovascular function is assessed by evaluation of skin colour and temperature, heart rate, heart rhythm, pulses, and capillary refill time.

Disability- This refers to a child’s neurologic function in terms of the level of consciousness. An assessment of light reflex and use of either of the standard scores used in paediatrics. Any child with a depressed level of consciousness should be immediately assessed for abnormalities in cardiorespiratory status.

Exposure- Exposure is the final component after the child has been stabilized. This includes exposing the child to assess for previously unidentified injuries by performing a focused physical exam, and assessing for burns, bruising, bleeding, joint laxity, and fractures.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not a risk factor for the development of cholangiocarcinoma?

Initial workup by ultrasound shows dilation of the intrahepatic biliary tree, but definitive diagnosis requires visualisation of the biliary tree and MRCP or ERCP (biopsy possible) is preferred

questions.text: Reiter syndrome is associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HLA-B27

Reiter syndrome is associated with HLA- B27.

Reiter's syndrome has a triad of urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis, with or without iridocyclitis. The exact cause of the syndrome is not fully understood, but it typically affects young males who test positive for the HLA-B27 gene.

It has three forms: postvenereal, postdysenteric, and articular. Ocular symptoms may include acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis and non-granulomatous iridocyclitis in a subset of cases.

Treatrment -Iridocyclitis responds well to usual treatment and in cases suspected of being caused by Chlamydia infection, a course of systemic tetracycline (250 mg QID for 10 days) may be beneficial in postvenereal form.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On a chest radiograph, which of the following occupational diseases is most likely to be mistaken as a case of tuberculosis of lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

• Silicosis is the occupational lung disease most commonly mistaken for pulmonary tuberculosis on chest X-ray.
• Causative agent: Free crystalline silica dust.
• High-risk occupations: Mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting, foundry work, ceramics, and glass industries.
• Chest X-ray findings:

• Multiple small rounded upper lobe nodules
• Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)
• “Eggshell” calcification of hilar lymph nodes (classic finding).

• Major complication: Silicotuberculosis due to impaired macrophage function.
• Silicosis also increases the risk of lung cancer, COPD, and cor pulmonale.

Other Important Pneumoconioses

• Anthracosis (Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis): Coal dust exposure.
• Asbestosis: Lower lobe interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques; associated with bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma.
• Siderosis: Iron dust exposure; benign pneumoconiosis with little or no fibrosis.
• Byssinosis: Cotton dust exposure; presents with chest tightness and occupational asthma (“Monday chest tightness”).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Increased H+ ions in the intermembrane space of mitochondria are due to?
options: Water retention in inner mitochondrial space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased oxidative phosphorylation

Increased H+ ions in the intermembrane space of mitochondria are due to decreased oxidative phosphorylation.

ATP is synthesized in mitochondria by a process called oxidative phosphorylation. The oxidation of substrates like carbohydrates, amino acids, or fats produces reducing equivalents (NADH, FADH2). These equivalents enter the electron transport chain and transfer a proton (H+) to the inter-membrane space. The inner mitochondrial membrane is not permeable to protons leading to the accumulation of H+ in the intermembrane space. The flow of these protons through the Fo releases the energy that phosphorylates ADP to form ATP.

Drugs that inhibit oxidative phosphorylation like oligomycin inhibit the flow of protons through Fo causing an increase in H+ ions in the intermembrane space.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the Nalgonda technique of defluoridation of water, which of the following plays a major role in flocculation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alum

Nalgonda technique is a cost-effective community method for defluoridation of drinking water, in which alum (aluminium sulfate) is the principal coagulant/flocculating agent that removes fluoride by forming flocs. Lime aids coagulation by adjusting pH, while bleaching powder is added for disinfection.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bleaching powder: Used for disinfection, not flocculation.
• C. Lime: Helps optimize pH and coagulation, but is not the primary flocculating agent.
• D. Activated charcoal: Used for adsorption of organic impurities, taste, and odor, not fluoride removal in the Nalgonda technique.
questions.learning: Alum Nalgonda technique is a cost-effective community method for defluoridation of drinking water, in which alum (aluminium sulfate) is the principal coagulant/flocculating agent that removes fluoride by forming flocs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient with lymphatic filarisis is being managed as shown in the image below. What is the level of prevention done here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Disability limitation

The image shows an established case of chronic lymphatic filariasis, where hygiene is being maintained to prevent further disability by secondary bacterial infection. Disability limitation is a mode of intervention in tertiary prevention.

Other options:

Option A: Specific protection is a mode of intervention in primary prevention which aims at limiting the number of cases of a particular disease. This includes immunization, use of specific nutrients, chemoprophylaxis, accident protection, and avoidance of allergens.

Option C: Primary prevention is a level of prevention which is defined as action taken prior to the onset of a disease, which removes the possibility that a disease will ever occur. It is accomplished by measures designed to promote general health and well-being.

Option D: Health promotion is a mode of intervention in primary prevention, and is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and improve health. Health promotion may be achieved through health education, environmental modification, nutritional interventions or lifestyle changes.
questions.learning: Disability limitation — The image shows an established case of chronic lymphatic filariasis, where hygiene is being maintained to prevent further disability by secondary bacterial infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with persistent itching, redness, and scaling of the skin. Skin scraping is performed for microscopic examination, revealing a pathogen with a characteristic pencil-shaped morphology. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for the patient’s dermatological symptoms?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytosis, or fungal skin infection, is diagnosed by the microscopic appearance of macroconidia in skin scrapings. Trichophyton species are characterized by their "pencil-shaped" or cigar-shaped, thin-walled, multi-septate macroconidia. They are the most common genus of dermatophytes causing infections of the skin, hair, and nails (tinea). Microsporum (Option B) produces spindle-shaped macroconidia with thick, rough walls, which look very different from the smooth "pencil" shape of Trichophyton. Epidermophyton (Option C) produces club-shaped or "snowshoe-shaped" macroconidia, often occurring in clusters of two or three. The patient's symptoms of itching, redness, and scaling are the standard clinical manifestations of tinea. Since the microscopic evidence specifically identifies a pencil-shaped morphology, Trichophyton is the correct genus. Identifying these microscopic features is essential for differentiating between the three main genera of dermatophytes that cause clinically similar skin lesions
questions.learning: Dermatophytosis, or fungal skin infection, is diagnosed by the microscopic appearance of macroconidia in skin scrapings. Trichophyton species are characterized by their "pencil-shaped" or cigar-shaped, thin-walled, multi-septate macroconidia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with chronic pancreatitis undergoes a Puestow procedure. What is the preferred route for providing postoperative nutritional support in this patient?
questions.explanation: After a Puestow procedure (longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy) in chronic pancreatitis, the preferred postoperative nutritional support is TPN. This is because the primary goal is to provide adequate nutrition while ensuring complete pancreatic rest. Any enteral feeding (oral, gastric, or jejunal) can stimulate pancreatic exocrine secretion through hormonal and neural mechanisms, potentially stressing the anastomosis and worsening inflammation. TPN bypasses the gastrointestinal tract entirely, thereby minimizing pancreatic stimulation, reducing pain, and allowing optimal healing in the early postoperative period. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Oral feeding: Not advised early postoperatively, as it directly stimulates pancreatic secretion and may aggravate symptoms or disrupt healing. (C) Feeding gastrostomy: Feeding into the stomach triggers hormonal responses (like gastrin and CCK release), leading to pancreatic stimulation, which is undesirable. (D) Feeding jejunostomy: Although it reduces stimulation compared to gastric feeding, it still causes some pancreatic secretion. Hence, it is not preferred immediately after surgery when complete pancreatic rest is required
questions.learning: After a Puestow procedure (longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy) in chronic pancreatitis, the preferred postoperative nutritional support is TPN. This is because the primary goal is to provide adequate nutrition while ensuring complete pancreatic rest.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Radical neck dissection spares which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digastric muscle

Digastric muscle is spared in radical neck dissection (RND). RND is used in the treatment of malignant lesions of the neck with local spread or metastasis.

In 1905, Crile described RND where Level I-V LN, sternocleidomastoid (SCM), internal jugular vein (IJV), and XI cranial nerve (spinal accessory nerve) are removed.

In 1962, Suarez described modified RND (MRND) where Level I-V LNs are removed and the following are preserved:

1. MRND I - XI cranial nerve
2. MRND II -  XI cranial nerve and IJV
3. MRND III - XI cranial nerve, IJV, and SCM

Note: RND with an additional LN/muscle/nerve is called extended RND.
questions.learning: Digastric muscle Digastric muscle is spared in radical neck dissection (RND). RND is used in the treatment of malignant lesions of the neck with local spread or metastasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common primary source of brain metastases?
questions.explanation: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults, and the lung (Option B) is the primary site of origin in approximately 40% to 50% of all cases. Lung cancer cells frequently spread hematogenously to the brain due to the direct vascular pathway from the pulmonary circulation. Breast cancer (Option D) is the second most common source, particularly in women. Thyroid cancer (Option A) and liver cancer (Option C) can occasionally metastasize to the brain, but they are significantly less frequent primary sources compared to the lung and breast . Brain metastases often present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, such as headaches, or focal neurological deficits and seizures. Multiple lesions are more common than solitary ones in metastatic disease. Radiologically, these typically appear as ring-enhancing lesions with significant surrounding edema. Therefore, when an adult presents with new-onset neurological signs and multiple brain lesions, a primary lung malignancy is the first suspicion
questions.learning: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults, and the lung (Option B) is the primary site of origin in approximately 40% to 50% of all cases.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following tests cannot be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Electron microscopy

Among the given options, electron microscopy will be the least useful in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Other tests mentioned can be used in humans to detect mucociliary transit time and total nasal clearance in humans.

Electron microscopy can be used to best assess the normalcy of cilia structure and its function, but it might not be able to detect any other abnormality that might interfere with nasal mucociliary clearance like any obstruction in the nasal cavity.

Test for mucociliary clearance include:

• Saccharine with or without color test in vivo (Option A)
• Radioisotope transport testing in vivo
• Measuring ciliary activity in vitro
• Nasal nitric oxide
• Scintigraphy (Option D) is the nuclear medicine equivalent of the dye disappearance test to assess functional and anatomic obstruction

The charcoal method (Option C) is a less commonly used method to detect nasal mucociliary clearance. In this method, a very small amount of charcoal is placed behind the head of the inferior turbinate. The pharynx is then observed to detect the presence of charcoal.

Mucociliary clearance tests are used to diagnose inborn disorders of mucociliary transport such as primary ciliary dysfunction and cystic fibrosis.
questions.learning: Electron microscopy Among the given options, electron microscopy will be the least useful in assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Other tests mentioned can be used in humans to detect mucociliary transit time and total nasal clearance in humans.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification of bile duct injury considers bile duct and vascular injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hannover

Hannover classification  Includes:

• Bile duct injury (site)
• Type of damage (thermal/mechanical)
• Associated vascular injury

❌Bismuth

• Based on level of injury (relative to hepatic duct)
• No vascular component

❌ Strasberg

• Expanded version of Bismuth
• Includes minor leaks + major injuries
• Still no vascular injury

❌Stewart-Way

• Based on mechanism of injury (how injury occurred)
• Not vascular injury.

Strassberg bismuth classification:-

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| A | Leak from cystic duct stump or small ducts (e.g., duct of Luschka)

| B | Occlusion of part of biliary tree (usually aberrant duct)

| C | Transection of aberrant duct with bile leak

| D | Lateral injury to major bile duct

| E1 | Transection >2 cm below hepatic duct confluence

| E2 | Transection <2 cm from confluence

| E3 | Injury at confluence (right & left ducts intact)

| E4 | Destruction of confluence (separate ducts)

| E5 | Injury to aberrant right duct + main duct

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old mentally challenged pregnant female was brought to the hospital for MTP. Consent in this case will be given by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Legal guardian

A legal guardian provides consent in the case of a mentally ill patient.

Consent of parent/legal guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.

questions.text: 2-year-old was brought to the ED following choking on a peanut. The child was unresponsive. What is the next step for managing this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chest compressions

•

Unresponsive child with choking (foreign body airway obstruction)

•

Treat as cardiac arrest → start CPR immediately

•

Begin with 30 chest compressions

• Then open airway → look for visible foreign body
• Give 2 rescue breaths
• Repeat cycles

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the co-test in cervical cancer screening?
questions.explanation: Co-testing for cervical cancer screening involves the simultaneous performance of HPV DNA testing and a Pap smear (cytology). This dual approach is highly effective because HPV testing identifies the presence of the causative virus (high-risk strains 16 and 18), while the Pap smear detects pre-malignant cellular changes. VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) (Options B and C) is a low-cost screening method used primarily in resource-limited settings. Colposcopy (Option D) is a diagnostic follow-up tool used to investigate abnormal screening results rather than a primary screening "co-test". In standard guidelines, co-testing with HPV and Pap smear is the gold standard for women aged 30–65
questions.learning: Co-testing for cervical cancer screening involves the simultaneous performance of HPV DNA testing and a Pap smear (cytology). This dual approach is highly effective because HPV testing identifies the presence of the causative virus (high-risk strains 16…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus?
options: Sensory level is from T10 to L1
Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8
In the 1st stage of labor, pain is due to the fibres at level of T10 - L1
In early labor, pain is usually because of the uterine contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8

The incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus is statement B. Uterine contractility is mainly mediated by hormonal mechanisms. Estrogen, prostaglandin, and oxytocin produce contraction, while progesterone causes relaxation.

Uterine sensory supply is by ascending afferent fibers which pass through the inferior hypogastric plexus and enter the spinal cord through T10-T12 and L1 roots.

Labor pain is due to stimulation of nociceptors in the genital tract caused by ischemia.

• First stage labor: Pain is mediated by T10 to L1 spinal segments. It is caused by distension of the cervix and low uterine segments along with isometric uterine contraction.
• Second stage labor: Pain is carried by T12 to L1 and S2 to S4 spinal segments. It is caused by tissue damage in the pelvis and perineum

Analgesia in labor is achieved by intramuscular injection of pethidine 50 mg. Metoclopramide is added to prevent vomiting. Pethidine is avoided within 2 hours of delivery as it is a known respiratory depressant to the fetus. When relief of pain is required throughout labor, regional analgesia is preferred through pudendal nerve block, epidural analgesia, spinal anesthesia or combined epidural-spinal anesthesia.
questions.learning: Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8 The incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus is statement B. Uterine contractility is mainly mediated by hormonal mechanisms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with pain abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was done. What is the likely source of pain in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kidney

The history of an elderly male presenting with pain abdomen and an axial CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal origin of pain likely renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

It is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50–70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It usually presents with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, or painless flank mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for RCC. On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis. The clear cell subtype may show much stronger enhancement is a differential for angiomyolipoma. Still, it is essential to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Surgeries done for RCC:

Partial nephrectomy, the goal is the complete removal of the primary tumor while preserving healthy renal parenchyma. It is used for renal tumors <7cm in size.
Classic radical nephrectomy involves the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes.
Targeted therapies for RCC include tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sorafenib, sunitinib), anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) monoclonal antibodies (bevacizumab), and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (everolimus and temsirolimus).

Given below is the image showing the anatomy in the axial section of the CT scan

1- Liver, 2-Spleen, 3-Pancreas, 4-Gallbladder, 5-Right Adrenal Gland, 6-Left Adrenal Gland, 7-Inferior Vena Cava, 8-Aorta, 9-Portal Vein, 11- Ascending Colon, 12-Descending Colon, 14- Stomach.
questions.learning: Kidney — The history of an elderly male presenting with pain abdomen and an axial CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal origin of pain likely renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding mechanisms of depolarisation, repolarisation, and hyperpolarisation in a skeletal muscle action potential?

1. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through voltage-gated channels
2. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through ligand-gated channels
3. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a voltage-gated channel
4. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a ligand-gated channel
5. Hyperpolarisation due to efflux of K+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, and 5 are correct

Statements 1, 3, and 5 are correct.

Action potential in skeletal muscle:

• Motor-neuron discharge causes end-plate potential, which when reaches to a threshold value, causes action potential in the muscle fibre.
• The depolarization of the muscle fibre is caused by the activation of the voltage-gated sodium channels, which causes the influx of sodium.
• During repolarization, the sodium channels are closed, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, which causes efflux of potassium.
• The voltage-gated potassium channels close slowly. As a result, the potassium efflux continues, leading to hyperpolarization of the membrane.

The steps in an action potential in muscle fibre and the neuron, are similar except for the quantitative differences, such as:

• RMP is -80 to -90 mV in skeletal muscle fibres, while it is about -70mV in neurons.
• The duration of the action potential in skeletal muscle is 1 to 5 msec, which is about 5 times longer than in the largest myelinated nerve fibre.
• The velocity of conduction is about 3-5m/s, which is about 1/13th of the velocity of the nerve fibre.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The Gold Standard for diagnosis of Celiac disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic small bowel biopsy

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). While serologic tests are useful for screening, the gold standard for diagnosis is an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple duodenal (small bowel) biopsies, which confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating characteristic mucosal changes.

Characteristic histopathological findings:

• Villous atrophy
• Crypt hyperplasia
• Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification)

Key points:

• Best initial screening test: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) antibody (along with total serum IgA).
• Gold standard: Endoscopic duodenal biopsy.
• Treatment: Lifelong gluten-free diet.
questions.learning: Endoscopic small bowel biopsy Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: At physiological pH, the buffering action in blood is caused by which amino acid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histidine

At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine.

The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

Histidine is a positively charged amino acid which can exist in both its protonated (positively charged) and deprotonated (neutral) forms.

It acts as a buffer by accepting or donating protons (H+ ions) in response to changes in pH, helping to maintain the blood's pH within a narrow physiological range.

Hence, histidine has the maximum buffering capacity at physiological pH.
questions.learning: Histidine At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine. The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the evaluation of a female patient with unexplained urinary leakage, a diagnostic test using methylene blue along with a three-swab technique is performed to determine the source of the leak. During the procedure, the middle swab becomes stained with the dye. What is the most likely diagnosis based on this finding?
questions.explanation: The 3-swab test (Moir's test) is used to differentiate between various types of urinary fistulae. Methylene blue dye is instilled into the bladder, and three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina at different levels. If the middle swab (or upper swab) turns blue, it indicates that the dye has leaked from the bladder into the vagina, confirming a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF). In a Uretero-vaginal fistula (Option C), the swabs would remain white but become wet with urine, because the dye in the bladder never reaches the ureters. In a Urethrovaginal fistula (Option B), the lowest (most distal) swab would turn blue. VVF is a common complication of prolonged obstructed labor or gynecological surgery. The test effectively localizes the site of communication, which is essential for planning surgical repair. Therefore, the "positive dye" result on the middle swab specifically identifies the bladder as the source of the leakage
questions.learning: The 3-swab test (Moir's test) is used to differentiate between various types of urinary fistulae. Methylene blue dye is instilled into the bladder, and three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina at different levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of the primary survey?
options: Removing clothes to inspect for wounds
Taking CT scan of the patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Taking CT scan of the patient

Taking a CT scan of the patient is a part of secondary survey.

Primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

The secondary survey includes investigations that help identify all other injuries, excluding the apparent ones. This includes X-rays of the spine and extremities and a CT of the abdomen, head, chest, and spine.
questions.learning: Taking CT scan of the patient Taking a CT scan of the patient is a part of secondary survey. Primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden-onset right leg pain. An investigation was done, and the obtained image is shown below. What is the investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ultrasound Doppler

The image shows a triphasic pattern of the arterial waveform, which is seen in the ultrasound doppler.

Doppler ultrasound is used in diagnosing peripheral arterial disease. It uses a handheld doppler ultrasound probe placed at an arterial site. This transmits a continuous wave. A receiver inside the probe picks up the reflected beam. The change in frequency between the reflected beam and the transmitted beam gets converted to a pulsatile audio signal.

A normal arterial wave has a triphasic signal. A triphasic wave has three waveforms consisting of a sharp systolic wave with a forward uprise and fall, a second wave with reverse flow occurring in diastole, and the last wave with a forward flow taking place during diastole.

Doppler ultrasound can detect moving blood. However, it does not provide information on whether the blood flow is sufficient for the maintenance of limb viability.

Other options:

Option A: Digital subtraction percutaneous angiography (DSA) is a procedure wherein a radiopaque dye is usually injected percutaneously into the femoral artery. Images obtained are digitalized and the background may be removed for a clear image. It provides information on dynamic arterial flow and can be combined with endovascular intervention if needed.

Option C: Plethysmography is a semi-quantitative method to measure segmental blood flow and velocity in the carotid and peripheral vascular systems.

Option D: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or MR angiography, is an imaging modality that can be used when duplex ultrasonography cannot be done or if it cannot produce a clear image. MRA avoids ionizing radiation.
questions.learning: Ultrasound Doppler — The image shows a triphasic pattern of the arterial waveform, which is seen in the ultrasound doppler. Doppler ultrasound is used in diagnosing peripheral arterial disease.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An Autopsy was conducted on a male with history of drowning. However, no water was found in his lungs, and he was determined to have experienced ‘dry drowning’. What is the cause of death:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laryngospasm

Dry drowning occurs due to reflex laryngospasm, which prevents water from entering the lungs and leads to asphyxia without fluid in the airways.

• Water entering upper airway → reflex closure of vocal cords (laryngospasm)
• Results in airway obstruction → hypoxia → death
• Hence, lungs may appear dry on autopsy

Types of drowning:

• Wet drowning: Water present in lungs (common)
• Dry drowning: Due to laryngospasm, no water in lungs
• Immersion syndrome: Sudden death due to vagal inhibition

Why not other options:

• Asphyxia: Final mechanism, but laryngospasm is the cause
• Vagal inhibition: Seen in sudden immersion (cold water), not typical drowning
• Ventricular fibrillation: Not primary mechanism here

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are noted. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with shortness of breath, fatigue, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds, which strongly suggest chronic cardiac compression. These findings are classical for constrictive pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrotic, and sometimes calcified, restricting normal cardiac filling. The chest X-ray in such cases often shows pericardial calcification, which appears as curvilinear radio-opaque shadows around the cardiac silhouette. This radiological feature is highly suggestive of constrictive pericarditis and helps differentiate it from other causes of heart failure. Why other options are wrong: (B) Bronchial asthma : Presents with wheezing and hyperinflated lungs, not JVD or muffled heart sounds (C) Acute pericarditis : Causes chest pain and pericardial effusion but not calcification (D) Atrial myxoma : May cause obstruction but does not show pericardial calcification on X-ray
questions.learning: The patient presents with shortness of breath, fatigue, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds, which strongly suggest chronic cardiac compression.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the adjuvant therapy in fungal corneal ulcer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atropine Sulfate eye ointment

Atropine sulfate (1%) eye ointment or eye drops is used as the nonspecific supportive treatment in both bacterial as well as a fungal corneal ulcer.

Atropine sulphate (1%) is a cycloplegic drug that is used as an adjunct in the treatment of corneal ulcers to

• reduce pain from ciliary spasm
• Prevent posterior synechiae formation that can develop from secondary iridocyclitis
• Increase blood supply to the anterior chamber that gets more antibodies into aqueous humor
• Reduce exudation by decreasing hyperpermeability of the vessels

Another cycloplegic that can be used as an adjunct is homatropine 2%.

Topical steroids such as Dexamethasone(option C) will increase fungal replication and corneal invasion and hence are contraindicated in the treatment of fungal corneal ulcers.

Management of fungal corneal ulcer includes

Definitive treatment:

• Topical antifungal eye drops: used for 6-8 weeks

• Filamentous fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium- Drug of choice (DOC) is natamycin (5%). Others include amphotericin B (0.1-0.3%), fluconazole (0.2%) or voriconazole 10%.
• Yeast such as Candida- Drug of choice (DOC) is Amphotericin B. Others include Nystatin 3.5%.

• Intracameral or intracorneal administration of Voriconazole in cases with intraocular extension or anterior chamber involvement.
• Systemic antifungals such as tablet fluconazole are given in severe cases of deeper fungal keratitis.
• Therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty for unresponsive cases.

Adjunct therapy:

1. Cycloplegics : Atropine sulphate 1% or homatropine 2%
2. Systemic analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs such as paracetamol, ibuprofen to decrease pain and edema.
3. Vitamins A,B-complex,C- to aid healing of the ulcer.
4. Hot fomentation, dark goggles, rest, good diet.
questions.learning: Atropine Sulfate eye ointment Atropine sulfate (1%) eye ointment or eye drops is used as the nonspecific supportive treatment in both bacterial as well as a fungal corneal ulcer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the term used to describe the demise of a twin in the second trimester, accompanied by maceration? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fetus Papyraceus

Fetus papyraceus refers to the compressed, mummified remains of a dead fetus retained in a multiple pregnancy after demise in the second trimester.

Pathogenesis:

• One twin dies in utero
• Dead fetus undergoes dehydration and compression between the uterine wall and surviving twin
• Produces a flattened, parchment-like fetus

Important distinction:

• Vanishing twin → early first-trimester fetal loss with resorption
• Fetus papyraceus → later fetal demise with retained macerated fetus

Complications:

• Preterm labor
• Coagulopathy (rare)
• Neurologic injury in surviving monochorionic twin due to shared circulation
questions.learning: Fetus Papyraceus Fetus papyraceus refers to the compressed, mummified remains of a dead fetus retained in a multiple pregnancy after demise in the second trimester.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following criteria: 1. Pleural fluid protein:Serum protein ratio > 0.5 2. Pleural fluid LDH:Serum LDH ratio > 0.6 3. Pleural fluid LDH > Two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH Which of the above criteria, if present in pleural fluid, will indicate an exudate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

The Light’s criteria are the most widely used criteria to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusions. A pleural effusion is classified as an exudate if any one of the following criteria is present:

1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5
2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6
3. Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

Common causes:

• Exudative effusions: Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, connective tissue diseases.
• Transudative effusions: Congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.

Limitations:

• Light’s criteria are highly sensitive for detecting exudates but may misclassify some transudates (especially in patients with heart failure receiving diuretics) as exudates. In such cases, the serum–pleural fluid albumin gradient (>1.2 g/dL) or protein gradient (>3.1 g/dL) can help identify a true transudate.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The Light’s criteria are the most widely used criteria to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusions. A pleural effusion is classified as an exudate if any one of the following criteria is present: 1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Following a punch injury to the face during a fight, which anatomical site around the eye is most commonly fractured?
questions.explanation: A direct blow to the orbit by an object larger than the orbital rim (like a fist or a ball) can cause a "blowout fracture". The orbital "floor" is the most frequently fractured area because it is thin and composed of the maxillary bone, which lacks robust structural support. A sudden increase in intraorbital pressure causes the floor to buckle or break, potentially entrapping the inferior rectus muscle. The medial wall (Option A), specifically the lamina papyracea, is the second most common site. The lateral wall (Option B) and roof (Option C) are composed of thicker bone and are much less frequently involved in isolated orbital trauma. Clinical signs of a floor fracture include periorbital ecchymosis, diplopia on up-gaze (due to muscle entrapment), and infraorbital nerve paresthesia. Diagnosis is confirmed via thin-cut CT scan. Surgical repair is indicated if there is persistent diplopia or significant enophthalmos

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Most common heart defect in congenital rubella syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PDA

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common congenital heart disease associated with rubella, followed by pulmonary artery stenosis (PS).

Cardiac anomalies have been observed in 50% of children infected during the first 8 weeks of gestation. The incidence of heart disease in congenital rubella syndrome is: PDA > PS (right >left) > ventricular septal defect > atrial septal defect.
